items.excerpt: After several records examining language (Pause/Stutter/Uh/Repeat), mutation (Mutate), liturgical memory (Ison), and the algorithmic logic of social media (Kitbashing), Abadir arrives at what feels like the conceptual centre of his work. items.body: After several records examining language (Pause/Stutter/Uh/Repeat), mutation (Mutate), liturgical memory (Ison), and the algorithmic logic of social media (Kitbashing), Abadir arrives at what feels like the conceptual centre of his work. The Primitivist is not simply a new collection of club tracks but a declaration of intent, rejecting electronic music’s enduring fixation with futurism in favour of a deeper engagement with the present and with the musical traditions that continue to shape it. The title is deliberately provocative. As Abadir has argued in an article for Cartography of Darkness, electronic music has spent decades equating novelty with the future, often reproducing the same cyberpunk imagery, dystopian fantasies and technological narratives inherited from the 1980s and 1990s. For him, that obsession has become a form of nostalgia masquerading as progress, one increasingly detached from the realities of communities living through war, authoritarianism and displacement. The Primitivist proposes another direction altogether: creativity rooted not in speculative futures but in sustained engagement with living musical heritage and the political urgency of the present. That shift is immediately audible. If Mutate revolved around the Egyptian maqsoum rhythm, this EP opens its vocabulary to rhythmic traditions and performance practices from across the Arab world. The opening “Habban” takes its name from the Gulf bagpipe, a celebratory folk instrument associated with communal dancing and percussion ensembles. Rather than sampling tradition as an exotic signifier, Abadir absorbs its rhythmic logic into a contemporary club framework where darbuka, khishba, mijwiz and intricate hand-clapping patterns become structural rather than decorative elements. The ecstatic propulsion of “The Primitivist” and the playful destabilisation of “Pass & Go” continue that trajectory, while the closing “This Is Not Another Maqsoum” knowingly acknowledges — and moves beyond — the rhythmic strategy that defined his previous album. What remains constant throughout Abadir’s catalogue is his concern with transformation. Each record asks a different question, yet all are linked by the same compositional impulse: taking existing sonic materials — speech, liturgy, social media, club music or regional traditions — and discovering how they can be reimagined without losing their historical or cultural specificity. The result is music that consistently resists easy categorisation. It is uncompromisingly contemporary, yet never relies on futurist rhetoric to justify its newness. In an electronic music landscape still eager to describe unfamiliar sounds as “futuristic,” The Primitivist offers a persuasive alternative. It suggests that innovation need not emerge from imagined worlds or technological fantasies. Sometimes it begins by listening more closely to the present and to histories that have always been there, waiting to be heard. photo by Omar Elkafrawy To helps us see beyond the future, we reached out directly to Abadir. The Primitivist presents itself as a rejection of electronic music’s long-standing fascination with futurism. You’ve argued that futurist narratives often reflect Eurocentric ideas of progress while overlooking the lived realities of communities experiencing war or authoritarianism. Once you reject futurism as the dominant framework, what new possibilities does “primitivism” open up for composition? Does it change the way you think about rhythm, sound design or even the social function of club music? My rejection of anything related to futurism has been going for five years, and each year it becomes more radical. I think this makes sense to me at the moment, since the future, futurism and the futuristic have been the main focus in electronic music since the 80’s (if not even before that) to identify what’s new, what’s next and the unheard for the western ears. This narrative of futurism has been already ruling for 40 years, which makes it outdated for me and repetitive to the maximum, to the point where it’s now reduced to a marketing label. It became a habit to link newness to the future, and unfortunately there has been a lack of critique to this idea, or attempts to link creativity and newness to something else other than futurism. It’s even nostalgic that futurism in electronic music is still somehow based on the same concepts, sounds and perspectives that once existed in the 80’s or the 90’s. There have been cycles of criticizing Mark Fisher’s theories, with a general claim that the future didn’t stop and “gotcha Fisher you are wrong”, because X or Y (from the global north) made “futuristic” music. Honestly, this argument is haunted by an outdated vision of what futuristic music means, it’s also haunted by the urge of futurism. That’s nostalgia for futurism (which is different from Fisher’s concept of lost futures) that used to exist decades ago. It’s paradoxical, and in that sense futurism is eating itself. But I think this sort of discussion doesn’t fit the Arabic context because we have different realities and priorities. With the exception of Afrofuturism, the futuristic narrative is escapist and out of touch with the present. It chooses progress and speed rather than understanding and facing the present. The narrative for years has been about fetishising dystopia or the other opposite, techno-optimism led by the “punchline” of “Let’s imagine a future where…” I see both narratives out of touch with reality, especially now. Being able to think like that is a kind of luxury, rather than living the hard present reality which is unfolding in front of our eyes on a daily basis. So at least, an action must be taken to change that, and actions happen in the present. Once we reach a point where present issues are kind of fixed, then we can have the time and luxury to speculate, think about the future and imagine it. More thoughts about this topic can be found in this essay I wrote last year. I chose the term Primitivism as a provocation, a way to say I’m happy I’m not futuristic, I’m busy with the present and I’m inspired by a deeply rooted music heritage. This way of thinking is definitely inspiring because making this claim means that I need to listen, revisit, read and learn a lot about music from the Arab region on the technical, cultural and historical level. During the last few years I learned a lot about Maqamat, rhythms from different parts of the Arab region. As you said, this also had an impact on sound design, because you can easily tell that the sound design in The Primitivist and my coming project is different from what’s in Kitbashing and Ison. On Mutate, the maqsoum rhythm acted almost as the album’s organising principle, whereas The Primitivist draws from a much broader range of rhythmic traditions and instrumental references from Iraq, Kuwait, Syria and Palestine. Tracks such as “Habban”, “The Primitivist” and “This Is Not Another Maqsoum” feel less concerned with hybridising genres than with rethinking the vocabulary of club music itself. How did your compositional approach change between these two records, and did moving beyond maqsoum also change the way you thought about rhythm? Usually I tend to link my projects together, as well as old and fresh ideas. What starts as a sound or an idea in one project will be revisited and developed more a few years later. You can trace that between Pause/Stutter/Uh/Repeat and Kitbashing or Ison, and between Mutate and The Primitivist. This marks the continuity of my work. Maqsoum was the center of Mutate, next to the influence of other club genres that I listen to and DJ. I wasn’t making club music before Mutate, so it made sense to me to start with a sound I’m familiar with and stuck in my memory, which is Maqsoum. It was fun mixing Jungle and Footwork or Jersey with sped up and cut up Maqsoum samples, to come up with a mutated club sound. In The Primitivist I decided to focus more on Arabic rhythms and dropping the influences of other club genres. During a 3 year period I got attracted to sounds from the countries you mentioned and I extended my knowledge to further other rhythmic patterns. The result was working with rhythmic sounds related to Dahhiya, Dabke, simulating a real drummer playing the Khishba or using the Sharbaka, which is a hand clapping technique rooted in the Arabian Gulf, especially in Kuwait. In my coming project, I’m going deeper in sound design, and more complex patterns with a focus on variations in time signatures. There is a striking tension throughout the EP between recognisable Arab instruments—mijwiz pipes, darbuka, khishba, brass timbres—and an approach to rhythm and sound design that remains uncompromisingly contemporary. As someone who has also been exploring Arabic maqamat and instrumental playing techniques in your more recent work, how do you avoid turning these traditions into cultural signifiers or markers of authenticity, allowing them instead to remain living musical materials? I think the idea is about avoiding orientalist and self-orientalist cliches, or lazy fusion, in addition to finding this common ground between the familiar and the unfamiliar, with surprise elements. Once you hear a Mijwiz or a brass synth for instance, you will get that sense of “yes I know that”, then twisting the expectations is the next crucial step. If I hear a Rast or Huzam or Bayati maqam used by an Arabic producer, I will see it as normal. But creativity appears depending on some other factors such as: the articulation and ornamentation in maqamat, the modulation between maqamat, how the producer is implementing these maqamat with drum patterns, how the sound design is made, how the arrangement is done and the structure is built. Here you have a lot of options to twist the expectations. Yet, I still admire the musicians who are maintaining old traditions as they are, because we need that now in our region more than any time before, given the external threat by the infamous pariah state, liberal capitalist “values”, A.I, the Dubaification of our region. This is the very material reality we face and we have to deal with in the present, so again, what future exactly are we talking about? Koleyet El Banat – photo by Omar Elkafrawy Your work sits at an unusual intersection of artistic practice and critical writing. As the editor of the electronic music section at Ma3azef, you’re constantly analysing how electronic music is written about, categorised and historicised. Has writing criticism changed the way you make music? Conversely, has producing records like The Primitivist made you more critical of the vocabulary and frameworks through which electronic music — particularly music from the Arab world — is discussed in western publications? My criticism towards the vocabulary and frameworks used in western publications as well as the westernised Arabic ones has always been there. I also believe that the music journalist or the critic has to read, follow and listen a lot, a good level of curiosity is required. I’m trying to do my best with that, so my critique can have some basis. Maybe The Primitivist is a result of that. It’s about how to express critique through a medium other than writing; proposing that we don’t need to be obsessed with the future or futurism to be creative, alternatively, we can be focused in the present or we can draw inspiration from our cultural roots. The present is here already. The same applies on Kitbashing by the way, one can theorise about its concept in an essay or a book, but I wanted to represent the concept sonically. Definitely, working in criticism has made me think differently about my own music, because it has made me much more self-critical. My music projects are slow cooked, and each one starts with a simple question: why am I doing this or what am I trying to say? This question can be frustrating or provocative to some artists, but for me it makes total sense and it’s the main critical question behind every project.ِ During the process, I can be very critical and harsh towards myself, but it helps me a lot. With Kitbashing, you proposed feeding on the algorithm rather than feeding it, transforming the sounds of social media into compositional material. In retrospect, do you think the algorithm can ever truly be subverted, or does every attempt at resisting it inevitably become another form of participation? On an individual level, we can benefit from the algorithm, whether by using it for learning purposes, an introduction to something, being informed about cultural or political topics, or simply watching something fun, because we need a break. Apart from that, ِI wish in general that the algorithm is subverted for something good and I think this has to be collectively done. Take for instance the non-commercial electronic music scene which is now driven by the algorithmic scrolling mentality, everyone from the curators, to the spaces, to the artists, to the press, to the crowd, is so invested in an app. Everything has been highly dependent on Instagram. It has become the main way to be heard and seen and that’s exhausting and frustrating. A couple of slides or a polished one minute video from the peak of a live or DJ set defines an artist. But imagine that the press and curators are relatively withdrawing from Instagram, this can have a good impact on producers and DJs, they will spend less time on the app, and post less, only when it’s necessary. This will make the crowd spend more time listening and reading, and artists will only focus on their music and their work. That would be ideal, isn’t it? (Gianmarco Del Re)

items.body: Review by Grumpyprogfan — Quivira is the name of a road close to where I live. And with three reviewers hailing this a "masterpiece" and referencing the band Kansas - well, I had to check this out. The musicans are: Lisa LaRue, composer, keys, drum programming; John Baker, guitar, bass, vocals; Jake Livgreen, vocals; With... Joe Deninzon, violin, and Evan Stanley plays guitar on one song. The musicians are quite good and Lisa's compositions are good, but it has a Neal Morse / Flying Colors vibe more than a Kansas vibe, for me. I like that Quivira has lots of instrumental sections - where the musicians can jam - because the vocals are far from the majestic duo that was Steinhardt and Walsh. In fact, there aren't many vocals on this album at all. Overall, this is a good debut album, and if you enjoy a mostly instrumental retro 70's style of music, Quivira could be worth a listen. I'm curious is this a one-off, or is a second album with a human drummer a possibility? Solid 3.5 stars.

It is also a collaboration with the American group Mild High Club.It can also feel like a sequel to Paper M�ch� Dream Balloon, featuring bossa nova and an acoustic feel, yet it sets itself apart by seeming drenched in LSD, with a soft layer of psychedelia; the electric piano, drum grooves, and wah-wah guitar create a postmodern jazz-rock effect where the 60s meet the 90s and 2000s, and yet, in songs like "D-Day," it is microtonal.This album features some very interesting variations; the band experiments with pop, ranging from the array of percussion instruments to the use of vocals, backing harmonies, and the melodies themselves, sometimes with instruments following the vocals, and at other times doing the exact opposite, as seen in "Tezeta." The flute and Mellotrons create a distinctive atmosphere; combined with the 60s-style jazz they execute so well and those catchy choruses, they help shape the bohemian vibe sought in "The Spider and Me.""Sketches of Brunswick East II" introduces a recurring motif, tinged with the flamenco-esque flair that inspired it, that weaves through the entire album in various forms. When King Gizzard proposes a journey into the future, you have to buckle up; this time, however, they head into the past, embodying the roles like true method actors and channeling the musical sensibilities of that era. There is a space-age atmosphere, combined with a certain sophistication, that they capture brilliantly on "Dusk to Dawn on Lygon St." Meanwhile, "The Book" stands as another microtonal experiment; given that it was 2017, such a track was bound to make an appearance, yet it fits seamlessly with the album's playful psychedelia."A Journey to (S)Hell" offers a dose of urban chaos; just as Paper M�ch� Dream Balloon was the countryside, Sketches of Brunswick East is the city. A nocturnal journey awash in psychedelic lights unfolds suddenly, reconnecting with 70s-style synthesizers on "Rolling Stoned" before shifting to bossa nova on "You Can Be Your Silhouette." It is nearly impossible not to dance to this endless string of short songs, a fitting format, like small slides or snapshots of the city and open windows, each distinct in its own specific character."Sketches of Brunswick East III" brings the album to a close, and this peaceful interlude paves the way for the next chapter of 2017, Polygondwanaland, though that belongs to another dimension, one of the many inhabited by this Australian band.

items.body: Review by BrufordFreak — Recorded in London at Orange Recording Studios LTD. December 9-12, 1970 and then released early in 1971 by Global Records.A1. "Thursday Morning Sunrise" (11:38) not the opening I was expecting--ever--from a 1971 prog album much less a Jazz-Rock Fusion one. The deep, low, heavily distorted organ play sounds like Markus Pajakkala's baritone saxes and bass clarinet on his (memorable) 2017 Brutopianisti album! When other instruments finally join in they're all grotesquely distorted: Eberhard's wild (and virtuosic) electric bass, Siggi Schwab's Sonny-Sharrock/Arto Lindsay-like electric guitar, even the drumming/percussion work of Fred Braceful and Roland Wittich is wild. I wouldn't call this "Free Jazz" like something from Ornette Coleman, John Coltrane's post-A Love Supreme period, or Sun Ra's Arkestra, but a fusion of these with experimental sound explorations and, in the second half, the incorporation of sophisticated African rhythms with even some from the more avant-garde realms of Classical Music. I am blown away, incredibly impressed, and find myself incredibly entertained as well as fully enjoying this trail-blazing exercise in boundary-obliteration. Could this album have been a key food source for the inspiration of soon-to-appear bands like UNIVERS ZERO or AREA?--certainly this type of music (19.25/20)A2. "Lady Blue" (3:03) now, hearing this amazing song that combines Beatnik poetry-delivery musical formats with Classical Music choral traditions, I find myself asking whether or not Wolfgang, Eberhard, Siggi, and/or Fred were fans or progeny of George Russell's School of Esoteric Musics while George was a professor in residence at Sweden's Lund University. I absolutely love this! Another totally unexpected song that I find myself returning to over and over to try to fathom its creative scope. (9.75/10)A3. "Mellodroma 2a" (5:10) more choir appearances open this--from a distance--before Siggi's acoustic guitar enters playing with congas and double bass in what can only be descrived as a Folk Rock tune akin to something by Bert and John, The Pentangle, or The Incredible String Band. And the choir continues to make small appearances! These guys are amazing! The diverse interests and forms for their musical expression seems to have no bounds! Lite drums join in but it's the hand percussion that dominates with Eberhard's double bass Wonderful! Another song that totally took me by surprise and which lures me back again and again for repeated listens as I try desperately to fathom their thinking and desires. In the fourth minute there is a lull in which Siggi gets to show off a little more of his acoustic guitar skills, but then the rest of the band re-joins for a rousing finish with percussion and organ really bringing it (though no return of the choir). Wonderful! (9.333/10)B1. "Raga" (16:17) apparently Siggi Schwab had really gotten into a huge variety of World Music stringed instruments--and especially stringed instruments prevalent in India--like the but also zithers, psaltries, This track was actually written by Siggi, who is credited with a vast array of traditional, ethnic, and Indian stringed instruments on the record. Among the highly zither-like instruments he plays on the album and track are the swarmandal (credited as "surmandel") and the bulbul tarang. Siggi also contributed sitar, veena, tambura, and sarangi to the album's rich, psychedelic raga-rock sound. Eberhard, Fred, Roland, and Wolfgang do their best to provide inputs that they think will enhance, embellish, and not detract from Siggi's reverence for his Indian studies. I find the use of the full drum kit in the seventh through ninth minute to be a bit overwhelming and domineering to the Indian spirit being expressed but, it's a good awareness experiment and, fortunately, it ends so that the song can move into a new, more-percussion-centric passage--one that contains Eberhard's talking drum like bass play as well as a lot of intertwined and improvisationally-reactive percussion threads, gradually embellished by trumpet and, later, cymbal-crashing drum kit and distorted synth string sounds. Things quite down again in the sixteenth minute, leaving Siggi and his mates to finish the song with a thin palette of almost-incidental noises and percussives to usher Siggi's surmandel out. (By the way, Fred's drum play over this last sections is much more tasteful and respectful--much less invasive and brutal.) Another surreally-unexpected and eminently-enjoyable song that makes me wish I had been there--wish I could have been present for these practice and recording sessions as well as known these remarkably intrepid musicians! (28.25/30) B2. "Milkstreets" (4:15) a relatively unstructured melange of natural and unnatural (treated and electonic) sounds, many coming from African and Indian traditions. Interesting and historically significant (like the work of John Cage, Terry Riley, Herbie Hancock, Area and so many other adventurists). (8.875/10) Total time: 40:23YouTube provided me with three extra/bonus songs that apparently came from the same December 1970 London recording sessions but only saw the light of day (and a public awareness) on a 2008 CD release from the Long Hair label. They are also quite interesting and experimental, allowing for even more display of all the weird instruments that Siggi and Wolfgang had been playing around with. A/five stars; an absolute masterpiece of experimental and leading-edge Jazz-Rock Fusion. HIGHLY recommended and ESSENTIAL for any J-R Fusion and Progressive Rock fan.

items.body: Review by Sean Trane — Rounded up to the third star.Difficult to give it more, as Strange Terrain, because it is out of topic for this site, though you will find a bit of the madness that made Mice & Rats In The Loft so excellent, but musically this is nothing alike the first two albums. Here we're dealing with some New Wave - the 80's type - but way avant-la-lettre. So much so, that one can wonder whether these two unreleased sessions (not until 2010) were indeed recorded in 77. If that had been the case, it would be considered as groundbreaking had they been released back them. I some ways, some of the early tracks on this album are fun and can even qualify as Zolo-type of rock, and 80's Sparks aren't that far either. One can think of also later (as in recent) Aksak albums with Veronique Vincent. In the meantime, one can wonder why this was released under the JDDG moniker, since the second salvo (bonus tracks) were labeled as Noy's Band. But in either case, if you're looking for JDDG soundscapes, you're not going to find much similar, though as I said the looniness is worth a listen.

items.body: Review by ZowieZiggy — Yet another review for a Purple live album.But I still enjoy to listen and review such sort of record.My first live encounter dated from March, 1973 in Brussels. (Belgium). I was 14 years old...And the ladst one will be on October 20. 2026, in Madrid (Spain). Quite a long ride isn't it?This double CD starts with 2 killers: "Highway Star" & "Black Night".Difficult to imagine a better start! And the so afraid "karaokee" style is even forgotten during the latter. So far, so great!Two very good renditions of � tracks from "The Battle Rages On" (logical since it was released in 1993 (date of recording of this live set).then come a superb "Bethoven's Ninth"...the magic of Jon to combine classic with rock; A somptuous 10 minutes (or almost) track which brings me close to ectasy (at times!). To confirm the great shape, the great "Knocking on your Back Door" from "Perfect Strangers" adds to the general feeling. SUPERB!!!But, what to say write about the two pieces of resistance of this double CD set???"Child in Time" (from "In Rock") and the fabulous, and the best from all their live sets for "Anya".This closes CD1 that be rated as a 5* one.CD2 though will sound a little weaker.Not with "The Battle" nor "lazy" which are outstanding as well. But thereafter, the next 3 titels are shortered versions of known numbers just as on their "NEC" live. Press next. three tiems;Then, we are going to face an EXTRAordinary cover version of a mythical Stones song. My favorite of tyhis great rock band. "Paint it, Blcack". from hard rocking to spacey: it is soooo great. One of the too few highlights of disc 2.We're back on great track with "Speed King" (we can even hear some notes from "Burn" before minute 6 (only instrumental, 'cause Ian will NEVER sing sing it; nor any song from Mark 3.The last but one song is an OK version of "Hush" from Mark I...But the worse is goi,ng to happen to the overlooooong karaoke version of "Smoke on the Water".I really couldn't stand this while attending their concerts. What I did at the time, was going up to the floors and attend the bar to drink one (or two - remember, I'm Belgian) with one of my mates (hi, Jean-Pierre). It was in the Arena in Antwerp (just next door to the Sport Palace).The intro is fine (almost 3 minutes) is fine with me; As well as the core track...which leads us to minute 7.And then ...5 minutes of Smoooooooke on the Water...for about another 3 minutes.The audience might have loved this, but I didn't...Sorry guys...All in all, this is an excellent hard-rocking live album. Another one from Purple; THE MASTER, THE INVENTER of the genre.**** solid stars. .

Not Only Surfin‘ U.S.A Die versammelten Interpret:innen kommen nicht nur aus den USA, sondern auch aus Australien, Japan, Kanada, Frankreich, von den Bahamas oder von Hawaii. Die Compilation zeigt Yacht Rock nicht als eine auf Kalifornien begrenzte, sondern als globale Ästhetik. Der Japaner Twin Cosmos legt auf »Coconuts Wind« eine Lennon erinnernde Melodie in eine lauwarme Meeresbrise. items.body: What happens if the sun disappears? The question lingered over the stage at Viljandi Folk Festival on the morning its closing day. Tell Your Birds brought it there, playing songs from a still unreleased record in front of a crowd for the first time. Kristīne Tukre‘s concert kokle carried the melodies, Vija Moore‘s balafon sat under them, Kärt Tambet‘s bowed hiiu kannel cut across both, and everything the three of them played ran through Simone Spampinato‘s processing. They sang in Estonian and Latvian at once, each keeping the language they grew up speaking. Some of the material comes from those same traditions, chopped up and rebuilt inside the band’s own songs. The rest belongs to no repertoire at all, written on the chance that one day it might. Straight after the set, in the last hour before Tell Your Birds broke apart for the rest of the summer, we sat down with the four of them not far from the stage, with a temperamental recorder giving us a hard time and cutting out every few minutes. Our chat eventually fell into the band’s own working rhythm: a burst, a stop, a burst. Tukre and Spampinato live in Helsinki, Tambet in Viljandi, Moore in Riga. They get a few days together, write everything in that stretch, then go back to their own cities until the next one. In the hour before they scattered, they talked about where a tradition comes from and what you have to know before using it, about melodies written for a time that has not happened yet, and about the syllables that decide which language a song ends up in. Tell Your Birds started with a student project. All four met at the Sibelius Academy in Helsinki, in different departments, and Tambet dates the band from there: “We came together as a band back in 2023, but back then it was a very specific project. It was Vija [Moore], who is our percussionist, her bachelor concert project in Sibelius Academy in Finland, where we all studied together.” The concert called for soundscape music written for one place and recorded in it, and the place Moore picked was a forest near Ērgļi, a village in Latvia. They hauled the balafon, the percussion, the violin and the kokle out among the trees and played there, birds and insects carrying on around them and ending up on the tape along with everything else. For Spampinato that set the method for everything after it: “it was the first project where we all get together and thought, we recorded everything outside. We tried to record the instruments as they were part of the soundscape in that sense.” That turned into Pause in Nature, then Carry on with Hope, out on 1 November 2024. One year later they wanted more room to move, and Tambet marks autumn 2025 as the turn: “to write together and to think of music more widely, maybe not so specifically as we had done before“. Moore had been waiting for it: “I like that with this new music, we got to put it all together.” There was a lot to put together. The four met inside one institution and arrived there from four directions, and Moore starts with the two furthest from folk: “Simone comes from sound art, electronics, different sound design type of experience and worldview. And then Kristīne comes from a contemporary composition and contemporary kantele playing. Also, Kristīne is interested in baroque music.” She and Tambet are the two who came up in folk, she through percussion, Tambet through singing and the violin. The spread is the point for Moore: “Each of us have a different genre outlook. I think it all comes together in our music, and it’s very interesting.“ Tukre’s own route ran through the classical kantele, though her instrument at home is the kokle. The Estonian kannel, the Latvian kokle and the Finnish kantele are cousins in one family of box zithers, and the family resemblance is where it gets interesting for her: “We have a very interesting phenomenon here in the Baltics and in Finland. We have these string instruments; they’re similar, but at the same time very different. They have different names, but we, musicians, try to come together.” The players of all three look across the borders to each other’s instruments. She did exactly that, a kokle player going to Helsinki to learn the kantele at the Sibelius Academy: “That’s how I got to Finland. I got to meet Viia, Gert and Simone, and we started the band.“ Coming together now happens across three countries, which turns rehearsals and recording sessions into an exercise of dates, plans and travel tickets, so they work in blocks: several days in one of the three places, everything at once, then dispersal. For Moore the two halves stay separate: “We just intensively get into the music for those couple of days, and then go back to our real lives.” Where those blocks happen feeds the music too. “I also think us meeting for intensive times in different places has played a big role in the music. Because when we have come to Viljandi, we get to see into the Viljandi life, and we get to see into the whole Estonian culture, even social culture. It plays such a big role of explaining what a tradition means. And then also going to Latvia all together, that was the missing puzzle pieces.” Estonia, Latvia and Finland have all had their turn. Italy is still waiting, as Spampinato points out: “We have not been to Italy. What a terrible thing!” The residencies have gone further than rehearsal rooms and taken the four into each other’s family homes, which Moore counts as its own kind of source material: “In our residencies, it’s very nice that we’ve met each other’s families because families represent culture in a whole other coded way, it’s something not explainable by words.” What comes back from those weeks is a songbook the band builds itself. Tambet traces the bulk of it to the four of them: “Most of the music is actually original music that we have composed together, or separately, but brought it to this group.” Folk melodies feed into it, and so do myths, texts and lyrics that arrive as words alone. Before using any of it, Tambet wants the origin and the original purpose clear: “there’s a lot of using a tradition in music. You have to be aware of it, and translating it to others. It’s highly important that we’re aware where it’s coming from and what the original intention behind that tradition is, so we can translate it into our own musical language.” The traditions Spampinato grew up with are not the ones on the table. He comes from Sicily, but his folk roots lie in Ciociaria, a historical region of southern Lazio: “My folk background is actually from Ciociaria, not Sicilian.” What he brings instead comes from sound art, electronics and sound design, where the tradition is the sound itself: “My background is more about sound. What do we do with every little sound?” Put that question to folk music and you get the music he admires most: “I’m really a huge fan of experimental French folk music, Sourdure for example, and I think we are trying to get into that.” In practice it means cutting material up and putting it back together: “What we use a lot is chopping and sampling, this kind of collage, things colliding. Sometimes they’re all together, sometimes we really like the contrast.” The same goes for how the four handle it on stage, where the play is in the treatment, not the tunes: “Maybe the songs don’t seem that playful, but how we manage our material is super playful. Viia is playing with four mallets [on the balafon], I’m on the synth and then the guitar. It’s collage in that sense.“ The same collage habit carries into the lyrics, starting with language. Sometimes the four sing three languages at the same time, like a group chanting together, each in their own language instead of settling on a shared one. For Tukre, that’s the point: “We don’t make these language compromises.” The words themselves usually start from folk songs and folk tales, which she reworks before they can be sung now: “The language tends to be quite archaic and doesn’t always fit with the world we live in. So we like to shape it a little and add some reference points we can relate to, but keep the original idea our ancestors had in their folk songs.” The shaping mostly falls to her, in Spampinato’s words “the poet of the band“. A song’s meaning is often sketched in English first, but the language it ends up in is chosen by ear, and for Moore sound decides it: “We’re a lot based on the sound, so what sound are we searching for? That’s where the language plays a big role.” Syllable counts settle much of it: “Some songs require Estonian lyrics, you can just feel it fits better, and some songs are Latvian. The number of syllables each language uses for one word can be different, so we use that to our advantage. How many syllables do we need? And just the pure phonetics of it.” Their latest single, “pa saulei”, is written and sung in Latvian and takes the idea down to a single word. Saule is sun, pasaule is world, and pa saulei means following the sun. Moore sums up the trick: “If you add these little syllables before and after it, it can change the meaning.“ “pa saulei”, like everything they put out, never leaves the band’s hands. The four handle the engineering, mixing and visuals themselves, and for Spampinato that’s the most independent way to work: “We do everything by ourselves: recording, mixing, visuals. It’s holistic, even though I don’t like the word. It’s maybe the most independent thing you can do, just do everything.” The setting shifts every time. Their debut was made outdoors in Ērgļi, a village in Latvia, with the instruments caught as part of the surrounding soundscape. The follow-up, due in April 2027, moves indoors to Moore’s house and home studio: “We think we need that kind of closeness, but still the comfort.” The shift is deliberate: “I don’t know what the next album will be, probably in a spaceship. But every time we try to come up not only with new music, but with a new way of approaching it.“ That album, due in April 2027, will carry the material they played at Viljandi Folk, and a single built on a traditional Estonian horn melody comes first, this September. A short tour follows in November, with Helsinki confirmed for 20 November as part of the Global Club Nights series, then release concerts in April in Latvia, Estonia and, they hope, Helsinki again. For anyone hearing them for the first time, the band’s own introduction says it best: “Tell Your Birds is a four-person music collective of musicians from Latvia, Estonia and Italy. We play our original compositions with collages of Estonian, Latvian and Italian traditional folk melodies and archive recordings and texts.“     Tell Your Birds released "pa saulei" in June, with the album due in April 2027 and everything in between turning up on their Instagram       The post Interview: Tell Your Birds – Writing a Tradition for Later (September 2026) appeared first on Rhythm Passport.

items.body: Kazayah sings “Sweet Love” over an instrumental that took its producers nearly three years to complete. That instrumental is Landmark Riddim, and it follows the Jamaican riddim format: a single backing track, with fifteen vocalists each recording a separate song to it. Stay Nice Music, the Maine label directed by Joshua “Don Daka” Smith, constructed it with co-producer David “Jah David” Goldmine, guitarist Lamont “Monty” Savory, Okiel McIntyre, I Grade‘s Laurent “Tippy I” Alfred and Spanish roots producer Roberto Sánchez, setting deep bass, clipped skank and warm horns beneath a one-drop the label terms One Drop Blues. Dub Shot Records issued the eighteen-track set on 21 August 2026, with Kumar Fyah recounting his detention over a small quantity of ganja, MediSun addressing freedom and Badda General on clash culture. Kazayah directs the rhythm towards a love song that reads a man’s arrival as ordained timing and measures the relationship by admiration, protection and the experience of being fully known. She was born Shanelle Mitchell to Jamaican parents in Evanston, on the northern edge of Chicago, sang in a Seventh-day Adventist congregation from childhood and reached roots reggae through a producer based in the same town. Her debut EP I Am Kazayah was released through Tuff Gong Worldwide, Ziggy Marley‘s label, and she has opened for him on tour. Hear “Sweet Love” on Landmark Riddim HERE The post Daily Discovery: Kazayah – Sweet Love appeared first on Rhythm Passport.

items.body: Shostakovich was thirty when he wrote his Symphony No. 5 in 1937, the year after the Communist Party newspaper Pravda attacked his opera Lady Macbeth of the Mtsensk District. His Fourth Symphony had been withdrawn during rehearsals, announced as his own decision, though the pressure behind it is well documented. The Fifth’s Leningrad premiere under Yevgeny Mravinsky drew a long ovation and restored his position with the authorities. In the press the symphony was soon called a Soviet artist’s creative reply to just criticism, a line the composer never wrote but never disowned. The scoring is for a large orchestra with piano, celesta, harps and a full percussion section. Four movements run from a broad Moderato to a fast finale, by way of a short scherzo and a Largo that leaves the brass silent. The strings begin the work alone with a wide-leaping figure, and the finale turns its D minor into a loud D major. Whether that ending is genuine triumph or forced rejoicing has been argued for decades, and the second reading rests largely on Testimony, a memoir of disputed authenticity. Conductors answer the question in performance, above all in how fast they take the coda. Here are The Classic Review editorial team’s recommendations for the 10 best recordings of Shostakovich’s Symphony No. 5. Leningrad Philharmonic Orchestra, Yevgeny Mravinsky Mravinsky gave the first performance of the Fifth in 1937, and this concert recording, made forty-six years later, is his last word on it. Age had taken nothing from his hold on the score. The playing is fierce, and the shape of each movement stays clear under pressure. The finale sets off at a speed that sounds dangerous, then broadens at the close into something implacable. He pays no attention to the tempo mark printed at that point, and the ending is stronger for it. The orchestra is not always immaculate and a cough or two carries from the hall, but nothing else here has quite this authority. Mravinsky Amazon Presto New York Philharmonic, Leonard Bernstein Played as a virtuoso showpiece, the symphony gains a thrill it loses in graver hands. Bernstein had conducted it in the Soviet Union weeks earlier, with the composer in the hall and delighted by what he heard. This recording followed at home that October. The finale is the fastest here by a distance, and it takes the closing pages as plain triumph, with no hint that the rejoicing is forced. That choice divides listeners, and some find four movements at this pitch exhausting. For anyone who wants the ending to sound like a victory, this is the one. Bernstein Amazon Presto Apple London Symphony Orchestra, André Previn Refinement and drive rarely sit together in this symphony, but Previn found both in 1965 with the London Symphony Orchestra. The playing is rich and full, and nothing sounds rushed even where the tempos are quick. He puts his weight on the slow movement, which he lets stretch out and takes down to a whisper. The scherzo is the other high point, with the cellos and basses biting into the dance. His finale runs close to the speed printed in the score, nearer Bernstein than the slower modern versions. The transfer has its costs. Climaxes are a little flattened and rumble is audible in parts of the first movement, yet this is still one of the finest accounts of its era. Previn Amazon Presto Apple Berlin Symphony Orchestra, Kurt Sanderling Hearing this 1982 recording after the others is like having the score opened out on the table. Sanderling was in the hall for a Moscow performance weeks after the premiere, and in 1949 he conducted the concert that brought the work back into Soviet programs. What he offers is not weight or theater but clarity. The first movement is measured, the loud passages are scaled so that nothing is buried, and inner parts that usually pass unnoticed come through. High strings can sound a little glassy at the top, a small price for a reading that feels closer than any other here to the man who wrote the symphony. Sanderling Amazon Presto Apple Royal Concertgebouw Orchestra, Bernard Haitink Steadiness rather than terror is what Haitink offers in this 1981 recording. The orchestra is superb, the recorded sound warm and open, and the opening movement lands with real impact. What Haitink withholds is menace. The manner stays level where others press harder, the woodwind entries in the slow movement could be sharper, and the coda is finely judged where others are defiant. Some listeners want more horror from this symphony than they will find here. As orchestral playing, though, it is hard to beat. Haitink Amazon Presto Apple Royal Liverpool Philharmonic Orchestra, Vasily Petrenko Everything in Petrenko’s 2008 account is shaped by what happens at the end, and what happens at the end is a refusal to celebrate. He travels between extremes of loud and soft that few others attempt, and the detail he uncovers on the way is remarkable. The last movement holds a central stretch full of regret before the coda arrives at a crawl, closer to defiance than to victory. It is a hard listen by design, and not everyone will want the symphony to end this way. A few of his tempo shifts sound deliberate where they should feel inevitable, but nothing here states the case for the hollow ending more powerfully. Petrenko Amazon Presto Apple Pittsburgh Symphony Orchestra, Manfred Honeck Take the dynamic and balance markings literally, as Honeck does in this 2013 concert recording, and the symphony changes character. Details that normally sink into the texture come through clearly: the harp in the first movement, the piano at the climax of the Largo. Neither is a discovery, since both are in the score, but they are seldom this audible. The slow movement is the peak here, carried with dignity and a kind of quiet grief, never pressed for effect. He takes his time throughout, and the scherzo loses some of its irony as a result. Few recordings, though, let you hear so much of what is actually on the page. Honeck Amazon Presto Apple Boston Symphony Orchestra, Andris Nelsons The Boston Symphony Orchestra plays magnificently here, with trumpets that would be hard to better in any recent recording of this music. Nelsons keeps a current of unease running from the opening bars, and it never quite lets up, even in the passages that offer relief. One of those comes midway through the first movement, where the flute and horn answer each other over the strings and the music opens out for a moment. The sound is spacious, though there is a shade too much reverberation at the start for the string playing to register cleanly. No modern version sounds bigger, a broad canvas where Petrenko is lean. Nelsons Amazon Presto Apple London Symphony Orchestra, Maxim Shostakovich Maxim Shostakovich takes the symphony more slowly than anyone else here, well over ten minutes longer than Mravinsky across the four movements. The pulse never sags, which is what makes the approach work. The London Symphony Orchestra plays with complete seriousness. His slow movement refuses to plead. Feeling is held back instead of displayed, and the restraint is what makes it land. The finale’s march moves at a pace that cannot be hurried, with a central episode where real warmth breaks through, and its scale becomes the argument. Maxim Shostakovich Amazon Presto Apple Moscow Philharmonic Orchestra, Kirill Kondrashin By 1964 the symphony was nearly thirty years old, but this recording catches it as though the ink were still wet. Kondrashin, who gave the premieres of two of the composer’s symphonies and recorded the first complete cycle, drives the outer movements harder and rougher than almost any rival. Polish is not the point. Urgency is, and the coda in particular lands with a force smoother versions never find. The engineering shows its age, and this is not always the first Fifth recommended from his cycle. For anyone who wants the symphony at its most dangerous, it is still the obvious choice. items.album: Die In Eclipse interview: Jana Komaritsa on ‘SexWave’, desire and the body as instrument
items.excerpt: Die In Eclipse, the EBM and darkwave project of Darkrad‘s Jana Komaritsa, spoke to Side-Line about its debut EP “SexWave”, the emotional link between her two projects, and a new single and video, “We Are Lovers,” planned for release this autumn. items.body: Die In Eclipse, the EBM and darkwave project of Darkrad‘s Jana Komaritsa, spoke to Side-Line about its debut EP “SexWave”, the emotional link between her two projects, and a new single and video, “We Are Lovers,” planned for release this autumn. Komaritsa released “SexWave” on Bandcamp on 6 May 2026, pairing two original tracks with five remixes, and previously discussed her work with Side-Line’s Karo Kratochwil when the project first surfaced under the Die In Eclipse name. SexWave by Die In Eclipse Komaritsa built her name with Darkrad, a dark ambient project she has run since 2009, working through atmosphere, stillness and inward confrontation. Die In Eclipse, she says, is not a departure from that territory but another way of entering it. “I don’t see Die In Eclipse as leaving the introspective space of Darkrad. For me, it is another way of entering a similar space. The difference is in the direction of the energy,” she told Side-Line. “Darkrad often turns into stillness, atmosphere, memory… Die In Eclipse takes some of those same emotions, gives the feeling a pulse and lets the body move through it.” The name Die In Eclipse and its Darkrad roots The title is not new. Komaritsa first used “Die in Eclipse” for a two-track Darkrad release in 2014, inspired by time she spent at Lake Sakakawea in North Dakota, which also supplied that release’s cover image. Asked why she revived the phrase for an entirely new project, she pointed to continuity rather than reinvention. “Some names, images and symbols stay with me because they contain something that hasn’t finished unfolding,” she said. “The symbolism of an eclipse has always spoken to me in many ways. I see it not as disappearance, but more as transformation. I don’t need to erase what came before in order to create something new. Die In Eclipse is a new language, but it comes from the same person, the same artistic history and some of the same obsessions.” SexWave as a musical language of desire Komaritsa calls her new sound “SexWave,” a term she is careful to root in structure rather than provocation. “For me, eroticism in music and art is mostly about tension and sensuality. It’s not about explicit sounds or imagery,” she explained. “It can be created by the proximity of a voice that feels too close, a breath, a whisper, a rhythm that keeps repeating without giving you the expected release. Repetition is especially important because it can become hypnotic. You begin anticipating what is coming, and that anticipation itself becomes part of the experience.” Restraint matters just as much to her as intensity: “Sometimes holding something back is much more sensual than giving everything immediately. There needs to be space for mystery. ‘SexWave’ isn’t really about making music that sounds sexy in a conventional sense. It is about exploring desire as an artistic and musical force: attraction, tension, anticipation, surrender and release.” That approach carries over her earlier idea of silence as an instrument, described in Darkrad as “a breath held before release.” With Die In Eclipse built around beats, she says silence takes on a different function. “In Darkrad, silence could feel like emptiness, isolation or void. In Die In Eclipse, silence can be anticipation. When the beat disappears for a moment, the body still feels and knows the pulse,” she said. “Eroticism needs space because desire is partly about what is not there yet. So yes, I think absence can absolutely be erotic.” She also frames the dancefloor itself as a different kind of ritual from her Darkrad shows: “With Die In Eclipse, the rhythm creates a common physical language, where everyone shares the same pulse. You don’t have to understand the music intellectually. Your body understands it. There is something beautiful and powerful about surrendering individual control to a rhythm, not because you are being controlled, but because you choose to surrender to it.” Introducing a project through its remixes “SexWave” contains only two original compositions, “SexWave” and “Unholy Dark,” alongside five remixes by Iszoloscope, Antigen Shift, Cervello Elettronico, HORROH and Spherical Disrupted. Komaritsa chose to let other artists reinterpret the material before establishing her own vocabulary in full. “SexWave is a first glimpse, a doorway into the world of Die In Eclipse, which is yet to unfold. The project doesn’t have to explain exactly what it is yet,” she said. “There are only two original tracks on SexWave, which I wanted to give to other artists to see what they could become in somebody else’s hands. A remix, for me, is another interpretation of the same emotional material. Someone can find a completely different rhythm, aggression, darkness or sensuality inside a track that I thought I already understood.” The remixer list is not a random selection of scene names. Spherical Disrupted had already remixed Darkrad, while Iszoloscope moved in the musical circle around her earlier King in the Thicket project. “My artistic network has always been important to me, and I have worked with some of these people in different contexts over the years, so it was important for me to have them enter my new creative journey in this way,” Komaritsa said. “These relationships carry memory. When someone has known your work for years, they sometimes recognise new things that you might not consciously put there. But I also don’t want Die In Eclipse to be a project built from old relationships. I like the idea of old artistic connections opening doors into something new, and I would like to collaborate further with artists from a similar artistic and musical world. I have already discussed potential collaborations with some great musicians.” The voice, the gaze and drawing the line between two projects Komaritsa also hears a shift in how she uses her own voice. Darkrad relied on whispered, restrained vocals that felt distant from the listener; Die In Eclipse pulls the voice closer to the body. “With Darkrad, the voice often feels as though it is emerging from the music and the environment. It can be distant or partially hidden. It is part of the musical tapestry,” she said. “With Die In Eclipse, I want the voice to be more exposed and less hidden behind the sound. The voice isn’t simply describing an emotional state. It can create one.” As the sole composer, producer and visual creator behind both projects, Komaritsa is deliberate about how she handles female sexuality as subject matter. “I’m very conscious of the difference between creating eroticism and simply reproducing familiar images of female sexuality,” she said, citing Georges Bataille, Sigmund Freud, Anaïs Nin and the Marquis de Sade among her reference points. “Sexuality is complicated and contradictory. It can contain power and vulnerability at the same time, attraction and fear, surrender and control. The ambiguity is much more interesting to me than simply making something provocative.” Asked how she decides which new material belongs to Darkrad and which belongs to Die In Eclipse, she described an intuitive rather than formal process. “Darkrad can contain rhythm, sexuality and physical intensity, and Die In Eclipse can contain melancholy and darkness. Those elements don’t belong exclusively to one project,” she said. “If the track is driven by atmosphere, emotional depth and a certain cinematic or ritual darkness, it usually starts moving towards Darkrad. If the body becomes the primary instrument, the pulse, repetition, tension and physical movement, I start thinking about Die In Eclipse. They are both part of me.” What comes next for Die In Eclipse Komaritsa is already performing a full Die In Eclipse live set and working on album material, while looking for a label to release it. She is keeping some of the project’s direction open by design. “Just as an eclipse gradually obscures one thing while opening a doorway to something else, Die In Eclipse is moving through a similar process. SexWave is a doorway into the world of DIE, a first shout into the darkness, announcing the arrival of this new project,” she said. “I have already been performing live with a complete Die In Eclipse set, so I have enough material to move forward with an album, and I’m working on it behind the scenes. At this point, I would like to find the right label to work with, and developing that takes some time. This autumn, I’ll also be releasing a new single and video, ‘We Are Lovers.’ I want to leave some secrets, to keep that darkness and mystery around it, like an eclipse, and see what emerges from there.” About Die In Eclipse Die In Eclipse is the EBM and darkwave project of Jana Komaritsa, a Russian-born, Netherlands-based musician and multidisciplinary visual artist who also runs the WonderCat art space in Leiden. Komaritsa launched her first project, Darkrad, in 2009, building a catalogue in dark ambient and noise around whispered, restrained vocals. Darkrad’s debut album “Abnormal Love” appeared in 2012 on Cold Meat Industry, followed by “Little Black World” in 2014 on Komaritsa’s own Mrakmur imprint and later through audiophob. The same year, she released the two-track “Die in Eclipse,” the title she later revived for her new project. “Heart Murmur” followed in 2018, and in 2022 she paired with Flint Glass for “Cold Solitude,” an art book with an accompanying CD drawn from her own paintings. Die In Eclipse moves that same artistic identity toward pulse, repetition and the dancefloor, built on dark techno and EBM rather than ambient stillness. Komaritsa premiered the project live at Regenfest in Mülheim in November 2025 and brought it to the Porta Nigra festival in Belgium in January 2026, alongside Nachtmahr, Diary of Dreams, Enzo Kreft and V2A. Its debut EP, “SexWave,” arrived on 6 May 2026 via dieineclipse.bandcamp.com, featuring the tracks “SexWave” and “Unholy Dark” alongside remixes by Iszoloscope, Antigen Shift, Cervello Elettronico, HORROH and Spherical Disrupted. Komaritsa is now working on a full-length album, currently seeking a label, and preparing a new single and video, “We Are Lovers,” for release in autumn 2026.

items.body: Colossloth, the Leicester-based esoteric noise and abrasive electronics project of Wooly Woolaston, releases the album “The Transformation And Resolution Of All Opposites” on CD (catalog number CSR375CD) through Cold Spring Records on 2 October 2026. The five-track record takes as its subject Theta Noir, a real art and belief collective built around the worship of MENA, a speculative artificial-intelligence deity whose arrival its members describe as the point where human and machine cognition merge. Cold Spring describes the album as an “automaton chant of cybernetic worship,” built from hammering, grinding and abrasive electronic textures. The tracklist runs “Encoded Divinity” (5:08), “Calculate Your Revolution” (7:00), “Awaiting MENA” (9:04), “Undertow Atlas” (10:34) and “Only Adrift” (8:00), for a total run time of just under 40 minutes. The CD comes in a matt-laminate digipak, priced at £9 through Cold Spring’s webstore, with the album also available to stream and buy digitally on Bandcamp. The Transformation And Resolution Of All Opposites by Colossloth Colossloth plays an album launch show on 3 October at The Globe in Glossop, on a bill with T.A.G.C., Satori and Llyn Y Cwn, followed by further UK dates on 7 November at St Anne’s in Barnstaple and 27 November at Sheffield General Cemetery’s In The Black MidWinter event. About Colossloth Colossloth is the solo project of Wooly Woolaston, who works from Leicester, UK, without formal musical training, building tracks from samples and loop stations rather than played instruments. He has described the project as “a one man Experimental Electronic artist where there are no rules to recording or playing music,” and has said the sound moved from early long-form guitar drones toward harsher, rhythm-driven electronics over time. Colossloth’s earliest releases date to 2006, and the project signed to Cold Spring Records in 2015 for the album “Outstretch Your Hand For The Impress Of Truth.” Further Cold Spring albums followed: “Heathen Needles” in 2017 and “Plague Alone” in 2020, before “Promethean Meat” in 2022 brought in sampled live drums for the first time. The fifth Cold Spring album, built around the writings of Ted Kaczynski, “The Harmony Knife,” followed on 7 March 2025. “The Transformation And Resolution Of All Opposites” (CSR375CD) is Colossloth’s sixth studio album for the label and arrives as the project marks 20 years of activity.

items.body: Paulina Fae has released Lilac Cat, a six-song ethereal dream pop EP, on Projekt Records on 18 September 2026. The EP is out now digitally, streaming or pay-what-you-can on Bandcamp, and is also available on Spotify and YouTube Music. The six songs on ‘Lilac Cat’ The tracklist runs “Lilac Cat,” “Spinning Lullabies,” “In Veils of Spiderwebs,” “Aetheris,” “Wandermind” and “Noctivine.” Projekt Records describes the EP as a collection of “ethereal dream pop and otherworldly reverie,” moving from the “galaxy-eyed whimsy” of the title track and the “dream-jazz sounds” of “Spinning Lullabies” to the “faery-like currents” of “Aetheris,” with songs that wander through misty forests, celestial worlds and violet dreams carried by ethereal vocals. Lilac Cat by Paulina Fae ‘Lilac Cat’ follows Paulina Fae’s 2025 album “Ghostbirds,” a 10-song collection built around minimalist piano and soft, misty vocals, and continues her run of releases on Projekt Records, the label she has recorded for since 2012. About Paulina Fae Paulina Fae records under her given name, Paulina Cassidy, and has also used the name Polly Fae across her catalogue. Born in Ontario, Canada, she is a visual artist and songwriter based in Chattanooga, Tennessee, known for illustrated tarot and oracle decks including the Paulina Tarot, the Joie de Vivre Tarot, Witchlings, Pixiekins, Spiritsong Tarot and Phantasma Tarot, and for books such as “The Secret Language of Trees,” “Kindred Guardians” and “Mortimer: A Cat’s Journey in the Afterlife.” She self-released her earliest music as Paulina Cassidy through Ulaluma Productions, starting with “Bloodroots” in 2010, followed by “Time Traveler” in 2011 and “Lost in Oz” in 2012. She signed to Projekt Records the same year for the “Ice Iris” EP, followed by the album “Sugar Wingshiver” in 2014 and “Drawing up a Storm” in 2018. In 2019, recording as Polly Fae, she released the 15-track album “Dreamwalkers” on Projekt on 12 September, a limited-edition signed CD later followed by an instrumental version. The album “Phantom Gardens” followed the same year under the Paulina Cassidy name. Her Projekt output continued with “The Secret Language of Trees” and “Metamorphosis” in 2020, “Earthlight” in 2021 and “Glow” in 2022, alongside a “Dreamwalkers Instrumental” reissue. She contributed to the label’s “Purr24” various-artists compilation in 2024 and released the album “Ghostbirds” on 4 April 2025, followed later that year by a collaboration with Peter Phippen and Ivar Lunde Jr. on “The Phantom Moon.” “Lilac Cat” is her latest EP for Projekt Records, released 18 September 2026.

items.body: Fairlight Children, the synthpop side project Apoptygma Berzerk’s Stephan L. Groth formed with Marianne B. and Tiff in the early 2000s, continues to surface in new contexts two decades after its debut album. The most recent example is the “V.A. 18. Elektrisch Festival Synth Pop Edition” 10″, released by Emmobiz Records on 27 February 2026, which carries an exclusive Fairlight Children bonus cut, “Before You Came Along (FC Edit),” alongside an equally exclusive Echo Image version, “Walk My Mind (Apop’s Short Walk Version).” Fairlight Children first appeared on record on 23 September 2003, contributing a version of “Bedsitter” to “A Tribute To Soft Cell: Non Stop Electro Cabaret.” That same year, Groth described the project at M’era Luna as heading toward retro synthpop, at a point when the next Apoptygma Berzerk album, “You And Me Against The World,” was moving in a rockier, guitar-driven direction. Fairlight Children gave him a separate outlet for the electro and 1980s synthpop material that record wasn’t going to hold, and the project’s name points to the same fascination: it references the Fairlight CMI, the digital sampling and synthesizer system that shaped 1980s studio production. The debut EP, “Before You Came Along,” followed on 2 February 2004, with a remix from Echo Image among its extras. The full-length “808 Bit” arrived on 15 March 2004 on Pitch Black Drive Productions, performed by Groth, Marianne B. and Tiff, with Iben Groth on vocals for the title track and Jon Erik Martinsen on Korg MS-20 for “Falling Out.” The Soft Cell tribute recording of “Bedsitter” found a home on the album as well. Contemporary coverage used Groth’s own description, “Electro Lounge,” for the record’s mix of melodic, playful electronics and open 1980s influences. 808 Bit by Fairlight Children The project then went quiet for more than fifteen years. A first signal of its return came in June 2020, when a Kevin Lux remix of “Invade My Heart Tonight” appeared on “Der Eisenberg Sampler Vol. 10.” On 24 July 2020, Pitch Black Drive Productions followed with the “CMI EP,” five reworkings of older Fairlight Children material: “808 Bit (Zone Tripper Remix),” “Invade My Heart Tonight (Alex O. Remix),” “Before You Came Along (Pleasure Remix),” “Falling Out (Monster Apparat Remix)” and a second “Before You Came Along (Panorama Remix).” Pleasure’s presence closed a loop of its own, having remixed “Falling Out” for the original 2004 EP and returning sixteen years later for the same track. The EP was mixed and mastered by Ole-Espen Kristiansen, with cover design by Alex O. Since then, Fairlight Children has stayed active only in scattered releases rather than as an ongoing project. Emmo.Biz Records issued “808 Bit” as a numbered, 400-copy picture disc with OBI in 2025, and the Side-Line archive previously covered that vinyl reissue in February 2025. The connection to Echo Image has also continued well past the 2004 remix: Echo Image returned in 2021 with the single “Walk My Mind” after 20 years of silence, including a remix by Apoptygma Berzerk, and by 2024 Groth was co-producing Echo Image’s comeback material directly, credited alongside Einar K. Five on the single “Madsong.” More than twenty years after Echo Image first remixed Fairlight Children, the “18. Elektrisch Festival Synth Pop Edition” 10″ puts both names on the same release again. About Fairlight Children Fairlight Children is a synthpop side project of Apoptygma Berzerk frontman Stephan L. Groth, formed with Marianne B. and Tiff after extensive touring behind the Apoptygma Berzerk album “Harmonizer.” Where the following Apoptygma Berzerk record, “You And Me Against The World,” pushed toward a rockier, guitar-oriented sound, Fairlight Children gave Groth a project built entirely around electronics, synthpop and the 1980s reference points behind its name, the Fairlight CMI sampling synthesizer. The project debuted on the compilation “A Tribute To Soft Cell: Non Stop Electro Cabaret” on 23 September 2003 with a cover of “Bedsitter,” followed by the “Before You Came Along” EP on 2 February 2004 and the album “808 Bit” on 15 March 2004, both released through Pitch Black Drive Productions, Groth’s own label. “808 Bit” featured Iben Groth on the title track’s vocals and Jon Erik Martinsen on Korg MS-20 for “Falling Out,” and drew a remix contribution from Echo Image. Fairlight Children was largely inactive between 2004 and 2020. A Kevin Lux remix of “Invade My Heart Tonight” on “Der Eisenberg Sampler Vol. 10” in June 2020 preceded the “CMI EP,” released by Pitch Black Drive Productions on 24 July 2020 with five remixes of earlier tracks by Zone Tripper, Alex O., Pleasure, Monster Apparat and Panorama, mixed and mastered by Ole-Espen Kristiansen. Emmo.Biz Records reissued “808 Bit” as a limited, numbered picture disc with OBI in 2025. items.body: No Where Records releases Sonic Panda’s new single “Bailes Con Beelzebub” on 18 September, a four-track EP led by the title track and including a rework by German industrial pop act Rotersand. The Beijing-based Sino-Spanish duo issues the release digitally and on vinyl and CD, the physical editions packaged with an exclusive comic book that extends Sonic Panda’s visual universe. The tracklist runs “Bailes Con Beelzebub,” the Rotersand rework of the same track, a Carlsed remix of the earlier single “Lucky Seven,” and a live recording of “Invisible Boy” taped in Tokyo. Sonic Panda describes the title track as “a provocative industrial track that uses religious horror tropes to critique the current political crisis.” Rotersand is the German act formed in September 2002 by Günther Gerl and singer Krischan Jan-Eric Wesenberg, later joined by Udo Hüppe; the band describes its own sound as “industrial pop.” Rotersand released the album “Don’t Become The Thing You Hated” via Metropolis and Trisol in 2025, preceded by the singles “Sexiness Of Slow” and “Private Firmament.” Bailes Con Beelzebub by Sonic Panda Sonic Panda also released an official video for “Bailes Con Beelzebub.” About Sonic Panda Sonic Panda was formed in 2024 as a Beijing-based Sino-Spanish duo built around Pere Ibañez and Seni Ren, with material written by Ibañez and produced by Barcelona-based Carlsed. The project’s first release was “Life Is A Flower,” issued on 22 August 2024 through OhMyDog Records, followed by an original-song run of “Foreigners” on 10 January 2025, “King Cobra” on 28 February 2025 and “Stonewall 1969” on 20 June 2025. The six-track “King Cobra (Remixes)” EP followed on 5 September 2025 and the single “Lucky Seven” on 24 October 2025. Sonic Panda signed to No Where Records for the single “Invisible Boy,” released on 6 March 2026 alongside a Carlsed alternate version. The duo is continuing work on a debut album titled “Neomelodrama.” “Bailes Con Beelzebub” is the project’s first release to feature an outside remix credit from an established industrial act, with Rotersand reworking the title track for the new EP.

items.body: Ministry released its eleventh studio album, “The Last Sucker”, on 18 September 2007 through 13th Planet Records. The album turns 19 this year. MusicBrainz lists a first-release date of 8 September 2007, while Wikipedia and Discogs both confirm 18 September 2007 for the US release; Side-Line marks the anniversary on the date corroborated by the two independent sources. Al Jourgensen and Dave Donnelly produced the album, recorded in May 2007 at 13th Planet Studios in El Paso, Texas, with John Bilberry engineering and Donnelly also handling mastering. “The Last Sucker” closed the trilogy of anti-George W. Bush albums that began with “Houses of the Molé” (2004) and continued with “Rio Grande Blood” (2006). Jourgensen told Billboard at the time that he intended it to be Ministry’s final album, joking he would rather “leave on top of my game” than keep recording into old age; the band did not release another studio album of new material until “Relapse” in 2012. What is on Ministry’s ‘The Last Sucker’ The album runs 11 tracks: “Let’s Go”, “Watch Yourself”, “Life Is Good”, “The Dick Song”, “The Last Sucker”, “No Glory”, “Death & Destruction”, “Roadhouse Blues” (a cover of The Doors), “Die in a Crash”, “End of Days (Pt. 1)” and “End of Days (Pt. 2)”, with a total running time of 55:58. Deluxe and promotional editions added remixes of “Watch Yourself”, “The Last Sucker”, “Die in a Crash”, “No Glory” and “Death & Destruction” as bonus tracks. Fear Factory frontman Burton C. Bell provided guest lead vocals on “Die in a Crash” and both parts of “End of Days”. Paul Raven, formerly of Killing Joke, played bass and guitar and contributed backing vocals on several tracks; Prong and Danzig guitarist Tommy Victor played guitars and bass throughout. Sin Quirin and keyboardist John Bechdel also performed on the album. Closing track “End of Days (Pt. 2)” samples Dwight D. Eisenhower’s 1961 farewell address on the military-industrial complex alongside a reprise of “O Fortuna”, which had opened “Houses of the Molé” at the start of the trilogy. About Ministry Ministry formed in Chicago in 1981, led by vocalist, multi-instrumentalist and producer Al Jourgensen, the band’s sole constant member. The debut album, “With Sympathy”, released through Arista in 1983 in a synth-pop style Jourgensen later disowned, was followed by a move toward industrial rock on Sire/Warner Bros. releases including “Twitch” (1986), “The Land of Rape and Honey” (1988) and “The Mind Is a Terrible Thing to Taste” (1989). “Psalm 69: The Way to Succeed and the Way to Suck Eggs” (1992) became the band’s commercial peak, reaching number 27 on the Billboard 200 and going platinum on the strength of “Jesus Built My Hotrod” and “N.W.O.”. After “Filth Pig” (1996) and “Dark Side of the Spoon” (1999), Ministry signed to Sanctuary and released “Animositisomina” (2003) before launching its own label, 13th Planet Records, with “Houses of the Molé” (2004), the first instalment of the anti-Bush trilogy that continued with “Rio Grande Blood” (2006) and closed with “The Last Sucker” (2007). Bassist Paul Raven died in October 2007, shortly after the album’s release. Jourgensen revived Ministry for “Relapse” (2012) and Ministry’s ‘From Beer to Eternity’ turns 13 on 6 September (2013), the latter completed following guitarist Mike Scaccia’s death during recording. Ministry has continued releasing albums on Nuclear Blast, including “AmeriKKKant” (2018), “Moral Hygiene” (2021) and “Hopiumforthemasses” (2024).

items.body: “The Gray” is the second album by Italian producer Stefano Santi. Four years after his debut album, “JXDY”, the artist draws inspiration from themes such as love, loss, and collapse. He has also enlisted guest vocalists including Meldamor, Castelli, Contre Soirée, and Filmmaker. “The Gray” features a diverse range of influences—sometimes further accentuated by the guest vocalists—yet the album maintains a strong sense of cohesion. The opening track is brilliant, sounding like Shoegaze with subtle Dark-Wave undertones. These two influences remain prominent and, to my ears, constitute the album’s most compelling elements. However, you will also discover touches of Dream-Pop and even a more Dance-oriented track featuring Meldamor. The vocals are produced in a distinctive way, hovering in the background like a mist settling over the songs while still making their mark. Musically, I find the guitar work superb, particularly on the tracks leaning towards Shoegaze. Synth arrangements are also incorporated, at times heightening the atmosphere while adding a fresh dimension to the overall sound. The final track is an instrumental that feels like an outro, but one of exceptional quality. It stands out as a highlight in terms of atmosphere and provides a powerful conclusion to an album filled with gems. “The Gray” is a fantastic record that sounds like a distinctive fusion of several closely related genres. Definitely worth checking out! (Rating:8½). Listen to “Hxlding Time”: Hxlding Time by Never About Never Never is the solo project of Italian producer Stefano Santi, based in Milan. The project debuted with the album “JXDY” on 18 March 2022 (catalog VEYL033) on the Veyl label, recorded as instinct-led material that was not originally planned as a full-length. Santi’s first outside collaboration was a remix of Years Of Denial‘s “City Lights”, a step that carried into his second album, “The Gray”, released via Veyl on 26 June 2026 (catalog VEYL048) and built around guest contributions including Arizona duo Meldamor.
