items.body: On the cotton candy sky Written every moment of life For all eternity Wonder why we are even alive Some records come from a scene, some from a city, and some seem to come from that ugly five-minute interval after you have stared at your phone too long and suddenly hate civilization. Faded Flowers, the latest album from Turkish Darkwave duo Ductape, belongs to the third category. It looks around at modern life: crowded rooms, digital selves, obedient routines, private disintegration, and finds a species that has become astonishingly good at maintaining appearances while quietly running itself into the ground. Çağla Güleray and Furkan Güleray formed Ductape in 2019 in Istanbul, where their mix of post-punk, darkwave, Turkish and English lyrics quickly carried them well beyond the usual underground boundaries. Four albums and two EPs later, they have relocated their creative base to France. Geography changes; the unease travels well. On Faded Flowers, that unease has acquired a larger target. The title gives you the central image without turning it into homework: people as flowers left too long beneath bad light, drained by repetition, expectation, isolation, and the exhausting business of becoming whatever the surrounding machinery finds acceptable. You can hear that pressure everywhere. The basslines have the cold discipline of public transport at six in the morning. Synthesizers cut through with little sympathy. Furkan’s guitar keeps finding ways to sound agitated without becoming decorative, sometimes stalking around Çağla’s voice, sometimes answering it, sometimes scraping at the walls. Çağla’s magnificent voice remains the great destabilizing force in Ductape. She can sound detached enough to frighten you, then suddenly let some exposed nerve show through before the song has time to make a ceremony of it. There is very little comfort in that delivery, which suits an album concerned with the absurdity of living among millions of people and still feeling marooned. That particular contradiction runs all through Faded Flowers. Everyone is visible now. Everyone is reachable. Everyone is encouraged to construct a public version of themselves, polish it, post it, improve it, defend it, sell it, then wake up tomorrow and do the same miserable maintenance all over again. Somewhere along the line, identity became administrative labour. Ductape sounds thoroughly fed up with the arrangement. The album keeps circling the false authorities people submit to without necessarily believing in them: social roles, digital identities, manufactured ideals, systems of power, inherited expectations, all those little invisible rules that become oppressive mostly because nobody remembers agreeing to them. There is anger in these songs, but also exhaustion, and the exhaustion may be more interesting. Rage still assumes you have energy to spare. Fine considers one dubious convenience of hitting bottom: at least you can stop pretending the view is lovely. The album’s first single follows a collapse through pain and disorientation toward an unexpected sense of ownership, as Çağla finds a place for herself inside the very circumstances that have undone her. A steady bassline and luminous synthesizers carry her weary composure, giving that uneasy acceptance room to develop. There is something wonderfully suspect about feeling comfortable down there, and the song lets the suspicion sit beside the relief. Within an album preoccupied with keeping up appearances, surrendering the performance becomes its own small freedom. The accompanying black-and-white video turns that process into a homemade alchemical experiment. Filmed at Misuc in Ankara, it casts the duo as silent-film experimenters collecting ingredients and tending a potion among curious specimens. Ductape handled the direction, styling, and production, with camera work by Mert Yalçın and editing by Çağla Güleray. Its antique laboratory makes an apt workshop for two people attempting to assemble another version of themselves. Standout track Obscure moves with a bassline so blunt and heavy it seems capable of carrying the song by itself, while Furkan Güleray’s distorted guitar keeps worrying at the edges, leaving abrasions rather than decoration. Synths hang overhead with an icy, almost antiseptic quality, giving the music the uneasy stillness of a room where something unpleasant has already been said. Çağla Güleray sings in English, her low register remarkably composed as she picks through disillusionment without dressing it up for sympathy. That restraint makes the words hit harder. Stolen light, dead idols, resentment calcified through repetition, the dull vacancy that follows years of believing in something that eventually reveals itself as another instrument of control: Obscure gathers these ideas until the song begins to feel less like despair than the slow recognition of how thoroughly faith can be exploited. There is damage here, certainly, but also the uncomfortable clarity that comes when the old explanations have finally stopped working. Its Berlin performance video brings that severity onto the stage. Directed by Altay Erlik, with cinematography by Emrah Celik and laser animation by Peter Isachenko, the clip concentrates on the duo’s physical presence, giving the song’s accusations the directness of an encounter across a crowded room. On Gölgesiz, the effort of continuing becomes almost physical. Sung in Turkish, the album’s second single carries accumulated sorrow through persistent drums and guitar figures that seem caught in the same argument with themselves. Çağla keeps her delivery measured, making fatigue audible through the weight she gives each phrase. The rhythm maintains its appointment with the next bar while the person inside it struggles to find a reason to follow. That uneasy relationship between bodily momentum and emotional depletion gives the song its force, extending the album’s concern with lives organised around obligations that have outlasted their meaning. Made during Ductape’s Latin American tour, the monochrome DIY video places Çağla against expanses of water and open space, her figure often reduced to a silhouette. Visual distortions make her outline appear unstable, as though even occupying a body has become difficult work. The images give the song’s isolation a scale that the surrounding emptiness only enlarges. Faded Flowers gains its pull from the sense that decay is something social as much as personal. The individual breaks down because the surrounding structure is already cracked. The city keeps moving. The screen keeps glowing. The machine keeps asking for another password. Somewhere inside all that, a person still has to decide who they are. Ductape leave that question open, with the bass still moving underneath it. Listen to Faded Flowers below and order the album here. Faded Flowers by Ductape To celebrate the album release, Ductape have announced headline shows and festival dates across Europe well into 2027. items.body: John X Belmonte’s Golden Lore understands a basic truth about goth clubs, doomed romance, and every terrible decision made after midnight: grandeur works best when there is something embarrassing hiding underneath it. The song moves with the confidence of a man walking into a ruined cathedral wearing sunglasses, fully aware that vanity and remorse have been sharing the same coat for years. Its synth bass keeps the floor moving with a steady, narcotic insistence, while Belmonte’s voice sits low in the mix, deep and controlled, as though he is delivering private evidence to a room that has already reached its verdict. The pitch-shifted echo curling around the vocal gives Belmonte’s delivery a doubled quality, part confession and part apparition, suggesting memory as a badly behaved accomplice rather than some sacred archive. Golden Lore keeps circling myth, beauty, regret, and self-invention, those old poisons that people pour into prettier bottles whenever reality starts looking cheap. The lyrics seem fascinated by how easily memory turns vanity into legend, and how legend eventually gets mistaken for truth. Golden Lore belongs to that hour when the dance floor becomes less a public space than a private reckoning set to a bassline. Belmonte gives the song enough romantic scale to make regret feel almost luxurious, letting memory dress its worst decisions in expensive clothes. By the final chorus, desire, vanity, and remorse have become impossible to separate, and the song leaves them circling one another beneath the club lights until closing time. As a dance track, Golden Lore has excellent instincts. The rhythm remains disciplined, the bassline stays heavy, and every element serves the forward motion. Nothing gets cluttered for the sake of drama. Then the chorus opens up, and this is where the song earns its black clothes. The melody is gorgeous without becoming sugary, large without losing its bruised center. There is a real sense of release in the refrain, the kind that makes a crowded room briefly feel communal even when everyone inside it is busy maintaining their own private disaster. You can hear why fans of Cold Cave, Drab Majesty, Then Comes Silence, and the Sisters of Mercy might find an immediate point of entry, though Belmonte keeps enough restraint in the arrangement to avoid drowning the song in borrowed gestures. The video takes a similarly direct route. Belmonte performs against images of a mysterious figure moving through a dark landscape with a giant ankh, the superimposition giving the clip the look of damaged film discovered in somebody’s locked drawer. The imagery is simple, but it suits the song’s obsession with memory, myth, and the ghostly versions of ourselves we keep polishing. Watch the video for Golden Lore below: Based in New York City, John X Belmonte is an independent darkwave and post-punk artist drawn to the romantic and cinematic possibilities of gothic music. His work pairs brooding atmosphere with rhythmic urgency, giving beauty and emotional intensity equal room within its electronic arrangements. Released September 18, 2026, Golden Lore brings that sensibility to its examination of myth, memory, and remorse. Listen to Golden Lore on Spotify here. Follow John X. items.body: In my head I am not dead A breakup is rarely finished just because somebody has delivered the closing speech. There are still arguments to rehearse, streets to avoid, and a suspicious number of reasons to take the long way home. Madison, Wisconsin’s Whippets give that unfinished business a suitably unhealthy bounce on Not Dead, a song in which announcing “This is the end” does very little to stop the next bad idea. Premiering today, Not Dead previews the trio’s second album, No Skulls, due October 2, 2026, through Bobby Hussy’s No Coast label. With Hussy on guitar and vocals, Tyler Spatz on bass, and Hart Miller on drums, Whippets bring post-punk, grunge, and garage rock into a close, uncomfortable embrace, leaving plenty of room for deathrock’s theatrical appetites. A thick, ominous bass figure gets things moving before the drums cascade into a serpentine guitar hook, bringing a horror-film leer to the song’s garage abrasion. Hussy’s voice quivers and twists around the words, making private misery sound like something that might require an exorcist. The rhythm soon acquires an infectious bounce, with Spatz’s bass holding the floor beneath the guitar’s crooked turns and Miller’s mounting commotion. There is something of Dance with Me-era T.S.O.L. in this marriage of morbid theatre and physical release: music for pogoing through a personal catastrophe, with an ’80s post-punk chorus sharp enough to remember the following morning. The lyrics make repeated attempts to draw a line under the relationship. “This is the end” and “We are not friends” sound decisive enough, until the other admissions begin slipping through. The refrain’s insistence on being alive comes with a revealing qualification: “In my head.” That is where the old attachment continues to conduct its business, untouched by whatever has happened outside it. By the closing “No need to lie / I still drive by,” the brave farewell has become an unwanted return visit. Whippets give that contradiction a beat you can jump to, allowing the uglier implications to catch up between choruses. Hussy says: “Our new record, “No Skulls” is by far the best record I’ve ever recorded….and I’ve recorded a few at this point in my life. I’m very proud of both the songs and the production on this album. “Not Dead” is the second single from the album and it perfectly represents everything I love about this band: Sharp guitar riffs, hypnotic dirty bass lines that pivot in all the right places and drums that escalate frantically as needed. Catch us shredding this one out on tour in Europe!” No Skulls features ten tracks, recorded and mixed by Hussy, produced by Bert Roberts and Whippets, and mastered by Justin Perkins. The cover artwork is by Erin Sullivan. The album comes out October 2 on LP, CD, and digital formats, with the chartreuse-and-black swirl vinyl limited to 100 copies. Listen to Not Dead below and pre-order No Skulls here. No Skulls by Whippets Whippets introduced themselves with a 2022 seven-inch EP on Italy’s Goodbye Boozy, which sold out within a week, followed by their self-titled debut album on No Coast in 2024. Readers may remember Splinter, whose deathrock inclinations made an early case for the band’s particular chemistry. Their shared history reaches further back: Hussy and Spatz have both played in The Hussy and Cave Curse, and also work together in Wristwatch, while Miller’s past bands include Tenement, MDC, and Wartorn. That experience gives the trio a useful feel for how much disorder a memorable song can accommodate. Whippets take the No Skulls on the road this autumn, with October shows alongside Busey and Brüder and a November date supporting The Faint. A 23-date European tour follows in January and February 2027. See the upcoming itinerary below. items.album: NYC’s Some Days Are Darker Explore the Anatomy of Obsession in Video for “Memorize You”
items.excerpt: Love songs usually get nervous around obsession because nobody wants to admit how close the two can live together. Everybody likes devotion when it comes with flowers, candy, and clean shirts. Start remembering somebody’s freckles individually, and suddenly the room gets quieter. items.body: Love songs usually get nervous around obsession because nobody wants to admit how close the two can live together. Everybody likes devotion when it comes with flowers, candy, and clean shirts. Start remembering somebody’s freckles individually, and suddenly the room gets quieter. New York’s Some Days Are Darker explores that uneasy proximity on Memorize You, a song with the posture of romance and the blood pressure of somebody who has been awake far too long thinking about one person. Lear Mason sings, “I want to memorize you, your freckles and scars, the longing in your eyes, the rhythm of your heart,” and the sweetness of the line grows more complicated with each detail. There is love in there, certainly, but there is also the ancient human urge to pin beauty to the wall before it can leave. A thick, metallic bassline gives Memorize You its physical weight, while the drums tighten the tension and chiming synth melodies introduce a nervous sweetness. Mason’s croon carries the seductive assurance of early ’90s alternative rock, making even the most exposed confession sound as though it has been rehearsed for one particular listener. Around him, Chris Martin and Robbie Williamson build pressure through the interplay of bass, drums, guitars, and keyboards, gradually filling the space his voice initially leaves open. The arrangement gives the song’s gothic romanticism a muscular foundation, allowing its tenderness and possessiveness to press uncomfortably close together. What begins as an intimate confession grows into a feverish rush, increasingly expansive and overwhelming, until desire and desperation become difficult to separate. The largely black-and-white video gives this fixation a distinctly New York setting, following a woman through Washington Square Park and beneath its familiar marble arch. Daylight smiles and close-ups alternate with nighttime walks past illuminated storefronts, parked cars, and iron railings, while Mason sings to the camera in a tightly framed interior. The repeated attention to her face makes a visual counterpart to the lyrics, collecting expressions as though enough looking might finally amount to knowing someone. But a masked figure brings a more literal threat into view, and her glances over her shoulder become increasingly uneasy. That unease develops into a pursuit through the streets and into narrow basement corridors, where exposed pipes and bare walls replace the park’s open space. The closing switch to colour brings pursuer and pursued face to face: two women whose similar hair and red lipstick give the encounter the unsettling suggestion of a double. It is a fitting complication for a song so concerned with committing another person to memory, leaving the desire to recognize someone tangled up with the fear of what recognition might reveal. Watch the video for Memorize You below: Mason began Some Days Are Darker in 2019 as a solitary songwriting project after years playing metalcore guitar. It has since become a three-piece built around his chemistry with bassist, guitarist, and keyboardist Chris Martin and drummer, multi-instrumentalist, and producer Robbie Williamson. Between them, the musicians bring decades of experience to songs that draw on gothic grandeur, synth-driven alternative rock, and the charged intimacy of noir cinema. Their self-titled 2022 debut introduced a musical world in which longing can become obsession and physical closeness offers no guarantee against feeling alone. That combination has found a home on stages alongside The Chameleons, Vision Video, and House of Harm, with the trio also touring the US East Coast and Canada with Pink Turns Blue and the US West Coast with Theatre of Hate. Further East Coast dates are planned around the November release of their forthcoming album, Black Box Warning. Recorded with Dave Catching at Rancho de la Luna in Joshua Tree, California, Black Box Warning expands these concerns across twelve songs about desire and its consequences, making room for love, loss, lust, and the possibility of beginning again. The desert studio, whose visitors have included Iggy Pop, Queens of the Stone Age, and PJ Harvey, provides the setting for some of the band’s most intense and expansive material alongside its most exposed performances. A solo acoustic piece and a closing piano ballad extend the album’s emotional range, bringing the same difficult questions into quieter rooms. For Some Days Are Darker, the attraction lies in that uncertainty: whether giving yourself over to someone will bring you closer to life or further from yourself. Memorize You makes the surrender sound seductive enough to postpone the question. Learning someone by heart is a beautiful ambition; expecting the heart to survive the exercise unaltered is another matter. items.body: Seduction gets complicated when one person knows the future, and the other is still getting accustomed to being human. Geneva Jacuzzi takes that imbalance to an entertaining extreme on Nu2U, a song she described in a 2024 interview with The FADER as an encounter between a primordial being and a caveman. Sex comes with a preview of the centuries ahead, including the suffering humanity has yet to invent for itself. Some lovers bring emotional baggage; this one brings the entire future of civilization. The Los Angeles musician and multimedia artist now gives that peculiar proposition a theatrical setting in the video for Nu2U, taken from her third album, Triple Fire, released on Dais Records in August 2024. Produced by Jacuzzi with co-production from Josh da Costa, the track supplies an appropriately crooked dance floor for an encounter across the ages. Nu2U bubbles and clangs with eerie, clamorous synths and foot-stomping percussion, making a persuasive case for synth music for cavemen. The occasional, emphatic keyboard stabs have an unmistakably prehistoric character, placing the track in the same mischievous tribe as Toto Coelo’s “I Eat Cannibals,” but if they ate edibles instead of flesh. Beneath that primal stomp, an intricate, melodic bassline curls through the arrangement, deepening the groove and giving its heavy steps a supple, sensual movement. Jacuzzi’s cool delivery, evocative of Erotica-era Madonna, presides over the gathering with a shamanic poise, her voice suggesting secret knowledge passed between bodies. The whole thing acquires a ritualistic pull, as though the discovery of electricity has given an ancient fertility dance some intriguing new possibilities. Directed and edited by Jacuzzi, with cinematography and art direction by Shannon Cornett, the video places its performers inside a set that recreates a work by artist Steven Arnold. Costumes are credited to Stacy Ellen Rich and Jacuzzi, with lighting by Tom Nixon and Fred Joseph. The official video credits make clear how many hands went into this compact, extravagantly strange production. Jacuzzi presides over a miniature theatre of cutout flames, suspended shapes, spirals, and stars, wearing an enormous geometric headdress above a pale costume punctuated with black circles. Her painted face and deliberate gestures suggest a celestial hostess who has been repeating this demonstration for several thousand years. Around her, figures pose in sculpted torso pieces, metallic-looking body paint, and elaborate accessories, turning the human form into another decorative element in the set. Deep blue lighting gives way to hot pink, red, and green, while stark monochrome close-ups interrupt the wider tableaux. Faces fill the frame; arms lift and bend; a crescent becomes a frame within the frame. The visibly handmade scenery lends the spectacle the intimacy of a toy theatre, even when its inhabitants look capable of rearranging the cosmos. There is a lovely absurdity to the scale of it all: the future of humanity appears to be under discussion in a cabaret small enough to pack into a van. Watch the video for “Nu2U” below: That meeting of pop music, costume, and performance has long been central to Jacuzzi’s work. Following Lamaze and Technophelia, Triple Fire brought her songs into sharper focus while preserving their appetite for strange characters and exaggerated situations. With Nu2U, another of those characters gets a stage, a formidable hat, and a captive audience. Triple Fire is available through Dais Records and Bandcamp. Triple Fire by Geneva Jacuzzi Geneva Jacuzzi is set to perform at The Chapel in San Francisco on September 19, 2026. She will be joined by EX-HEIR, Diesel Dudes, and Nick Moss, who will also DJ. Doors open at 8 p.m., and the all-ages show starts at 9 p.m. Tickets are available here. items.body: alarm!systemen self-titled Antibody Belgian newcomer alarm!systemen’s debut LP has a range of sounds and approaches which often belies a lack of direction or aesthetic, but that’s definitely not the case here. At large, the ten tracks on offer draw from long histories of coldwave and dream pop, but eschew slavish adherence to lo-fi nostalgia for its own sake. The classic Slowdive-isms of “Goes Again” are offset by clean, if minimal modern programming, and later on album closer “Void” serves as a reminder of how that act and other shoegaze giants found new life lifting from ambient electronics at large. On the more direct side, “Kapot” juxtaposes bricked-out synthpop drum programming with excellently reverbed guitar, and the dead simple but wonderfully executed dream pop nod of “BURN” shows just how far some wistful melodies and airy production can take you when they’re done with a measure of taste and restraint. Written over the course of five years, it’s perhaps not surprising that there’s this much variety here, but alarm!systemen’s real forte is in pulling it all off well enough to refresh familiar styles and serve as an example of how younger acts drawn to these classic sounds can rework and rethink them in their own manner. alarm!systemen by alarm!systemen Zataar First Crush CRVSH While based in France, the material released by producer Zataar draws from both her Morrocan and Belgian heritage. From the latter, you funky rhythmic electronics that hearken back to the New Beat era with a healthy dose of classic body music, where the former comes through in the melodies and instrumentation that reference North African folk music. Cuts like “Ali Sawtek” lean into the blend especially well, finding a swinging groove in the bass and drum programming, while Zataar’s vocals and the track’s melody are kept low and swirling in the mix, with big string stabs cutting through the thick reverb. As a contrast, “In the Lights You Call My Name” injects polyrhythmic complexity into the drum track, its belchy resonant bassline flowing beneath rich waves of plucks and pads. The cleverness in the arrangements really comes through on “Moments in Love”, which manages transitions between deep house styled rhythm programming and sections of Chaabi folk melodies, before combining them smoothly into a hypnotic whole. Far from a gimmick, it’s a fully realized approach that recognizes the commonality and contrasts inherent in blending multiple styles and genres, and then reconciles them handily. items.body: Top Pick?Game Over – Face the End (2025)No, that's not a mistake. Nothing's really doing it this week. Once upon a time, a Carly Rae Jepsen double-abum would be cause for celebration, but not in September of 2026. Similarly, while I seemed to enjoy 2016's For All Kings a lot more than most, and while the new Anthrax album isn't as bad as its AI Babadook magician-laden promo cycle suggested it might be, it's still far from recommendable. The need for some better thrash had me looking in the direction of Italian thrashers Game Over, but their new one—while perfectly fine— isn't really all that either. However, I remember referring to last year's Face the End in our Discord as "the best Anthrax album in years", but never ended up actually writing about it anywhere, so I'm choosing to give it a belated highlight here, in lieu of any better options.Going back to it now, my assessment of the album still stands. New vocalist Danny Schiavina gives hints of both John Bush and Joey Belladonna and the riffs are about as righteous as you can hope for from a longrunning re-thrash band these days. The quality of Game Over's records has always hovered "decent but not exciting", but I'd say Face the End sits only behind Crimes Against Reality (2016) in their discography and is well worth a listen if you overlooked it last year, or—like me—are just looking for a good thrash fix. items.body: I’ll admit, the announcement of a new Uncle Acid and the deadbeats album hardly registered with me. It’s been a damn long while since I’ve had them in regular rotation, as I sorta fell off after 2015’s The Night Creeper. Not that that record really spoiled anything for me—it just didn’t seem to do anything that my favorites, Blood Lust and Mind Control, hadn’t already handled better. That said, it took almost a decade for them to catch my ear again, this time with the (respectfully) weird and adventurous detour of 2024’s mostly instrumental Nell’ Ora Blu. Its soundtrack-y, synth-forward nature showcased the group as genuinely astute mood-setters, even if it ultimately felt more suited to passive listening than the kind of record I’d actively return to. Still, it was enough to remind me that there’s something uniquely compelling about the way Uncle Acid and the deadbeats can set a tone—and maybe that I’d been a little too quick to give up on them.While their occult proto-metal contemporaries Ghost shapeshifted from similar stripped-down beginnings to achieve varying degrees of critical success and significant popularity, I’ve always felt that UA’s comparatively reserved, less immediately theatrical approach offered more potential. Where Ghost have increasingly embraced the spectacle and lore, UA hit me as less clownish and gimmicky, finding ways to be genuinely unsettling and music-focused without resorting to this razor-blade-in-my-Halloween-candy sort of Trojan-horsing Satan into pop music that everyone seems to find so clever. So I admit, I have a little rooting interest and bias here. Not that this guided my listening so much as brought to light an interesting contrast in how things just happen to shake out sometimes. I’m not passing judgment on either approach or trying to yuck anyone’s yums, I just find it curious how what seemed to be similar bands a decade-and-a-half ago have taken such different paths. Shapes Of Midnight by Uncle Acid and the deadbeats So, that leaves us with actually getting into Shapes Of Midnight and where UA find themselves in 2026. While some bands trickle in new flavors over time, their hard pivot on Nell’ Ora Blu, though head-scratching at the time, nicely paves the way for Shapes Of Midnight. Here, the analog synths and horns are again essential, coloring a more metal-forward (oh, we’re beyond proto-metal now, babes) sound while also establishing these textures as something utterly integral to the UA sound, making them sound fuller and more complete and compelling than ever.The title track is a prime example, delivering that signature UA haunted bounce, recalling one of my all-time faves from Mind Control, “Poison Apple,” here with synths lending a cosmic warmth akin to Zombi that significantly ups the ante on the spooky factor. This fuller, more robust sound enhances their more metallic edge on this go, even with some Thin Lizzy-esque harmonies and more nuanced, detailed songwriting. Still catchy as all get-out, thankfully, but structurally, Shapes Of Midnight has way more meat on its bones, earning every second on the record’s longer compositions. The melodies, while a strong point on previous records, are at full-tilt here in many forms. B-side opener “Psycho on the Loose” delivers a well-timed 80s metal gut- punch in the vein of Judas Priest with one of the best hooks of their entire discography. Similarly, “Don’t Let It Control You” finds a surfy, classic rock ‘n’ roll backbone where keys bang away, and yet again, the way things come together feels so right, not homage-y, schtick-y, or experimental, but rather that UA is just dripping in such rich horror and throwback atmosphere that the juxtaposition of these tracks doesn’t even make me flinch.The pieces they've put into motion and the world they’ve built over the last couple records feels like it’s fully realized here. “When Evil Wakes” gives the synths and horns even more room to shine, hitting this sort of Doors-y stride, even dipping toes in a pitch-black boogie before gathering steam and building to a Sabotage-era Black Sabbath peak where leads flirt and dance around one another, richly layered vocals froth up a hypnotic haze, acoustic guitars lend a metallic ring, and the bass and drums lock into a groove both nimble and rock solid. It’s an early highlight representative of their comfort, confidence, and vision. “The Other Side of the Sky” connects with another stellar metal hook, matching this buzzy, near-sci-fi synth with a cowbell-laden stomp that will satisfy Mountain fans. Bigger yet is “I Won’t Sleep (‘til You’re Gone)” which captures glam and psychedelia through a veil of sepia-tinged goth rock, boasting bombasts of horns that are as infectious as they are curious—it’s almost surprising there’s not an Iggy Pop guest spot on this track. It’s sassy, sultry, and downright chilling. (“We’ll be turning the soil while your bones start to boil on the stove”? Oof!) Again, the production is phenomenal, every element hits with clarity, power, and purpose. Truly and expertly orchestrated.Ultimately, Shapes Of Midnight offers a complete, well-rounded, and fully actualized version of the Uncle Acid we’ve all …kind of… heard before. The retro flavors are absolutely on point with the additional instrumentation, the songwriting is as sharp as ever, and the horror storytelling inspired by Poe’s The Masque of the Red Death offers depth and intrigue. It’s exactly what I didn’t know I had been waiting for, and by the time the oddly bluesy, almost Danzig-esque closer “Sleep No More” drives its artful and unnerving final nail in the coffin, Shapes Of Midnight has revealed itself as not just a fantastic record in its own right, but also as the culmination of years of harrowing work. (Un)Safe to say, the time to reconnect with your old Uncle Acid has never been better.

矢代秋雄のソナタとベートーヴェン「ソナタop.109」 ピアノ・ソナタ（1961） （田所） チケット申し込み： 朝日ホール・チケットセンター Tel. 03-3267-9990（日・祝除く10:00～18:00） https://www.asahi-hall.jp/hamarikyu/ticket/ 問い合わせ： 音楽之友社楽譜部 Tel. 03-3235-2135 近年演奏が話題となった演奏家 山田和樹 ～N響やバーミンガム市響で矢代作品を指揮して 「交響曲」は自筆譜で演奏させていただいたのですが、その筆致をよく見てみると、一音一音にすごく確信がある。 最初に指揮した矢代作品である「ピアノ協奏曲」（演奏：NHK交響楽団／ピアノ：河村尚子）や、昨年バーミンガム市響と「交響曲」を演奏したときのエピソードを交えて、矢代作品のオリジナリティについて語っている。（取材・文＝西村祐） 河村尚子 ～「ピアノ協奏曲」を二度演奏して ご自身がピアノの名手であったこともあり、「ピアノ協奏曲」でもピアニストに要求されるものがとても大きいのです。（中略）たくさんの音色を描いていかなければならない。 「ピアノ協奏曲」を指揮者の下野竜也さん、山田和樹さんと共演して以来、「ピアノ・ソナタ」や小品にも取り組むようになった河村さん。「ピアノ協奏曲」においては、繊細さをきわめるような情景から、暴力的でアグレッシヴなシーンまで、常に音色を変化させていかなければならない。その多彩さこそが矢代作品の特徴のひとつだという。 上村文乃 ～2025年に初演者だった堤剛さんの代奏をして （チェロ協奏曲は）チェロのレチタティーヴォ（朗唱）と歌が非常に印象的です。（中略）オリエンタルな空気を感じつつ、西洋的な美や趣きがあるように感じられます。 日本に勢いのあった1960年に作曲された「チェロ協奏曲」。その時代性へ思いを寄せ、矢代と同級生である黛敏郎の無伴奏チェロ作品《BUNRAKU》を引き合いに出しながら、作品の魅力や音のつくりかたの細部などに言及している。   堤剛さんの弾く「チェロ協奏曲」が収録されたアルバム 矢代秋雄の関連本 「音楽の友」2026年10月号（9月18日発売）。特別企画として「没後50年記念 矢代秋雄の世界」を掲載 飾らず率直に綴られた、みずみずしい息吹を味わえる矢代秋雄の名エッセイ集 矢代秋雄 特設ページ 関連記事「ヨーロッパとのはてしない距離──矢代秋雄の孤独」

items.excerpt: 2026.09.18 海外クラシックNEWS～from アメリカ 海外のクラシック界のニュースやコンサート、オペラ公演の様子を、現地在住の筆者がいちはやくお届け。今回はアメリカの8月の音楽シーンから、ニューヨークで行われた公演をレポートします。 小林伸太郎 Shintaro Kobayashi 音楽ライター ニューヨークのクラシック音楽エージェント、エンタテインメント会社勤務を経て、クラシック音楽を中心としたパフォーミング・アーツ全般について執筆、日本の戯曲の英訳も手掛け... 詳しく見る 音楽の友 編集部 月刊誌 1941年12月創刊。音楽之友社の看板雑誌「音楽の友」を毎月刊行しています。“音楽の深層を知り、音楽家の本音を聞く”がモットー。今月号のコンテンツはこちらバックナンバ... 詳しく見る ウクライナ・フリーダム・オーケストラが8月25日と26日、リンカーン・センターのデイヴィッド・ゲフェン・ホールで演奏会を行った。同団は、ウクライナ国内のオーケストラ所属メンバーやウクライナ国外に逃れた音楽家らをメンバーとして、ロシアのウクライナ侵攻に対する反応として、2022年にウクライナ系
items.body: 2026.09.18 海外クラシックNEWS～from アメリカ 海外のクラシック界のニュースやコンサート、オペラ公演の様子を、現地在住の筆者がいちはやくお届け。今回はアメリカの8月の音楽シーンから、ニューヨークで行われた公演をレポートします。 小林伸太郎 Shintaro Kobayashi 音楽ライター ニューヨークのクラシック音楽エージェント、エンタテインメント会社勤務を経て、クラシック音楽を中心としたパフォーミング・アーツ全般について執筆、日本の戯曲の英訳も手掛け... 詳しく見る 音楽の友 編集部 月刊誌 1941年12月創刊。音楽之友社の看板雑誌「音楽の友」を毎月刊行しています。“音楽の深層を知り、音楽家の本音を聞く”がモットー。今月号のコンテンツはこちらバックナンバ... 詳しく見る ウクライナ・フリーダム・オーケストラが8月25日と26日、リンカーン・センターのデイヴィッド・ゲフェン・ホールで演奏会を行った。同団は、ウクライナ国内のオーケストラ所属メンバーやウクライナ国外に逃れた音楽家らをメンバーとして、ロシアのウクライナ侵攻に対する反応として、2022年にウクライナ系カナダ人指揮者、ケリー＝リン・ウィルソンによって結成された。 以来、ウクライナの文化とレジリエンスを世界に示し、犠牲者を追悼するとともに平和を訴えることを目的とするという同団は、夏のオフシーズンを中心に活動を続けている。いまだに停戦の明確な兆しは見出されないなか、この8月に行われた欧米ツアーには、「2026年インヴィンシブル（無敵）・ツアー」と、かなり直接的な名称が与えられている。 設立当初から同団には広報から芸術面までメトロポリタン歌劇場（MET）が深くかかわっており、METは昨シーズンの公演プログラム冊子にも、毎回ウクライナ支持のメッセージを掲載した。ポーランド国立歌劇場やウクライナ文化省も協力し、2023年以来、ウクライナ大統領夫人オレナ・ゼレンスカの後援を得ているという。 そのような背景を意識せずとも、民族的なつながりが感じられるメンバーの顔、演奏が終わったあとに抱き合ってお互いを讃えあう姿などに、このアンサンブルの成り立ちが特殊であり、特別であることが感じられる。 はたしてウィルソン率いる同団の演奏は、一糸乱れぬアンサンブルというわけではないものの、全体として柔軟なつながりで聴かせる魅力的なものだった。 ウィルソンはニューヨーク・フィルハーモニックからNHK交響楽団まで、すでにさまざまなオーケストラとシンフォニー指揮者としての経験を積んでいるが、少なくともニューヨークでは、これまでオペラ指揮者としての印象のほうが強かったように思う。 しかし25日に演奏されたベートーヴェン「交響曲第7番」では、同曲のような人気交響曲でも豊かな音色を聴かせるダイナミックな統率力が印象的だった。最終楽章は現代の演奏らしく猛烈に速いテンポだが、疾走感が持続して息切れするところがなく、爽快だ。 もっとも8月25日の最大の呼び物は、休憩前に演奏されたリーゼ・ダーヴィドセンがソリストのR.シュトラウス《4つの最後の歌》であった。今回のツアーはヨーロッパ5都市とニューヨークを回るものだったが、ヨーロッパ5都市ではダーヴィドセンは登場せず、曲も別のものとなっている。彼女の登場が実現したのは、彼女とMETのつながりが深いことに加え、9月のシーズン初日にヴェルディ《マクベス》でマクベス夫人を歌うため、たまたまニューヨークに滞在していたためと思われる。 ダーヴィドセンの歌は、言葉一つひとつのニュアンスを枝葉末節にこだわって抽出するより、真正面からたゆたうように聴かせる。その現代随一の声の力があってこその表現であり、年齢を重ねることによる解釈の深まりを予感させる余裕も感じさせてくれた。ウィルソンの指揮も、そんなダーヴィドセンの現在の美点を支える推進力のあるものだった。 ウクライナ・フリーダム・オーケストラのヴェルディ「レクイエム」から（8月26日、デイヴィッド・ゲフェン・ホール）© Richard Termine / Met Opera 8月26日にはヴェルディ「レクイエム」が演奏された。ここでは何よりも、METの合唱団メンバーによって構成されたMETコーラス・アーティスツの好演が印象的で、冒頭から最後まで緊張感を保ちながらも柔らかに深く響いた合唱は、この日最大の立役者であった。 METの中堅的存在であるアイリーン・ペレス（S）とソロマン・ハワード（Bs）に加え、ナタリー・ルイス（Ms）、ルネ・バルベラ（T）らソリストの歌唱も安定感のあるもので、とりわけペレスの声と歌唱は、現在のMETの水準を表すものとして興味深いものだった。 ウィルソンの指揮も、よく指摘されるこの曲のオペラ的なダイナミックさを抽出したものだった。そしてそのダイナミックさは、現代の戦争に対する恐怖と怒りにふさわしく感じられるもので、全体を鎮魂曲としてインスパイアされるものにしていた。 ちなみに両日とも冒頭にはウクライナ人作曲家の作品が演奏され、25日はマクシム・コロミレツ（1981年生まれ）の《The Mothers of Kherson》（ヘルソンの母たち）からの組曲が、26日にはボフダナ・フロリャク（1968年生まれ）の《グローリア》が演奏された。そしてアンコールとして最後には、弦楽曲として編曲されたウクライナ国歌が美しく演奏された。

東京藝術大学大学院修士課程（音楽学）修了。東京医科歯科大学非常勤講師。オペラを中心に雑誌やWEB、書籍などで文筆活動を展開するほか、社会人講座やカルチャーセンターの講... 詳しく見る 『ドン・ジョヴァンニ』あらすじ 欲望のままに自由に生きるドン・ジョヴァンニは、若く魅力にあふれた貴族。ある夜、忍び込んだ邸宅で騎士長の娘ドンナ・アンナに抵抗され、父の騎士長を刺殺。アンナやその婚約者オッターヴィオらに追われても、放蕩をやめない。ついに亡き騎士長の石像に悔い改めることを迫られるが、拒否し地獄に堕ちてゆく。 ドン・ジョヴァンニの放蕩な生き様に翻弄される周囲の人々の心情や人間の欲望と倫理の狭間が、モーツァルトの美しくも劇的な音楽で描き出される。 モーツァルト作品の難しさと面白さ ——生田さんは今回が3回目のオペラ演出ということですが、そもそもオペラとの出会いは何だったのでしょうか。 生田 私がオペラを演出したいと思ったきっかけは、2010年から14年にびわ湖ホールが主催したペーター・コンヴィチュニーのワークショップでした。モーツァルト作品に取り組み、コンヴィチュニーさんから“スコアに全部書いてある”と学びました。モーツァルトの音楽は繰り返しが多いので、同じ音楽でどう変化をつけるかを戦略的に考えているところはとても勉強になりました。 園田 確かに、オペラを観たことがない人にとって、モーツァルトの音楽は繰り返しが多いし、人物も入り組んでいるのでわかりにくいところがあるかもしれません。でもモーツァルト作品の奥深さは、謎解きのような面白さで、名曲が随所に散りばめられ、世界中で長く愛され続けています。 生田みゆき（演出） 文学座所属、演劇ユニット「理性的な変人たち」メンバー。東京藝術大学大学院音楽研究科修士課程修了。 ドイツ文化センターの文化プログラムの語学奨学金（芸術分野対象）を得てドイツに滞在。『占領の囚人たち』『海戦 2023』『屠殺人ブッチャー』にて第31回読売演劇大賞優秀演出家賞、『占領の囚人たち』ほかで芸術選奨文部科学大臣新人賞を受賞。 園田隆一郎（指揮、フォルテピアノ） 2006年、シエナのキジアーナ夏季音楽週間《トスカ》を指揮してデビュー。翌年、藤原歌劇団《ラ・ボエーム》を指揮して日本デビューを果たす。その後、国内外のオペラへの出演、オーケストラとの共演を重ね、オペラ、シンフォニーの両分野で活躍する指揮者の一人。パシフィックフィルハーモニア東京 指揮者。藤沢市民オペラ芸術監督。 ドン・ジョヴァンニの人物像 ——そんなモーツァルト作品の中でも、『ドン・ジョヴァンニ』は比較的わかりやすいと思います。なにしろドン・ジョヴァンニがめちゃくちゃ魅力的です。 生田 今回演出するにあたって過去のプロダクションをいくつか観たのですが、強く印象に残ったのは、ドン・ジョヴァンニがどういう人かというよりも、ドン・ジョヴァンニの周りの人たちの生き方でした。 近くに露悪的な人がいるといろいろな意味で気になりますよね、彼に惹かれてしまう人もいれば嫌悪感を抱く人もいます。逸脱した彼によって自分も自由になれるところもあるけれど、やっぱりついていけないところもある。周囲の喜びと辛さを描けたら、そこからドン・ジョヴァンニ像が浮かび上がってくるのではないかと考えています。 園田 僕はドン・ジョヴァンニに100%共感できないんですけど（笑）、彼が鏡のような存在だというのはよくわかります。周りがどういう反応をするかによって、ドン・ジョヴァンニの人物像が見えてくる。 それともうひとつ、これは音楽的に言えることなのですが、ドン・ジョヴァンニが誰と対峙しているかによって、音楽がガラリと変わっているんです。相手によって態度を変える、そういう社会性が身についているのが彼の特徴だと思います。 善悪を超越したカリスマが放つ熱を表現したいと語る、ドン・ジョヴァンニ役の池内響（写真右）と大久保惇史（写真左）。二者二様の熱とたたずまいからも魅力がにじみ出るドン・ジョヴァンニに心奪われる。 キーワードは「逸脱」 ——今、生田さんから「逸脱」というキーワードが出てきましたが、ドン・ジョヴァンニは当時の貴族としても異質な人だったのでしょうか。 生田 園田さんのおっしゃることにつながりますが、彼は人が欲しい言葉をひじょうに上手に与えられる人物だと思うんです。もちろんそれはその場しのぎかもしれませんが、相手がもっとも欲している言葉を瞬時に理解して、的確に言える能力があるんですね。 園田 たとえばドンナ・エルヴィーラとの場面で、彼女も気持ちを吐き出したいだろうからとちゃんと言わせてあげる。「あなた、今怒りたいんですよね、私の悪いところを言いたいですよね」と相手の求めるものを察知して与えているのではないでしょうか。ドン・ジョヴァンニほどの男性であれば、あの場を丸く収めるなんて簡単なことなのに、敢えて怒らせる、吐き出させる。それはやっぱり普通じゃない、かなり「逸脱」した人物だったと思います。 演劇とオペラの違い ——生田さんは普段は演劇の演出を手がけていらっしゃいますが、オペラの演出との違いはどこにあるとお考えですか。 生田 演出の組み立て方が全然違いますね。演劇では、最初の1週間はセリフのテンポ感を共有する作業があるのですが、オペラではそこはもうある程度決まっているので。 園田 その前に音楽稽古もありますしね。でも、そういう決まってしまっている状況は嫌だな、と思うことはありませんか？ 生田 いやいや、それはないです（笑）マエストロもいらっしゃいますし、歌手の方もその作品を何度も演じていて理解度が深い場合が多いですし。オペラの演出は、マエストロや歌手の意向を汲み取りながら、パズルのように最適解を考える作業になります。音楽の制約を制約と考えず、その中での自由を探して楽しむのが醍醐味だと思います。 初めてオペラを観る人にも楽しんでほしい ——11月10日から13日に中高生のための芸術鑑賞教室「日生劇場オペラ教室2026」もありますが、オペラを初めて観る方にメッセージをいただけますか。 生田 私は高校時代は演劇部に所属していて、オペラを観る機会がなかったのですが、その後大学時代にワンコインで聴けるコンサートで初めてオペラに接して、そこで面白いなと思ってオペラ公演に通うようになりました。初めて劇場に来る前に、少しだけでも予習してきてもらうといいかなと思います。 園田 中高生の鑑賞教室にご参加の方は、日生劇場では毎回事前学習教材を作っているので、それを利用してくださるのもありがたいです。一般のお客様も、今はインターネットで映像を観られるので、アリアを1曲でも聴いておくと、劇場に来たときに「あ、これ知ってる！」と興味が湧くのではないでしょうか。 写真左から、生田みゆき（演出）、池内響（ドン・ジョヴァンニ）、大久保惇史（ドン・ジョヴァンニ）、園田隆一郎（指揮、フォルテピアノ）。四人が組み上げる『ドン・ジョヴァンニ』の新しい世界に期待が高まる。 11月14日（土）・15日（日）NISSAY OPERA 2026『ドン・ジョヴァンニ』 公演情報 NISSAY OPERA 2026『ドン・ジョヴァンニ』全2幕 items.album: 【ARBAN WEEKLY／今週の話題まとめ】ソニー・ロリンズとコルトレーン、唯一の共演盤に耳を澄ます
items.excerpt: 今週は、二人の巨人が一度きり交わした共演盤の再発から、101歳のサックス奏者が今なお更新し続ける現在進行形の音楽まで、時間の幅そのものがテーマになるようなニュースが並んだ。ジャズという文化が抱える「継続」の意味を、それぞれの記事から読み解きたい。 1956年、一度きりの夜—ロリンズとコルトレーンの共演盤が甦る Jazz Journal UKの新譜コラムに、ソニー・ロリンズとジョン・コルトレーンの唯一の共演を収めた録音『Tenor Madness』（1956年）のリイシュー情報が上がっている。二人は1956年、まだそれぞれが自身のスタイルを確立しきる前の時期に一度だけ同じセッションに立ち会った。これが二人の唯一知られている共演録音である。 この一枚が特別なのは、単に「二大テナーの共演」という肩書きのためではない。ロリンズとコルトレーンはその後、それぞれ全く異なる道をたどったことがジャズ史ではよく知られている。一般に、ロリンズはテーマを掘り下げる即興、コルトレーンはモード・ジャズを経てスピリチュアル・ジャズへと向かったとされる。まだ分岐する前の一夜の記録として、聴き直す価値がある一枚だと言
items.body: 今週は、二人の巨人が一度きり交わした共演盤の再発から、101歳のサックス奏者が今なお更新し続ける現在進行形の音楽まで、時間の幅そのものがテーマになるようなニュースが並んだ。ジャズという文化が抱える「継続」の意味を、それぞれの記事から読み解きたい。 1956年、一度きりの夜—ロリンズとコルトレーンの共演盤が甦る Jazz Journal UKの新譜コラムに、ソニー・ロリンズとジョン・コルトレーンの唯一の共演を収めた録音『Tenor Madness』（1956年）のリイシュー情報が上がっている。二人は1956年、まだそれぞれが自身のスタイルを確立しきる前の時期に一度だけ同じセッションに立ち会った。これが二人の唯一知られている共演録音である。 この一枚が特別なのは、単に「二大テナーの共演」という肩書きのためではない。ロリンズとコルトレーンはその後、それぞれ全く異なる道をたどったことがジャズ史ではよく知られている。一般に、ロリンズはテーマを掘り下げる即興、コルトレーンはモード・ジャズを経てスピリチュアル・ジャズへと向かったとされる。まだ分岐する前の一夜の記録として、聴き直す価値がある一枚だと言える。 同コラムでは他にも、スピリチュアルジャズ系五重奏やヘンリー・パーセル解釈作、サティをめぐるトランスアトランティック・トリオ、ユセフ・ラティーフへのトリビュート盤が紹介されている。まずはこのロリンズ×コルトレーン盤を軸に、ジャズ史の “ある分岐点” を聴き直す機会として楽しみたい。 出典：https://jazzjournal.co.uk/2026/09/13/new-releases-august-september-2026-r-s 101歳、いまも更新される音——マーシャル・アレンの新作 UK Jazz Newsが、101歳のサックス奏者マーシャル・アレンによる新作『101 – an Audio Odyssey』をレビューしている。アレンはサン・ラ・アルケストラの長年のメンバーとして半世紀以上を過ごしてきた人物で、サン・ラの没後はアレンがバンドを率いる立場になった。 サン・ラが説いた「宇宙」という主題は、しばしば神秘主義や奇矯なパフォーマンスの側面ばかりが語られがちだが、その根にあったのは既存の音楽語法・楽器編成・演奏形態そのものを問い直す姿勢だった。 アレンが101歳になった今もアルバムを作り続けているという事実は、その姿勢が個人の意志を超えて、ひとつの音楽的伝統として続いていることを示している。ジャズ史の生き証人がまだ現役で鳴らしている、という一点だけでも記録に値するニュースである。 出典：https://ukjazznews.com/marshall-allen-101-an-audio-odyssey グレッチェン・パーラト新作をガーディアン紙が賞賛 ジャズシンガーのグレッチェン・パーラトによる最新作『The Wise Ones』を、ガーディアン紙の評者ジョン・フォーダムが今月のジャズ・アルバムとして取り上げた。 本作では、フォークロックやジャズの影響を受けたマルチインストゥルメンタリストのアラン・ハンプトンや、パーカッショニストである夫のマーク・ジュリアナといった長年のパートナーに加え、ロバート・グラスパー、ミシェル・ンデゲオチェロ、ベッカ・スティーブンスといったゲストミュージシャンが参加している。 出典：https://www.theguardian.com/music/2026/sep/11/gretchen-parlato-the-wise-ones-review チャールス・ロイド、インドとの対話を続ける理由 ジャズの長老チャールス・ロイドが、インド古典音楽の伝統との交錯を試みるプロジェクト「Sangam」の新作『Sangam & Friends』を発表した。Sangamは2004年から継続的に取り組まれてきたロイドのライフワークのひとつであり、今作でも複数の文化的背景を持つミュージシャンとの共演が展開されている。 ロイドはこれまでも、ジャズという語法の外側にある音楽的伝統との対話を繰り返し試みてきた奏者である。老境に差し掛かってなお、その探究を止めない姿勢は、ジャズという音楽が本来持っていた「異なるものを取り込みながら形を変え続ける」性質を体現しているとも言える。 出典：https://www.jazzthing.de/review/charles-lloyd-sangam-and-friends 投稿 【ARBAN WEEKLY／今週の話題まとめ】ソニー・ロリンズとコルトレーン、唯一の共演盤に耳を澄ます は ARBAN に最初に表示されました。

items.body: 高知県立美術館で学芸員として働く筆者の専門は日本の現代美術だが、扱う作家や作品の多くは日本国内にあり、これまで仕事で海外と関わる機会は限られていた。それが、ここ数年でにわかに事情が変わった。仕事を通じて海外、とりわけアメリカとの接点が生まれた。昨年はニューヨークとロサンゼルスを訪れた結果、ふたつの都市のあまりの違いに、30代も半ばを過ぎて、久しぶりに大きなカルチャーショックを受けた。そして、もう少しアメリカを見てみたいという思いが育ちはじめた。 ピッツバーグへの関心 アメリカの地方都市におけるアートシーンとはいかなるものなのか。そんなことを考えていた頃、ペンシルヴァニア州ピッツバーグという街が視野に入ってきた。ニューヨークとシカゴの間に位置するピッツバーグは、周辺地域まで含めれば人口は約240万人。市域人口に絞ると約30万人で、筆者が暮らす高知市とほぼ同規模だ。いわゆる大都市ではない。 関心をもつきっかけとなったのは、1896年に始まった北米最長の歴史ある国際展「カーネギー・インターナショナル」の存在だった。ヴェネツィア・ビエンナーレ創設の翌年から、世界各地の現代美術をピッツバーグに紹介し続けている。 国際的な現代美術のコンテクストと、そこに暮らす人々の生活はどこで接続するのか。あるいは、接続しないのか。近年、日本でも国際芸術祭が相次ぐなか、ひとつの土地で100年以上にわたり国際展が続くとはどういうことなのかが気になった。 そのような折、学芸員を対象とする海外研修の助成を得て、この7月にピッツバーグを訪れる機会に恵まれた。 ピッツバーグの風景。中央にそびえるのは、ピッツバーグ大学の象徴であり、街を代表するランドマークのひとつ「学びの聖堂（Cathedral of Learning）」［筆者撮影］ カーネギー・インターナショナル この国際展を理解するには、その主会場となるカーネギー美術館の歴史から見ておく必要があるだろう。仕掛け人は、鉄鋼王アンドリュー・カーネギー（1835-1919）。鉄鋼業で莫大な財を築いたカーネギーは、1895年、ピッツバーグにカーネギー・インスティテュートを設立した★1。 カーネギーは、自身のコレクションを美術館に寄贈して充実させるのではなく、展覧会の開催を通して美術館が作品を収集していくという構想を抱いた。同時代の優れた美術を世界から集めて展覧会を開き、そこから作品を購入する──そのために翌1896年に始まったのが、現在の「カーネギー・インターナショナル」へと続く年1回の年次展である。 以来130年、過去のインターナショナルから収蔵された作品は520点を超える。日本の美術家との関わりも深い。たとえば、20世紀初頭に岡山から単身渡米した画家の国吉康雄は、1931年から52年にかけて、現在のカーネギー・インターナショナルへと連なる年次展に17回出品している。そのほか主要なところでは、草間彌生、井上有一、猪熊弦一郎、桂ゆき、河原温、宮島達男、杉本博司といった作家が参加してきた。そして今回の第59回展には、画家の杉原玲那と、いけばなを軸に彫刻や書など多岐にわたる領域で制作した勅使河原蒼風、そして彼が創始したいけばなの流派「草月流」の作品が出品されている。 第59回カーネギー・インターナショナル「If the word we」 世界各地から61組の作家・コレクティブが参加する第59回展のタイトルは「If the word we（もし、私たちという言葉が）」。解説によると、「we＝私たち」を単一で固定された集団ではなく、異なる者同士がともに存在し、互いに耳を傾け合うための、複雑で開かれた関係として捉えているという。筆者が美術館を訪れた際には、本展のキュレーターのひとり、ライアン・イノウエ（Ryan Inouye）さんの案内を受けながら、会場を巡ることができた。 会場入口の風景［筆者撮影］ 入口にあたる、美術館1階から2階へと続く吹き抜けの空間では、渦を巻くようにたわめられた無数の竹を用いたダイナミックなインスタレーションが来場者を迎える。日本人として馴染みのある素材とその風合いが目に入った瞬間、それが草月流の「いけばな」だとわかった。 会場でいくつか気になった作品を挙げてみよう。 色とりどりのテキスタイルが森のように上下へ張り巡らされた《Tewok: the river we weave》は、アルゼンチン北部の先住民族ウィチ（Wichí）の女性たちによるコレクティブ、シラット（Silät）が織り上げたものだ。100人を超える織り手が関わりながらも、そこに繰り返し現われる形やパターンからは、個人を超えて受け継がれてきた共有知の存在がうかがえる。 また、中国のアーティスト、ジャオ・ヤオによる、卵の殻を用いた繊細でミニマルな絵画のシリーズは、一見すると同規格の均質な画面が並んでいるように見える。だが近づいてみると、用いられた卵殻の色やひび割れの違いによって、画面ごとの微細な差異が浮かび上がる。 広大な彫刻ホールでは、巨大な緑のカーペットが視界いっぱいに広がる。ブラジルの国家権力の中枢である連邦議会に敷かれていたカーペットを参照して、シンシア・マルセル（Cinthia Marcelle）が手掛けた大規模インスタレーション《Green Hall Annex》である。カーペットの裏面には外交や移民をめぐる新聞記事や資料が配され、ブラジルという国家がそうした問題をいかに語ってきたのかを壮大な構造体として身体的に体感させる。 一方で、杉原玲那と勅使河原蒼風の作品は、異なる角度からこの展覧会に生気を与えていた。褐色を基調とする杉原の絵画は、粘度のある筆致による臓器のようなモチーフが不穏な気配を醸し出す。それらと連続する空間に、勅使河原の大規模な木彫《八雲》をはじめとする作品群が置かれることで、双方の有機的な形態が呼応しているように思われた。移動や離散、植民地主義、共同体、信仰、記憶──政治や歴史をめぐる重厚な主題が繰り返し現われ、作家の出自や作品のコンテクストへと意識を向けさせる本展にあって、ここでは色や形そのものに目を凝らし、しばし息をつくことができた。 カーネギー・インターナショナルの展示風景（シラット）［筆者撮影］ カーネギー・インターナショナルの展示風景（ジャオ・ヤオ）［筆者撮影］ カーネギー・インターナショナルの展示風景（シンシア・マルセル）［筆者撮影］ カーネギー・インターナショナルの展示風景（杉原玲那）［筆者撮影］ コレクションとの差異 他方、会場では「カーネギー・インターナショナルはこちら」という動線案内が至る所にあるのが目につく。なぜなら、美術館全体が国際展の特設会場となっているのではなく、コレクションと国際展の展示エリアとが入り組んでいるからだ。つまり、国際展とコレクション展示とが完全に切り離されるわけではなく、壁一枚を挟んで併存している。両者の絶妙な距離感は、筆者がこれまで訪れた展覧会では経験したことのないものだった。 常設のコレクション・ギャラリーでは、所蔵品を「継承」「市場」「土地」といった複数のテーマから読み直す展示が展開されていた。例を挙げると、「カーネギー・インターナショナルの歴史」と題されたセクションでは、過去のこのシリーズに出品され、その後カーネギー美術館に収蔵された作品群が壁を埋め尽くしている。ゲルハルト・リヒターやブルース・ナウマンといった日本でもよく知られた巨匠から、香月泰男や岡田謙三といった日本人作家まで、多様な作品がひしめく空間は圧巻だ。定期的に国際展を開き、作品を購入し続けてコレクションを育ててきたからこそ生まれる、日本の美術館ではなかなか見ることのできない風景だった。 もうひとつ興味深かったのが、コレクション展示と今回のインターナショナルとのあいだに横たわる、ある種の差異である。コレクション・ギャラリーで展示されている作品は、遠目でも作者名が識別できる有名作家が少なくない。ところが今回のインターナショナルでは、ジャオ・ヤオや杉原玲那、勅使河原蒼風、そして草月財団を除けば、筆者にとってほとんどが初見の作家だった。もちろん、それは偶然ではない。 「we」が示すもの 出品作家の顔ぶれには、本展が掲げる「we」の考え方がよく表われている。アジア、中東、アフリカ、中南米をはじめ、従来の欧米中心のアートワールドからは見えにくかった地域で活動する作家が数多く参加している。また、キャプションの作家プロフィールには、先住民族や土地との関係が明記されている例も目につく。たとえば、アメリカとカナダにまたがる、先住民族による連邦「ハウデノサウニー★2」の芸術と文化を長年にわたり支えてきたG・ピーター・ジェミソン（G. Peter Jemison）の紹介はこのようにはじまる。 セネカ族、ヘロン・クラン。1945年、ニューヨーク州シルバー・クリーク生まれ／ニューヨーク州ヴィクター在住。 基本的な作家紹介の段階から、国家や都市名だけでは捉えきれない帰属や土地との関係を可視化しようとするキュレーションの、あるいは美術館運営の意思が表われている。 もっとも、正直にいえば、こうしたプロフィールは決して読みやすくはない。見慣れない民族名や土地の呼称を前に、何度も立ち止まり、Google翻訳を立ち上げることになる。しかし、その「わからなさ」自体が、自分がこれまでどのような地理や分類の仕方に慣れ親しんできたのかを逆照射するようでもあった。 カーネギー・インターナショナルの展示風景（G・ピーター・ジェミソン）［筆者撮影］ ピッツバーグのアートシーン では、130年にわたって国際展が続いてきたこの街には、どのようなアートシーンが育っているのだろうか。実のところ、カーネギー・インターナショナルという老舗国際展が100年以上にわたって継続的に開催され、アンディ・ウォーホル美術館、マットレス・ファクトリーといった有力な施設が存在する一方、ピッツバーグには現代アートに特化したコマーシャルギャラリーは意外なほど少ない。 カーネギー美術館から徒歩10分ほど。現代美術ギャラリーのROMANCEはそのうちのひとつだ。筆者は東京のギャラリーMisako & Rosenから紹介を受け、ROMANCEのギャラリスト、マーガレット・クロス（Margaret Kross）さんに話を聞く機会を得た。 折しも開催されていたグループ展「details to follow」は、第59回カーネギー・インターナショナルの開幕にあわせて企画されたものだった。この展覧会は、Misako & Rosen──カーネギー・インターナショナル出品作家の杉原玲那も所属している──、ジャカルタのROH、ソウルのWhistleなど、各地のギャラリーとの共同展であり、まさに国際展をきっかけに生まれた交流の一例といえる。元診療所を改装した待合室のようなROMANCEの展示空間には、サイズこそ小さいものが多いが、そうして世界から集結した絵画、映像、立体といったさまざまな形態の作品が並んでいた。 ROMANCEの入口［筆者撮影］ 「details to follow」の展示風景［筆者撮影］ マーガレットさんによれば、主要なギャラリーや展示施設が集まる大都市とピッツバーグとの接続は、決して十分ではない。だからこそ、自分たちのようなギャラリーが、アーティストを外へとつなぐ「conduit（導管）」、あるいは「feeder（送り出す経路）」になりたい──そうした言葉が、とりわけ筆者には印象に残った。 4年に一度のカーネギー・インターナショナルが開かれると、キュレーターやコレクター、アーティストが街を訪れ、ピッツバーグのアートシーンには活気が生まれる。しかし、その合間には、停滞とまではいわずとも、凪いだ時間が訪れる。一度起こったエネルギーを次の国際展までどう持続させるかも、地元のギャラリーが向き合う課題のひとつだという。 マーガレットさんに紹介されて訪れたギャラリーのApril Aprilでも、よく似た問題意識を聞くことができた。共同運営者のひとり、ルーカス・レガッツィ（Lucas Regazzi）さんは、「多くのvisibility（可視性）が大都市に集中する一方、小都市にも、本当に面白く刺激的な場所になる可能性はある」と話した。ただし、そのためには「少し庭仕事が必要。種を蒔くようなもの」なのだという。 こうした話は、日本の地方都市にも重なる部分があるように思われる。国際展によって一時的に多くの人や作品が行き交うことと、その土地に持続的なアートシーンが生まれることは同義ではない。外からもたらされる刺激を受け止め、作家を地域の外へとつなぎ、次の機会までその動きを絶やさずにいること。それが何よりも難しい。ピッツバーグで見聞きした風景は、筆者自身にとっても、決して他人事ではなかった。 ピッツバーグでのリサーチにあたり、ライアン・イノウエさん、ジョン・テイン（John Tain）さん、ダン・リアーズ（Dan Leers）さん、マーガレット・クロスさん、ルーカス・レガッツィさん、ローゼン美沙子さん、ジェフリー・ローゼンさんをはじめ、多くの方々にご協力いただきました。ここに記して御礼申し上げます。 ★1──現在、カーネギー美術館は、カーネギー自然史博物館、アンディ・ウォーホル美術館、カミン・サイエンス・センターとともに、Carnegie Museums of Pittsburghを構成する4館のひとつである。 ★2──北アメリカの先住民のひとつで、おもにイロコイ語系の部族から構成されていることからイロコイ連邦ともいう。 “If the word we” 59th Carnegie items.body: Our third iteration of the " Sculpting Silence " series, brings us to France, for a trio with Alexandra Grimal on saxophones, voice, harmonium, nōkan, shakuhachi, Naoto Yamagishi on percussions and Alexandre Saada on piano and harmonium. The title, Marée Basse , is French for “low tide”: the moment when the sea withdraws, leaving behind a wide, empty stretch of beach scattered with shells, tiny creatures, and fragments the waves have carried ashore. The music evokes much the same landscape. It takes this open space for granted, allowing the notes of saxophone, piano, and percussion to appear sparsely, sometimes only for brief moments before disappearing again. All three musicians are minimalists, deeply attentive to the overall sound yet reluctant to impose themselves upon it, as though the tones themselves should determine whether, and when, they wish to interact. Every sound feels tender and fragile, unobtrusive and gentle—and often completely absent. Silence is not merely the space between the notes; it is an essential part of the music itself. This is particularly striking in the thirty-minute second track, where, roughly halfway through, there is almost a full minute of near silence, with only faint crackling sounds barely audible in the background. When the music gradually returns, the instrumentation has subtly shifted: the harmonium introduces a handful of sustained tones, joined by Grimal's wordless singing, equally elongated and sensitive. Towards the end of the piece, the sound becomes fuller and more agitated, as though a sudden gust of wind were stirring the waves and awakening the distant cries of seagulls. Once again, silence plays an essential role in this music, much as it does in Japanese art, which has fascinated Grimaldi in recent years. Here, absence is not a lack but a presence of its own—a space in which the smallest sounds can emerge, linger for a moment, and then quietly disappear. Enjoy! Listen and download from Bandcamp . items.body:
ROSÉ is stepping into a playful new chapter with 'new trick'.

Released on 17 September, the dreamy alt-pop single sees the BLACKPINK member moving through heartbreak with a newfound sense of resilience. The track brings together the nostalgic energy of '90s romantic comedies, early-2000s punk-rock touches, and an upbeat pop attitude.

'new trick' arrives alongside a music video directed by Dave Meyers, whose credits include work with Taylor Swift, Kendrick Lamar, and Ariana Grande. Shot entirely on the iPhone 18 Pro, the visual forms part of Apple's latest Shot on iPhone campaign and places ROSÉ in a vibrant, youthful setting that matches the song's playful energy.

ROSÉ described the track, which she created with songwriter Amy Allen, as “possibly the cutest thing” the pair have made together. She also shared that she has been working on new music as she explores the sound and world of her next era.

The release follows ROSÉ's debut studio album rosie and 'APT.', her collaboration with Bruno Mars.

items.body:
Eight years is a long time to wait, but Rachael Yamagata made her return to Singapore feel remarkably familiar.

Taking over Foo Chow Hall on 16 September, her Starlit Alchemy Tour marked her first show here since 2018, her 10th Singapore performance, and the tour’s only Southeast Asia stop. Early in the night, Yamagata spoke warmly about her history with the country and thanked Bandwagon for bringing her back — a fitting sentiment for an artist whose relationship with Singapore audiences has been built across numerous visits, long meet-and-greets, and years of songs that fans have carried with them.

The show itself embodied what makes Yamagata such a compelling live performer: enormous emotional weight without ever becoming oppressively solemn. There was tenderness and vulnerability, certainly, but also plenty of humour, stories, and an easy rapport with the room.

Opening with ‘Heaven Help’ and ‘Empty Houses’, Yamagata moved through a set that brought different eras of her catalogue into conversation. ‘Meet Me By the Water’ and ‘Saturday Morning’ appeared alongside ‘Break Apart’ and ‘Backwards’, before ‘Elephants’, ‘Over and Over’, ‘Dealbreaker’, ‘Sunday Afternoon’, and ‘You Won’t Let Me’ traced the emotional terrain she has explored across more than two decades of songwriting.

One of the night’s standout moments came with ‘Be Be Your Love’. Rather than its familiar piano-driven form, Yamagata presented the Happenstance favourite through a guitar-led arrangement that lost none of the original’s emotional force.

She dedicated it to opening act Charlie Lim, before jokingly protesting when Lim revealed that he had first heard the song when he was 15 — an admission that prompted Yamagata to playfully confront the passage of time.

The joke soon gave way to something more reflective. Yamagata acknowledged ‘Be Be Your Love’ as the breakthrough that helped open the doors to record deals and touring, making its return here feel especially poignant more than two decades on.

Lim, who recently returned with his third studio album DAYDREAM, was an inspired choice to open the evening, with his own emotionally direct, genre-fluid songwriting sharing natural ground with Yamagata’s. He later joined her for ‘Duet’, turning one of her best-loved collaborations into a distinctly Singaporean moment.

Then came an even more unexpected full-circle encounter.

Singaporean singer-songwriter, fitness personality, and content creator Tyen Rasif joined Yamagata for ‘I Wish You Love’. But Rasif’s connection with Yamagata did not begin backstage that evening.

Around 14 years ago, Rasif attended one of Yamagata’s Singapore concerts as a fan. Instead of joining the lengthy post-show meet-and-greet queue, she and her then-boyfriend happened to strike up a conversation with a stranger nearby. He turned out to be Yamagata’s producer, and after learning that the pair were aspiring singer-songwriters, invited them along for supper.

Yamagata was there — and the night eventually ended with them jamming together by the side of the road at around 5 AM.

14 later, Rasif was no longer singing with one of her musical heroes on a roadside. She was sharing a stage with her at Foo Chow Hall.

That full-circle moment captured much of what made Yamagata’s Singapore return so affecting. There were songs about loss and longing, but the night itself was filled with connection — between artist and audience, between old songs and new ones, and between musicians whose paths had crossed years earlier in very different circumstances.

Presented by Bandwagon Live in partnership with The Rock Promotions, MAILIVE, and MAISEAT, the concert ultimately showed why Yamagata’s relationship with Singapore has endured across 10 performances. She may have been away since 2018, but once the songs started, the distance did not feel quite so long.

items.album: Boris, DAVID BORING, Srirajah Rockers & more highlight an unforgettable Baybeats 2026 — festival report
items.excerpt:
25 editions in, Baybeats 2026 proved that there is still plenty of room for discovery at Singapore's longest-running alternative music festival. Across 3 – 6 September, 48 acts filled Esplanade with everything from crushing experimental rock and abrasive post-punk to homegrown hip-hop and Thai roots reggae. It was diverse, unpredictable and, most importantly, a whole lot of fun. Here are five sets that stayed with us.

Boris

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by borisheavyrocks (@borisd
items.body:
25 editions in, Baybeats 2026 proved that there is still plenty of room for discovery at Singapore's longest-running alternative music festival. Across 3 – 6 September, 48 acts filled Esplanade with everything from crushing experimental rock and abrasive post-punk to homegrown hip-hop and Thai roots reggae. It was diverse, unpredictable and, most importantly, a whole lot of fun. Here are five sets that stayed with us.

Boris

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by borisheavyrocks (@borisdronevil)

Few bands can make sheer volume feel as nuanced as Boris. The Japanese experimental rock veterans shifted through sludge, drone, noise, psychedelia and shoegaze with an almost elemental force, building enormous walls of sound before pulling them back into quieter, more hypnotic passages. Heavy without ever becoming one-dimensional, their set was a masterclass in how distortion, dynamics and atmosphere can work together to completely swallow a room.

DAVID BORING

Credit: danspixelgraphy, courtesy of Esplanade – Theatres on the Bay

There was something almost hypnotic about DAVID BORING, even at their most confrontational. The Hong Kong outfit constantly alternated between danceable, propulsive grooves and sudden bursts of abrasive post-punk noise, creating a tension between release and unease that kept the room locked in. That push and pull between raw dissonance and meticulous control became considerably more visceral onstage. Chaotic without feeling careless, this was a set that made it difficult to look away.

Kin Leonn x pureblue Ensemble

Credit: chrawme, courtesy of Esplanade – Theatres on the Bay

Kin Leonn x pureblue Ensemble took the collective's already intricate, ambient and contemporary compositions and gave them new depth. Joined by Bryan de Rozario on saxophone, Lucas Tee on drums and Mervin Wong on viola, the ensemble added breath, movement and physicality to music built on delicacy and restraint. Combined with the breathtaking visuals, every small detail seemed more textured and visceral, turning the performance into an incredibly immersive audiovisual experience. The result was a set that felt expansive, tactile, and completely absorbing.

Mediocre Haircut Crew

Credit: alvieisalive, courtesy of Esplanade – Theatres on the Bay

Mediocre Haircut Crew's return to Baybeats felt less like a comeback set and more like a block party with a few hundred friends. Backed by a full live band led by music director Kenzo Nagari, omarKENOBI, mickeyLEANO and daniKIDDO sounded bigger without losing the easy chemistry, impeccable live flow and stage charisma that have always made them such a fun act to watch. They debuted new material alongside favourites including 'Lose Your Love' and 'Fuck Da System', before ending with a full-crowd sing-along to 'WANNABES'. If there was any rust to shake off, you certainly couldn't hear it.

Srirajah Rockers

Credit: won997, courtesy of Esplanade – Theatres on the Bay

Srirajah Rockers brought a completely different kind of vibe to Baybeats — one driven by groove rather than sheer volume. The Thai veterans' blend of roots reggae, heavy dub, Thai soul, lovers rock, ska and funk unfolded with an easy confidence, leaving plenty of space for deep bass and laid-back rhythms to breathe. Warm, hypnotic and effortlessly danceable, the set showed why more than two decades together have made the group such an enduring presence in Thailand's reggae scene. Amid a weekend of wide-ranging sounds, Srirajah Rockers stood out by locking into an irresistible groove.

items.body: Happy golden anniversary to the International Computer Music Conference! This special album honors founder David Wessel (1942–2014). The full title of the 2025 theme: Curiosity, Play, Innovation—A 50th Anniversary Celebration of Creativity in Music, Science and Technology. This generous collection showcases electro-acoustic music from around the world. Each piece is intricate and unique, while many touch upon contemporary themes, starting with Jiajing Zhao‘s “Glitchopolis,” a commentary on information overload. The very first sound is that of an alarm, doubled and then tripled, set against London traffic, which begins to fracture, stutter and glitch. Garbled human voices emerge from a processed vat; construction and technology intertwine. A bee – real and metaphoric – buzzes by, followed by a flock of birds, fireworks and a police siren. How many inputs can one brain handle? “Pardon me, ‘scuse me, sorry,” a commuter apologizes at the end. By refusing to mute the signals, the composer imitates the feeling of being overwhelmed, not only aural, but emotionally. “Rumors, approximated” by Shane Turner with Simone Pitot (Delorca) uses algorithms to translate sound into data. The textures are the key, but as patterns emerge, questions of value arise: are these patterns authentic or unintentional? And how much of the human remains after technology has had its say? While Pitot purposely subjected her vocals to this process, other parts of life are unwittingly fed to the whims of the machine. Zeo Lin‘s Escape, whose opening minutes flirt with the dance floor, is filled with glass crashes and computer beeps, percussion and synth, piano and breath, representing a clash between the organic and the electronic, its movements marked by the click of a cassette. At the end a church bell tolls, only to by subsumed by static. Daniele Valenti‘s “CAN you hear them?” is particularly clever, derived almost entirely from the timbres of cans. Without knowing this, one might only guess at the nature of these sounds. The knowledge allows one to lean in,, to cherish the sounds made by the humble object that one often kicks down the road or discards without any attention to its aural qualities. Can a can sound like traffic, or rain? Yes, it CAN. In contrast, “Hammerklavier” uses the piano as its acoustic source, with Antonio Argentieri doing pretty much everything but playing the keys. Think of Matmos’ Ultimate Care II, which performed a similar feat with a washing machine. Few would ever guess that this is a piano piece, which exponentially increases its appeal. How does it feel to be “an international student with limited English proficiency” in London? Hongquan Yang and Fan Zu attempt to translate the experience in “Rambling,” starting with a traditional classroom speech about sound, then feeding it through echo, loop and reverb, injecting their own language to return the favor. Soon everyone is confused, yet finds common ground in the tempo and the playful approach. Passing grade! The chimes and choral tones of the beautifully titled “A Poem for Little Things” turn out to have been taken from children’s toys; as the mother of twins, Chung Eun Kim‘s aural environment has been altered, and she has responded by altering it right back, finding rhythm and melody, wonder and awe, in a castanet, maraca or toy xylophone. “Decorate beauty” is the concept behind Peter Dickson Lopez and Ensemble MISE-EN. “Mise En Series I” begins as a pure chamber piece before the electro-acoustic elements enter; the timbre approaches drone, as the instruments swell with sound, underpinned by pensive electronics. As if coming full cycle, Liu Yurai‘s “The Shackle” is inspired by a visit to the thousand-year-old Daci Temple, an oasis of peace located in the heart of Chengdu. The contrast between peace and overload (as first addressed in “Glitchopolis”) is palpable. Tapping and texting sounds overlap and threaten to undo all calm; a train clacks by; passengers chatter. Soon the bicycle bells are replaced by temple bells, the incoherent conversations with chants, the traffic with birdsong, and a sense of balance is restored. Unfortunately, albeit realistically, the outside world keeps rushing back in. “Seascape Serenity” readjusts the scene. Yu Chia Kuo and SinYu Deng pack the soundscape with hydrophone recordings that reflect the ecosystems of Taiwan. Just as one wished for the serenity of the temple in “The Shackle,” one wishes for humans to stop polluting the biophony of this piece. And yet, this is part of the lesson: that marine life is at least as stressed as we are and that we have caused both. While the piece attempts a happy ending, increasing the number of species calls, one wonders how realistic this might be; the title becomes less a reflection of the piece than an elegy. Taken as a whole, Best of the Listening Rooms demonstrates incredible range while managing to flow beautifully as a whole. The collection is sociologically enlightening yet retains a sense of fun, honoring the theme. Most couples are winding down by their golden anniversary, but we have a feeling that the International Computer Music Conference is just getting started. (Richard Allen)

items.body: Cuban drummer Francisco Mela’s free jazz odyssey continues on four new releases, writes Daniel Spicer in The Wire 512 Francisco Mela Carnaval De Oriente 577 CD/DL Jowee Omicil & Francisco Mela OM BasH! Village DL Rafael Zaldivar Zaldivar/McBride/Mela: Meeting In New York Vol 1 577 DL Matthew Putman/Hill Greene/Francisco Mela Bright Sun Outside 577 CD/DL Cuban drummer Francisco Mela’s route into the mysteries of free jazz has been a circuitous one. He started out as a teenager working in the bands of Latin jazz pianists and fellow countrymen Emiliano Salvador and Gabriel Hernandez before moving to the US at the turn of the millennium and building a reputation as an in-demand straightahead jazz drummer, playing with Joe Lovano and enjoying nearly a decade in pianist McCoy Tyner’s trio. Following Tyner’s death in 2020 and the forced hiatus of the pandemic, Mela emerged with a new fascination for and commitment to freedom, forging a fruitful partnership with the Brooklyn based 577 label and collaborating with heavy-hitters including William Parker, Cooper-Moore and Matthew Shipp. His journey is not entirely without precedent. Milford Graves cut his teeth in the early 1960s playing congas and timbales in Latin and Afro-Cuban outfits and led The Milford Graves Latino Quartet, featuring a young pianist by the name of Chick Corea, before a 1962 encounter with the volcanic eruptions of Elvin Jones alongside Tyner in John Coltrane’s quartet inspired him to turn to the drum kit and become a key architect of the mid-60s free jazz New Thing, entirely rewiring the possibilities of time and timbre in the process. In Cuban pianist Rafael Zaldivar’s trio, Mela teams up with Christian McBride, who held bass duties in Corea’s trio with drummer Brian Blade, as heard on the 2013 live album Trilogy. In fact, on Meeting In New York Vol 1, Zaldivar at times channels a strikingly similar feel to Corea’s sophisticated and sentimental tunefulness, embraced by McBride’s muscular lyricism. It’s a temptation Mela resolutely resists, avoiding Blade’s deep swing in favour of a constant flickering fizz of cymbals and snare, dancing playfully around the idea of time. At other moments, Zaldivar summons puckish declamations more akin to Paul Bley, eliciting a brawnier churn from Mela punctuated by sudden gunshot snare cracks while, in a diaphanous free ballad, his subtle brush work shushes and sighs in gaseous textures. Here, McBride – not often heard in a free context – sounds a little out of place, cramming as many notes as possible into solos perhaps more suited to a contemporary post-bop milieu. There’s no such mismatch in the trio with pianist Matthew Putman, where the low end is held down by Hilliard Greene, a bassist with considerable avant garde credentials, having worked with the likes of pianists Don Pullen and Cecil Taylor, and saxophonist Charles Gayle. Bright Sun Outside navigates more familiar free jazz terrain and isn’t afraid to ramble. Even some of its fairly brief improvisations, lasting just a few minutes, convey a sense of loose and leisurely meandering, with Putman flicking out spontaneous melodic gambits that seem quite content to never fully commit to a destination – like a succession of half-formed thoughts bubbling up in an unhurried internal monologue. Mela is happily along for the ride, laying out a rattling commentary dominated by an arrestingly dry snare, each stroke deftly placed with neat precision. When Greene leans into rasping arco shrieks and Putman chops out sudden staccato stabs, Mela flexes his muscles with a more aggressive energy, like fresh flames springing up from glowing embers. Mela’s first solo album Carnaval De Oriente proposes a wholly different mood. Inspired by the sounds of the eponymous street carnival heard in his childhood, he rolls around the drum kit – revealing a loose, earthy sound reminiscent of Graves – adding shakers, cowbell and sundry percussion. All the while, he chirps spontaneous vocal chants and snatches of song that recall percussionist/vocalist Juno Lewis’s mythically resonant Afro-Creole vocals on his song “Kulu Sé Mama (Juno Sé Mama)”, recorded with John Coltrane in 1965. On one track, Mela tinkers with rudimentary innocence on a glockenspiel; on another, he picks clumsily at an acoustic guitar. What he lacks in chops, he makes up for with unabashed enthusiasm. Whistling absentmindedly and chatting contentedly to himself, he sounds like he’s having a fine time. When the full kit breaks through in a burst of dense polyrhythms, you can pretty much hear the smile on his face. His concise improvised duets with Canadian-Haitian multi-instrumentalist Jowee Omicil are in a similar vein, as the pair explore the shared musical traditions of Haiti and Cuba. On saxophones and clarinet, Omicil displays some of the loquacious unpredictability of Eric Dolphy, while Mela rolls out a nimble undertow that occasionally comes close to a standard jazz sound, replete with full-bodied rolls and tumbles. Omicil’s lip-smacking pocket trumpet works Mela up into a frenzied freakout of ecstatic vocal cries. Intuitive piano splashes invite a thoughtful drizzle of snare and ride. Mela sings with lusty abandon and thwacks out hambone rhythms on his own body. Again, a palpable sense of spontaneous joy reigns throughout. There’s an obvious similarity to Don Cherry’s duets with drummer Ed Blackwell, as documented on the twin Mu albums: while reaching back past the dim origins of jazz, Mela and Omicil conduct imaginary Pangaean rituals bursting with the same omnivorous exuberance that colours all of Mela’s music. This review appears in The Wire 512 along with many other reviews of new and recent records, books, films, festivals and more. To read them all, pick up a copy of the magazine in our online shop. Wire subscribers can also read the issue in our online magazine library.

items.body: For all its stunning virtuosity, the tumbling fingerstyle guitar of Swedish guitarist Finn Loxbo is always in service to a set of brilliant compositional ideas Digging through the various improvised solo and duo recordings Swedish guitarist Finn Loxbo has made over the last decade is like witnessing a slow-motion creative winnowing, observing how a feverish pile of ideas and experiments has gradually coalesced into something inscrutable. items.body: Review by BrufordFreak — The first BS &T album I bought. I found it greatly disappointing but it served my musical education process by helping me to define the kind of musics I did not like. 1. "Hi De Ho" (4:25) never a favorite of mine though I recognize the talent, skill, and hard work that went into pulling this one off. (8.75/10)2. "The Battle" (2:43) the harpsichord opening and recorder joining in as Steve Katz provides the serious vocals of this anachronistic tune. Inspired by THE ASSOCIATION's "Requiem for the Masses"? I've always liked the Baroque Revival trend of the 1960s. (9.125/10) 3. "Lucretia MacEvil" (3:03) trying to make more out of the success of "Spinning Wheel." Great performances but, come on, Guys! Once is enough! (8.875/10)4. "Lucretia's Reprise" (2:35) now, isn't this a little embarrassing and tacky?! Two times through the same song (though this one is less "Spinning Wheel" and more Brass-Rock expos�. And, yes, David really does let his full TOM JONES come shining through. (9/10)5. "Fire and Rain" (4:02) trying to make James Taylor's masterful and iconic tune more serious, more poignant. I can understand but this is the kind of stuff that should be saved for live concert encores. I'm not really a fan of the brassification of the tune, either. (8.875/10)6. "Lonsome Suzie" (4:35) piano jazz-blues over which David shows off his softer, subtler LOU RAWLS side. The soft, subtle horn arrangements are quite a sublime touch but the rest is kind of . . . unnecessary. (8.75/10)7. "Symphony for the Devil/Sympathy for the Devil" (7:49) now this is an interesting version/take on an all-time rock classic. It feels quite a bit like Andrew Lloyd Weber's material for Jesus Christ Superstar, which was written and partly recorded and being rehearsed when BS&T were recording the songs for this album. In fact, many of the themes and palettes seem to mirror the JCS album quite directly--despite the fact that JCS didn't get released until October of 1970. (BS&T 3 was released by Columbia Records in June of 1970.) So, which came first? Were BS&T playing this in their controversial European tour during the fall and winter of 1969 and 1970? I do, in fact, really like this rendering of of the Stones iconic song--maybe even better than the original (especially the "Sympathy for the Devil" half). (13.5/15)8. "He's A Runner" (4:15) my favorite song on the album, it's a cover of a Laura Nyro composition, there's just such a cool lounge vocal jazz vibe to this music and these performances, start to finish--like real professionals of the club scene, American and European. (9.5/10)9. "Somethin' Comin' On" (4:33) my second favorite song on the album. It's a cover of a Joe Cocker tune. Too bad when I was young I never gave this album's Side Two much attention cuz as I hear it now I hear/feel the best of this band as well as the best of the Brass Rock phenomenon. It's as if they've snuck Terry Kath to sing over the BS&T band's music while using both Chicago and BS&T's horn players. I love Halligan's organ play. (9.25/10)10. "40,000 Headmen" (4:40) a really interesting multi-part song attributed to the unknown Fred Lewis, it's got slow sections, child lullaby sections, brass rock passages, and lively uptempo jazz-rock parts. Great song! All hail Side Two! (9.125/10)Total time: 42:20A-/4.5 stars; despite the mostly flat renderings of the (to me) questionable song choices and Side One, the album only gets stronger as it leaves its "Spinning Wheel" past behind and chooses to explore its own preferred styles (on Side Two). For such a talented band I wish they could/would consider writing and exposing their own writing material and not just rely on covers. I find myself reluctant to include this album in the context of a pop or prog or even Jazz-Rock Fusion domain but it does contain some really finely crafted songs.

items.body: Review by kenethlevine — When your album is from 1970 and you manage to sound more stoned than your contemporaries, you're ahead in at least one area. This debut from DANDO SHAFT, while not actually a concert album in spite of the implications of its title, possesses a live feel that vacillates both shakily and tightly in at the intersection of JETHRO TULL, MOODY BLUES, JAN DUKES DE GREY, MUSHROOM, with a wink or two to FUCHSIA (which they do nonetheless predate) and LINDISFARNE. In all, this is, while not quite a missing link, a varied and more than competent collection with a few surprises to maintain freshness after so many decades, achieved through the harmony vocals, Celtic flourishes and just enough psych to keep the folk-weary from unhinging a jaw. To get a flavor for the best on offer here from the integrated styles, go for the EMTIDI-like "September Wine", the reflective ballad "In the Country", and the twangy and uplifting "End of the Game". Don't dismiss the later bonus tracks either if you can connect with then, but most of all, give this one a p.m with whatever comfort consumable you've been saving.

items.body: Review by ElenaNL — The music is simply amazing. This album feels quite different from the other music by Compassionizer. As I listened to the tracks, I felt as if I were taking a journey around the world?and then even farther, into the Universe.There are subtle folk motifs that seem to echo Slavic heritage, intertwined with oriental influences and sounds that somehow touch the rhythm of the heartbeat. The combination creates a feeling of movement, discovery, and something almost timeless.I'm a dreamer by nature, and I love to "travel" through time, imagine distant places, and create worlds that don't exist anywhere except in my imagination. The music on this album feels like a perfect companion for that kind of journey. It doesn't simply fill the background?it guides the dreams, opens space for deep thoughts, and gives the imagination somewhere to wander.The vocals are a beautiful addition to the overall experience. They add another layer to the music without taking away from its atmospheric and almost cinematic quality.What I especially appreciate is the feeling the album leaves behind. It doesn't feel heavy or overwhelming, and there is no unpleasant aftertaste or excessive excitement. Instead, it leaves me with a sense of freshness, as if my mind has been gently cleared and filled with new thoughts.Each track feels like a small story of its own, with its own characters, atmosphere, journey, and ending. Together, the tracks create something that feels like a collection of little worlds?each one inviting you to step inside for a while and see where it takes you.

items.body: Review by ElenaNL — absolutely love Aquarium. The music, the atmosphere, and the lyrics may not be immediately accessible to a broad audience, but they are filled with wisdom, light, and deep philosophy. I can listen to their music anywhere, and it never gets boring.Some of the humour and references require an understanding of Soviet history and everyday life in the USSR?the values, the absurdities, and all the little things that were part of that world. For example, for many people born in the USSR, a train is not simply a means of transportation. It represents a whole subculture and a particular experience: long journeys, conversations with strangers, and those unexpectedly deep talks that can last for hours. Not the short, polite kind?the long ones.With Aquarium, the lyrics and the music are inseparable. They fuse together to create something much bigger than either one on its own?the full experience of the band.

items.body: Review by RojerWilco — If you're a fan of early Kaipa, you'll enjoy this set. Has it really been 40 years? Roine and Michael are as excellent as you would expect, and Tomas and Ingemar have apparently picked up right where they left off 40 years ago, literally not missing a beat. To me, the surprise is Lalle Larsson. As with his work in Karmakanic, he makes everything he touches better.The track selection has been picked from Inget Nytt Under Solen (Nothing New Under the Sun) and Solo, with Det Tysta Guldet (The Silent Gold) coming from the Kaipa daCapo album. Unless you're actively cross referencing their music, you wouldn't notice the new track among the classic ones.Consider this the missing link in the Kaipa discography. It is an excellent addition to any Kaipa collection, and also makes a good entry point for those interested in early Kaipa.
