items.body: Review by Radisa50 — LP "Time" is the first album of the Zagreb rock group Time, recorded in the Jadran film studio in Dubrava, Zagreb, in April 1972, published by Jugoton in August 1972 (runout 160772), in many respects it is a copy and plagiarism of the music of the English progressive jazz-rock group Colosseum, and mostly the composition from their 2LP "Colosseum Live" from 1971.For the musical introduction of the song "For the life I was born into/Za koji ?ivot treba da se rodim"", the introduction of the composition "Walking In The Park" was taken literally, and in its sequel, such phrases from "Skelington" were plagiarized for the riffs!Also, "Hegedupa Upa" is nothing but a filler, an addition to the album, based on the playing of themes from "Colosseum Live", after all, like all Time album arrangements from that Colosseum live album.In a statement for Svet 1995, Dado Topić indirectly confirmed the copying of Colosseum when he said: "But the key moment was when we played in Zagreb's Dom of Sports as an opening act for the famous band 'Koloseum'." They sounded exactly the way I wanted 'Time' to sound."Also Time would not only not have been called that, but also would not have had Colosseum as a musical matrix if it had not been suggested by their future producer Vladimir Mihaljek Miha.He helped Dad Topić to create a new group after leaving the first Yugoslav progressive rock group Korni grupa in Belgrade.Namely, Miha appeared at a moment when Dado was helpless because the realization of the idea to reactivate Osijek's Dynamites was not possible.And not just gathering, creating a group, but also what and how to play, whose matrix to use.This conclusion was confirmed by Zlatko Gal in the accompanying text for the reissue of the album Time 2019 when he wrote: "Listening to what is happening on the global scene, which has been networked by prog-rock supergroups, but also the situation on the home ground, Mihaljek correctly concluded that the moment is right for a domestic response as well. And guessed!" Yes, he guessed by giving them the musical matrix of the then dominant English progressive rock group Collosseum!And not only did they plagiarize, they called themselves Time based on the name of Colosseum's third studio album "Daugher Of Time" from the summer of 1970, as well as the composition from that record "Time Machine" and the opening song of the first Time album "Istina ma?ina" is a consequence of that inspiration.By the way, Dado Topić was not telling the truth when he said that Time was the opening act for the Colosseum concert in the Zagreb Sports Hall.That English jazz-rock group was indeed a guest in Zagreb, but as Colosseum II with a concert in the Dom sportova on Sunday, September 26, 1976. as part of a three-day YU tour. Journalist Ante Batinović in a detailed review of that concert held in Studio be. 651 of 25. IX 1976 nowhere mentions any pre-group, and therefore neither Time as Dado asserted, of course wrongly, not to say falsely. Evaluate album?The studio performance of the Time album is impeccable, and if it weren't for the aggravating circumstances of the composition, i.e. the plagiarism of Colosseum, that album would deserve the highest rating.Their poor live performance of "Za koji ?ivot..." at the Pop Festival Ljubljana 72-BOOM, held on April 20 and 21, 1972, is also aggravating. This cannot serve to honor the great musicians of the Time group.

items.body: Review by BrufordFreak — An American band that has both an unusual back story as well as quite the unusual motivation. Veterans who are somehow collectively inspired to represent and express a blend of Spanish colonizer and Native American tradition, mythos, and spirit.1. "(Intro) The Coming Of The Spaniards" (3:54) Alan Parsons Project-like Western choir mixed into a musical pastiche that sounds like something from a Spanish "spaghetti western" like soundtrack. It's like throwing APP together with Novella-era RENAISSANCE. Powerful and most excellent! (9.667/10)2. "The Benefits Of Breathing Quietly" (5:56) excellent piano-based APP prog over which singers John Baker and Jake Livgren provide some excellent, appropriately bombastic vocals--entwined and mutually supportive. The music is excellent, the story in the lyrics powerful, the overall effect quite emotional. This is the kind of music and song that reaffirms the reason prog exists! And this Lisa LaRue: She is a FORCE! (9.333/10)3. "The Plains? Truth" (6:49) an instrumental symphonic rock soundscape that reminds me of the best of bands like Kansas, The Dregs, and modern day Prog Folk band SOLSTICE. Excellent programming and computer-generated violin--and sound engineering! Lisa: Maestra: you are nothing short of a genius! This is great prog! (14/15)4. "Quivira Bound" (5:33) this one feels more like old prog, old classic rock. Bombastic opening with piano-based lull for John and Jake's vocal presentation to begin in, we quickly find ourselves back in classic STYX/SOLSTICE/IONA/DAVE BAINBRIDGE/ALAN PARSONS PROJECT territory though, of course, you have to substitute male vocal tracks for most of the female ones--and EXCELLENT are the performances of both John and Jake. Though John Baker's choice of electric guitar tone is a little odd, it works well enough to take nothing away from Lisa's excellent music. (9/10)5. "Moving Forward" (6:51) an instrumental of exemplar weave of prog solos, violin, real and otherwise, keyboard play of the very highest caliber, interesting and very effective guitar sound and styling choices, and some rather stupendous programming of the drums and rhythm section. This could've been early FROST* or BIG BIG TRAIN or THE FLOWER KINGS or THE TANGENT or even Open Sky-era IONA. I call this song a prog lover's wet dream! (15/15)6. "The Turk/Follow The Wind" (5:58) despite the relatively "weak" realistic tone and talent of singer Jake Livgren's voice, the music behind this song is, again, of the highest quality and caliber. Wow! Great chord and melodic pathways drive the music of this band deep into the pleasure zones of my brain. (9.5/10)7. "Nothing Is Everything" (7:34) more sophisticated and virtuosic symphonic prog music that features, this time, a real, "live" violin (though the previous one--on "The Plains? Truth" sounded just as authentic). The song moves through several motifs, shifting in keys and tempos while maintaining the piano-based full-spectrum prog with violin palette until the fourth minute in which Lisa's gorgeous piano play is isolated with guest Joe Deninzen's violin for a spell before the rest of the prog instruments rejoin. The melody choices are so awesome: piano and violin going back and forth each with totally-engaging lines and dynamics. At the five minute mark we move into a heavier, more dynamic section with pounding piano chords, guitar power chords, and soloing electric guitar before we bridge into a Spanish guitar-led section beneath which Lisa has the drums programmed with some excellent tom-and-bass drum flourishes. And soon enough it is over! Nice! I never expected that one to be an instrumental the whole way through. (13.75/15)8. "Carved From The Sun" (8:03) another stupendous prog rock instrumental that takes the listener on an exciting journey of dynamic multi-stimuli, all encapsulated into an action-packed whirlwind of enjoyable romantic slightly-pastoral NeoProg. Great bass, drum pacing, and, of course, keyboard work. I'm coming to fully comprehend what total melodic genius Lisa is: Amazing! So easy and comforting while never sacrificing sophistication and active lines from all of her instruments in the weaves. John's wah-wah-ed distorted guitar in the third minute is quite fitting but Lisa's continuous display of melodic and harmonic genius never quits! So many endorphin/goosebump moments generated by melodies, chord progression surprises, as well as palette and textural shifts. I am simply in awe. This is not only great prog it is music that I can (and will be) listen(ing) to for a long time into the future. This is music that not only rivals but I think surpasses that of my other favorite 21st Century NeoProg/Prog Folk band/artist, Solstice. (15/15)9. "Kicking Rocks" (4:20) though another great instrumental rendering (with a Marc COHN "Walking in Memphis"-like piano approach). Active bass, steady drums, organ and synths, and intermittent electric guitar shredding all add their sounds over the lively piano foundation. There is a weird "no sound" solo section at the end of the second minute but Lisa's confident piano playing never wavers, continues to deliver some wonderfully engaging work (to which I feel like playing "air piano"). The synth-supported multiple guitar soloing that occurs in the fourth minute is cool, too, but I could listen to Lisa's piano playing all day long--especially with recurring support of bursts of near-djenty bass-&-guitar passages. (9.125/10)10. "Prelude To Anywhere/Weekend Conquistadors" (5:45) more of the same piano styling from "Kicking Rocks" over and within which synths, shredding violins and metal guitars, as well as periodic bass and drums help out. There's a lot of the TRANS SIBERIAN ORCHESTRA Christmas music feel to this sound palette. John and/or Jake join in during a solo piano lull around the three-minute mark, signifying the switch to the "Weekend Conquistadors" half of the song--a lament about modern man's use (and misuse) of the land that once supported herds of bison and Native American tribes. Weird "distant and fading" strummed electric guitar ending as a couple quotes from literature or legend as delivered as spoken word over the top. (8.875/10)11. "Still Breathing" (5:58) long introduction eventually pans out in the second minute into a hard-driving violin-topped prog instrumental passage. This is disrupted around the 2:30 mark to allow plodding piano notes and increasingly thickening rock palette to support more of Lisa's computer-generated violin. John's guitars begin to increase in layers, gradually revealing some solo ideas until another sudden stop at the end of the fifth minute signals a shift back into the hard-driving motif of the second minute, over which John's twangy guitar steps up to really solo before the song's final chord--which is followed by a neighing horse whose hooves can then be heard galloping off onto the Plains. Solid prog if not so "perfect" as some of the previous compositions. (9/10)Total time 66:41There are many who will bemoan so much of this music being computer generated and "cleaned" but the end result--great prog music--cannot (and should not) be denied. Keyboard specialist Lisa LaRue is expressing a level of genius that not many prog artists have ever achieved. An album that is definitely in the running for 2026's Album of the Year--and deservedly so!A/five stars; a masterpiece of wonderful progressive rock music that taps into the palettes and energy of both the NeoProg and Prog Folk realms of progressive rock music and represent the talents of a musical genius who is totally new to me: Native American Lisa LaRue. HIGHLY recommended!

items.body: Review by brainsuccasurgery — 1973 was a banner year for Italian progressive rock. Alongside the universally acclaimed masterpieces that the genre's "four tenors" were producing at the same time (Io Sono Natto Libero, Felona E Sorona, Photos Of Ghosts, Arbeit Macht Frei), other classics emerged that left a lasting mark on the genre, even though most of them were short-lived. Aside from often contrived?or even trivial?reunions, bands like Cervello, Campo Di Marte, Festa Mobile, Blocco Mentale, Museo Rosenbach, L'Uovo Di Colombo, Semiramis as one-album "meteor" bands, with their sole album released in 1973?even though the last two groups mentioned have recently reemerged with a noteworthy album (and it's impossible to overlook Apoteosi's seminal album, which falls into the same category, though it was released in 1975). One might be tempted to place Alphataurus in the same golden category, with its superb self-titled debut album?provided one disregards its second album, recorded the same year but released only in 1992 following the dissolution of its creator, as well as *AttosecondO*, the 2012 release, which is excellent but not as indispensable as its illustrious predecessor.More than 50 years after that annus mirabilis, Alphataurus is back, led by two founding members, keyboardist Pietro Pellegrini and guitarist Guido Wassermann (who sadly passed away after the recording was completed). A second keyboardist, Andrea Guizzetti, who already appeared on AttosecondO strengthens the lineup, rounded out by the inevitable fresh blood: Tony Alemanno (a defector from the new The Trip) on bass, Diego Mariani on drums, and Franco Giaffreda on vocals, acoustic guitar, and flute?the latter having already made a name for himself about fifteen years ago as a member of Biglietto Per L'Inferno. Is this new Alphataurus reunion a pleasant surprise, much like S�miramis's was a few months ago?Yes, but only partly, because "2084: Viaggio nel Nulla", a dystopian fiction with philosophical and existential themes, alternates between RPI tracks that still have that special spark (a good half of the album) and a sort of classy but generic prog that seems to meander nonchalantly over bluesy chords ("Pista 6," oddly placed at the beginning of the album, is saved by a magical Mellotron bridge), unfortunately verging on high-end Italian rock-pop ("Viaggio nel Nulla," disappointing despite a promising start and a catchy melodic theme), much like PFM has done recently in its least inspired moments (in fact, singer Franco Giaffreda's voice can be compared to that of Franz Di Cioccio). "Flashback (apocalisse)" is more convincing with its clearly syncopated, off-beat rhythm reminiscent of Gentle Giant, its unapologetic melodic breaks, its playful little Moog solo, its jazzy nods, and its infectious positive energy. "Meta e met�" (6:36) packs a punch in the same league?or even a notch above?with unpredictable, rhythmic footwork, powerful solo uppercuts, and a melody as strong as steel set against a velvety backdrop. The album closes tenderly with "E=mc2," featuring a smooth melody and emphatic, slightly saccharine harmonies that boldly combine acoustic guitar and chamber orchestra?though it lacks that distinctive tension that is the hallmark of the best prog.None of this is disgraceful?in fact, it's quite pleasant?conscientiously crafted with today's resources in a highly professional manner by true prog enthusiasts. But the album as a whole struggles to inspire overwhelming enthusiasm and will likely fall short of satisfying the most demanding among us, eliciting little more than a polite and benevolent listen. This assessment may seem harsh, even unfair, but it must be acknowledged that we're a long way from the success of S�miramis's earth-shattering comeback.Except that it's not quite that simple, because *2084: Viaggio nel Nulla* contains an epic track that's sure to make you forget everything else: "Wormhole" (10:15) is exactly what you'd expect from such a legendary band. A dynamic first section, full steam ahead, that owes a great deal to Banco's heyday with its Hammond organ arpeggios and repetitive piano; a second, more acoustic section, structured like PFM's "Impressioni di Settembre," with a sublime chorus?a true challenge to anyone who tries to resist singing along at the top of their lungs?everything is designed to set off fireworks in our ears, dazzle us, and make the twinkling of the stars fade into the background. A well-crafted modern RPI album that you can happily listen to again and again, whistling the melodies as if you'd always known them, *2084: Viaggio nel Nulla* becomes, with "Wormhole," a must-hear release from an RPI veteran worthy of his legendary status.

items.body: Review by BrufordFreak — I know nothing of this artist but I have had many encounters with idiosyncratic creatives like him, so I feel somewhat steeled, if not totally qualified (who is?), for the experience of listening to this album. 1. "I Had a Dream" (2:13) over a recording of a female student's English narration of a dream of hers a NuJazz multi-track weave of multiple horns, synth horns, pianos, xylophones, fuzzy electric guitars, and bass and drums and synthesizer noises all travel together like the start of a marathon race: with each instrument traveling an oscillating path of pitch, all at the same speed, each with their own individual, loose and idiosyncratic expressions of the same directional goal. Interesting. Reminds me of something Markuus Pajakaala would do (especially because of the prominent presence of low-end horns like bassoons or baritone saxophones mixed with multiple tracks of various tuned percussion instruments). (4.375/5)2. "Memories of a Loser" (3:39) a kind of bleed-over from the previous dream song turns into a kind of loose jazz lounge (or airport piano and sundry instruments and sounds that happen to show up--including honking horns from taxis) all given motion by a rolling bass, drums and piano. There are appearances from quite a variety of "passer-by" guests, including multiple horns, all acting as if they're just walking by and happen to have an instrument to throw into the mix for a few seconds before moving on. Interesting. (8.75/10)3. "I Want You (She's So Heavy)" (4:04) Yes, that "I Want You (She's So Heavy)"--here rendered by jazzy-blues-rock combo with a very active drummer, multiple guitar, keyboard/synth, and horn contributors, each throwing their Fred Frith-Sonny Sharrock-like interpretations into the increasingly-wild mix. Interesting. (8.875/10)4. "El lado oscuro de la calle" (3:31) synth- & electric guitar-generated noises, programmed drum/percussion, bass, and Holger Czukay-like random radio-recording tracks fed into the same David Torn/Stephan Thelen/SONAR-like Future Possible Jazz Musics mix. I happen to LOVE this! Sounds like the kind of music a self-assured terrorist might be listening to on his noise-cancelling headphones as he cased out a target airport, train station, bus depot or the like. (9.333/10)5. "The Narrow Way" (3:53) faded in BRAINTICKET-like melody pattern of synth/organ and piano with drums and synth-saw bass line in which voices, field recordings, pianos, keyboards, eerie synthesizers, and other instruments weave in and out of each other's presence with almost violent and reckless abandon despite all somewhat following the rising and falling oscillation of the main bass and synth melody line. (9/10)6. "La m�quina de los sue�os" (3:32) a cool jazz track that could easily occupy a soundtrack to a street-walking scene in a spy movie: there are tons of supplemental tracks woven in and out, panning across the soundscape, a lot of them treated field recordings of radio and/or passers-by voices. Very cool. (9.125/10)7. "Ostinato en Em" (2:36) hypnotic left-hand piano pattern is congested with many other layers of horns, guitars, drums, percussion, more piano tracks, all spewing forth their vomit and excrement like a scene of exhaust plumes flowing thickly into the air from factory smokestacks, all moving synchronously in the same direction, same pattern. Excellent, though I wish it would've morphed or transitioned. (4.625/5)8. "El trapecio" (3:16) jazz drums with descending chord bass line over/within which everything but the kitchen sinks thrown in from the listening drone flying around the airspace outside a busy mega-high-rise apartment complex. Okay as a dumping ground but under-developed. (8.75/10)9. "Onda Media" (3:15) the soundtrack to an hour in the life of an airport's robotic floor cleaner/vacuum, all recorded, filtered through a high-speed playback feature so that the sound and visuals are moving in 3x speed. We're starting to travel beyond the boundaries of what is acceptable as dance and entertainment music: something that would be more appropriate to a 22nd Century Ornette Coleman, John Zorn, or Sonny Sharrock (which is beyond my tolerance or enjoyment capacity). (8.667/10)10. "El final del camino" (2:57) the musical interpretation, capture, and/or expression of the cacophony of modern world mall life? (8.75/10)11."Los platos rotos" (5:15) drums and drones: the first playing free jazz, the second providing stable observer perspective. This one actually grew on me--began making sense as well as achieving NEON HEART-like sublimity for me. Why this one and not some of the others I cannot explain. Perhaps the grounding, pacifying effect of the heavily reverbed Fender Rhodes or dreamy infinity notes coming out of the electric guitars helping to balance/offset the angsty drum play. (9.25/10)12. "Ambient Loser" (1:57) gentle guitar and horn lullaby with glitch percussives. (4.5/5)13. "Carnaval" (3:35) a Latin percussion display with incidental synth-generated noises thrown in every few seconds for spice and futuristic sci-fi effect. Interesting. (8.875/10)Totla Time 43:42I really enjoyed the journey arc through "real" modern world soundscapes that this album took me through. Though there are several songs I would call "keepers"--that I will look forward to when they come up in my random shuffle playlists--a lot of it feels like �tudes or attempts to capture a single emotion or random life situation--which is not wrong or bad, just not universally appealing. B+/4.5 stars; an excellent collection of one artist's personal and very modern perspectives of the world as he sees/experiences it. Some of these often-unusual and hyper-stimulating songs are bound to connect while some are bound to rankle: each listener will experience it differently, according to his/her/their own personal experiences and moods. I do recommend the experience: who knows what you'll get out of it!

items.body: Review by ZowieZiggy — Some of youmight know that I'm a Purple maniac.Studio albums or alive!I witnessed their MIJ tour in Europe and was present at their concert in my hometown Brussels (Forest National -March 73) while I was just 14.This is a souvenir that still shines in my memory. In the meantime, I saw them quite a bunch of times through the (many) years. And on October 20, 2026 I will see them maybe for the last time! In Madrid (I live in Spain since 2014 but might relocate in Cambodia in a couple of years).I rate MIJ with 5*****.This triple CD is the rendition of their concerts in Japan in1972. Osaka (twice) & Tokyo.But even with the arrival of the CD, it was NOT possible to get the full encores on them.So "Speed King" is missing on the first CD."Black Night" as well "Lucille" (from Little Richard - R & Roll legend) on the second. For a total of about 14 minutes."Black Night" & Speed King" on the third CD for just a mere 14 minutes.Such a shame but that was a technical limitation So, no wonder that some people downloaded this work, right?The good thing here, is that we have the concerts in the right sequence. Which was NOT the case with MIJ.Again, due to lack of space on the vinyl. Each show started with "Highway Star" and ended with "Space Truckin". I mean the qhow without the encores.So, the first night, the were no "Smoke on the Water"."The Mule" was always played in 4, and "Lazy" as 6.And I will get "Highway", "Lazy" & "Smoke" in Madrid. As well as "Black Night" (the single that I bought in December 1970 and which turned me into a Purple freak).The sound rendition is perfect and is there any wonder that I should rate the triple CD version differently than the original MIJ?You have the answer I guess.5*****. A masterpiece of hard-rock live!!! FOR EVER!!!

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — Listening to Autobahn, both the album and the title track, one begins to notice just how many artists they have influenced, across both rock and electronic music. The sonic leap from the previous album is immense; there is a minimalist approach, repetition, and layers of sound that are subtly added one by one, like raindrops we don't notice until there are too many of them, and it is these layers that drive the changes.The structure is progressive, evolving even as the same central theme repeats, shifting in timing, speed, and ultimately, meaning. The synthesizers create a vast stereo universe; we were sensing modernity before it had even arrived. Atmospheres and moods were evoked; beneath that veneer of coldness lay substance and emotion, and I am thinking not only of Brian Eno, but also of David Byrne, Magazine, and Ultravox. Suddenly, it feels like a racetrack, and the synthesizers abandon the melody, though not the harmony.The synthesizers then reach a certain symphonic depth, before becoming a sort of religious choir as the electronic drums forever leave behind the mere science fiction of the 50s and 60s. And the Minimoog joins the vocals to create a new melody towards the end, creating within this staging, a certain form of new modern epic."Kometenmelodie 1" is dark and cinematic, with the lead synthesizer contrasting against the delicate piano whispering in the background, allowing the duo of Ralf H�tter and Florian Schneider to shine with their full theatricality."Kometenmelodie 2," on the other hand, is luminous, like its counterpart, representing the two faces of the theater. It once again features the synthesizer-and-keyboard duet, yet here it almost anticipates the modern 80s pop that would later draw upon its lessons. A symphonic-progressive air drifts through, much like that comet, complemented by Wolfgang Fl�r's electronic drums. "Mitternacht" holds echoes that reverberate in an almost ecclesiastical, yet psychedelic, manner; it gradually reveals itself as a musical painting, rich in textures to unravel, dissect, and try to comprehend, or simply to let wash over you and feel.There is something organic about Morgenspaziergang, the sound of the flute and the birds, yet at this point, it is entirely an experience for the senses, a matter of perceiving and surrendering to them. After so much overexposure to technology, and the coldness and concrete of highways and "musique concr�te", it is as if the earth and Kraftwerk are responding, much like their compatriots Popol Vuh, with a return to a certain kind of nature, one whose uniqueness is only revealed after having left it behind. There is nothing more modern than that.

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — As long as the Electric Light Orchestra maintained the premise of being a progressive rock band featuring strings, they could rely on those very strings, along with the right arrangements, to remain at the cutting edge. However, with each successive album following Roy Wood's departure, pop music began to take up more space in their compositions. "Fire on High" boasts a sweeping, powerful start, moving beyond the intro and the female chorus to showcase that signature element established in their first three albums: a classical-rock orchestra. Yet, while the compositions on those early records were daring and surprising, featuring dark, original arrangements that coexisted with rock 'n' roll, the music gradually became more predictable. Face the Music is an enjoyable listen, though it has its ups and downs; "Waterfall," for instance, is a ballad that, were the strings stripped away, I could easily imagine Freddie Mercury singing. Those strings could be mysterious, aggressive, or melancholic, and at times even reminiscent of the Beatles, echoing the production style of George Martin."Evil Woman" is a great song, the first of the nods to disco they would incorporate, yet played in a glam-rock and funk style. It's a spirited, groovy track featuring prominent drums and Bee Gees-style backing vocals; the strings serve the disco vibe, complemented by a funky clavinet part that made, and still makes, the song a lot of fun (proving that progressive rock can be fun, too). At times, the strings would play around and break the conventional mold, and whenever Jeff Lynne was in a festive mood, he really brought a great vibe to the music."Nightrider" is built upon the backing vocals and all the signature trappings they had established, the voices and the swirling strings that seemed to spin like a Ferris wheel. Yet, it still sounded fresh; at times, the music would hang suspended in mid-air, leaving the female backing vocals alone for a few seconds before everything instantly rushed back in. There was also a dreamlike section, a compositional triumph, infused with a burst of energy that snapped the listener out of that reverie; it was in moments like these that ELO truly shone with a symphonic brilliance."Poker" was another fast-paced rock 'n' roll track, yet Richard Tandy's Minimoog, Lynne's guitar, and the cellos combined to create magnificent sonic moments; meanwhile, "Strange Magic", which begins like Tchaikovsky's Swan Lake, transforms into a radio-friendly mid-70s ballad. For some reason, the influence of the Bee Gees and Queen hovers over the album, intertwining with the electric originality of this orchestra. "Down Home Town" succumbs to an inexplicable country vibe, though the string arrangements are effectively tailored to that style. "One Summer Dream" begins with the gravity of an opera's finale, with melancholy taking the lead, yet it balances out a solid, worthy album that delivers all the virtues and strengths one would expect from the band. The choruses and those robust string parts the band could latch onto saved it from the electric chair, which they could simply walk right past.

items.body: Faris Ishaq‘s uncle had got hold of some reed cane from Jericho and asked Faris’s older brother to cut holes in it so he could play it. The brother made the flute. Faris, sixteen at the time, picked it up before his uncle got the chance and kept it. He was four years into euphonium lessons at the Edward Said National Conservatory, but the sound of that homemade nay took hold of him completely. Nobody taught him what to do with it. There was nothing to teach, really: no mouthpiece, no keys, nothing mechanical to explain, just cane, breath, and whatever he could find by trial. Then he saw Dhafer Youssef play live and understood how far it could go. The nay is a Middle Eastern flute with 5,000 years behind it, answering to breath and nothing else. That is either a severe limitation or the entire point, and Ishaq has spent twenty years proving it’s the second. For the fifth episode of our Musical Road to WOMEX, we follow Faris Ishaq from that room in Bethlehem to Berklee’s Global Jazz programme, where a full scholarship took him and he was named top student for running Arabic maqam through jazz harmony. He has since released three albums, recorded with Grammy-winning bassist John Patitucci, featured the nay on the BAFTA-nominated Assassin’s Creed Mirage soundtrack, and premiered his own concerto for the instrument, A Wildscape, at Southwark Cathedral. Ishaq also trained as a music therapist, which shapes how he builds a piece from the ground up—meant to hold and heal as much as to perform. His new work takes all of that and strips it back to where he started. JASAD (Arabic for body) was recorded live in his own Bethlehem studio with no band and no overdubs: just the nay and a frame drum strapped to his leg. Coltrane runs through it via Arabic maqam. Palestinian dabke footwork, learned while dancing professionally at school, translates directly onto the drum. Underneath it all is tashbib, the melodic-percussive Arabic woodwind tradition he grew up with. He refuses to call what he does a “revival”, to him, the tradition never went anywhere. On 24 October, he brings all of it to WOMEX in Las Palmas de Gran Canaria, one stop on a tour running from Istanbul in September to the EFG London Jazz Festival in November. Below, he talks about breath, borders, and a living heritage, alongside an exclusive playlist of the tracks that shaped his sound. You play the nay while accompanying yourself on leg-percussion: one body producing melody and rhythm at once. For a first-time listener, how would you describe the sound and the setup? My sound is rooted in Palestinian and the broader Arabic musical tradition, while also drawing from Global Jazz and cross-cultural musical dialogue. I play the Nay flute and a leg-mounted frame drum at the same time. I sometimes describe what I do as similar to what an electronic music producer does, except my only playground is the Nay and the frame drum. I use them to build a live, layered and immersive sound, combining melodies, rhythms and acoustic effects in real time. I describe the frame drum as a natural extension of how I play the Nay, which involves a lot of percussive tonguing and playing with and around the rhythm. I also grew up dancing Palestinian Dabke professionally at school, which involves rhythmic stomping and movement. I translate some of the rhythmic footwork of Dabke onto the leg-mounted frame drum. It’s my own way of connecting movement to music. You were largely self-taught before Berklee, drawn to a reed flute dating back thousands of years. Was there a turning point that told you this instrument, and this path, were yours? The sound of the Nay was the turning point. I am largely self-taught on the Nay, but I started playing the euphonium at the Edward Said National Conservatory of Music in Palestine at the age of 12. When I was 16, my uncle had recently got some reed cane from Jericho and asked my older brother to make some holes in it so he could play. My brother made that flute, and my uncle never saw it again! This is how it started and I became obsessed with its sound. The other turning point was listening to Dhafer Youssef play live. His powerful presence and exploration of the voice touched me on a deep level, and I wanted to explore the Nay in a similar way. Your nay grows out of a shepherd’s music: you’ve revived the Palestinian tashbib. The Canaries have their own pastoral inheritance, including silbo gomero, the whistled language shepherds used to carry messages across the ravines of La Gomera. Is there anything in that shared open-air, herding root you’re curious to seek out while you’re in the islands? I wouldn’t say I revived Palestinian Tashbib. It was always there. The Nay has a long history across many cultures and countries, and similar reed flutes have taken many different forms and roles. I’m not sure the Nay grew only from shepherds’ music. I can definitely imagine that they started from that human desire to resonate with the natural beauty around us, open spaces, rivers and mountains. It’s fascinating how we developed such technologies through sound and our connection to the land. As you mentioned, silbo gomero is a beautiful example of this. In a similar way, Palestinian Tashbib is a melodic-percussive way of playing traditional woodwind instruments that goes by different names in Arab countries. In Palestine, we call it Tashbib, which literally means “to become young,” and it’s full of joy, rhythm and earthiness. Musically, it leaves space for improvisation and percussive interplay with and around the rhythms of traditional Palestinian songs and Dabke dance stomps. Essentially, to me, the rhythmic energy of Tashbib and the Dabke stomps are a way of showing dignity and our connection to the land and its soil. You bring the tashbib and jazz together on the nay. In a WOMEX line-up full of the world’s traditions, what makes yours stand out, and what do you hope people take from your showcase? I was particularly drawn to combining Tashbib and jazz because they both share an improvisational spirit connected with identity, as well as the rhythmic interplay of playing in and around the beat. But my album is not only about bringing Tashbib and jazz together. It’s about creating an immersive experience with the Nay that honours its roots and expansive musical potential, while also offering a grounding and healing space after the madness humanity has experienced in the past years. What stands out musically is that I create a complete world of musical expressions and sounds on the spot, using only the Nay and a leg-mounted frame drum. From that place, I combine Tashbib and Global Jazz influences with rich Arabic maqam modalities, Dabke and other rhythms, together with my original acoustic nay effects that have taken years to develop. All of these elements come together to create a singular musical language. The nay responds only to breath and intention: it’s an intimate instrument. How does playing to an attentive, close-listening delegate and music professional audience shape the way you perform? It will be an honour to share my music with music professionals from around the world. The very first thing the audience hears is how I feel in that moment, rather than a planned musical sentence. I shape my repertoire, improvisations, and textures according to how I feel at the start of the show and throughout the performance. For example, playing in a cathedral is very different from playing in a seated concert hall or to a standing audience. I enjoy resonating with the type of venue, atmosphere, and, most importantly, the audience, who mostly shape the musical journey. Playing for delegates and music professionals is the same. In the end, I want to create an immersive sonic journey that honours the sound of the Nay. You’re also a trained music therapist. Has that shaped how you think about what music is for, beyond the stage? Being trained as a music therapist has set the foundation for how I create music, helping me create work that is both musically and culturally rich, while carrying a sense of healing and grounding. Beyond WOMEX, what lies ahead: the JASAD project, new recordings, the concerto and orchestral directions you’ve been exploring? JASAD is currently set for an international tour, including the London Jazz Festival on November 14th, Melbourne Jazz Festival on October 18th, Arter in Istanbul on September 13th, and many other dates this autumn. Beyond this, I am working to expand my musical concerto A Wildscape, which premiered at Southwark Cathedral two years ago, while also working on a new album for jazz quartet.  https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VT4Tbz0gm3A   On 24 October in Las Palmas, Faris Ishaq carries the memory of a homemade Jericho flute straight to the WOMEX stage, weaving Palestinian tashbib and global jazz into a singular live performance   PLAYLIST: FARIS ISHAQ X RHYTHM PASSPORT   You can find all the previous episodes of Musical Road to Womex HERE   Cover Photo ©: Fadi Dahabreh The post Musical Road to WOMEX 2026 – Faris Ishaq appeared first on Rhythm Passport.

items.body: “Caminando Por La Playa” means walking along the beach, yet Aldo Zolev wrote it about a happy day marching through Bogotá, a city more than 2,600 metres up in the Andes and hundreds of kilometres from the sea. The percussion sets a brisk marching step through the instrumental, with Sandro Londoño on cymbals. Sandra Duque plays the melody on bassoon over Zolev’s double bass. Zolev describes the piece as energetic and lively, built on a memory of Colombian rhythms, and says the walk stands for a way through life, urging his friends to walk “por la vida hoy y siempre“, through life today and always, and to be happy. Zolev comes from Pamplona, a small Andean city in north-eastern Colombia near the Venezuelan border, where his grandfather, a professional double bassist, started him on the instrument. He moved to Bogotá to study double bass at the conservatory of the Universidad Nacional de Colombia and took jazz and harmony lessons with saxophonist Antonio Arnedo. He formed the world-jazz group Dos Aguas and later played in Bereket, an ensemble devoted to Turkish and Middle Eastern music. In 2007 he set up EnnO, the independent Bogotá label and studio that has since produced 25 albums and runs its own world music festival. Three years later he launched UVA Sexteto, bringing the oud in alongside his double bass. He has also recorded with MARIAZÚ, whose album Eau de Vie – Agua Ardiente was cut outdoors in the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta, with birdsong and running water around acoustic instruments and indigenous percussion. In 2025 Zolev relaunched Sensaciones Bajo La Lluvia, the album that carries “Caminando Por La Playa”, and he has just come back from a summer tour of Europe. Listen to “Caminando Por La Playa” and the full Sensaciones Bajo La Lluvia album HERE The post Daily Discovery: Aldo Zolev – Caminando Por La Playa appeared first on Rhythm Passport.

items.body: Belgian electronica pop act 808 Dot Pop has posted four videos since 14 August 2026, each pairing a track from an ongoing “-ism” naming series with a 20th-century building, ahead of two albums, “Minimalism” and “Maximalism,” due at the end of November 2026 via Alfa Matrix. The most recent, “Collectionism,” was posted on the artist’s official website on 17 September 2026. The four videos “Internationalism (Seagram)” was posted around 28 August 2026 and pairs the track with the Seagram Building in New York, an example of the International Style. The track itself is not available on the video’s own release: it appears exclusively on the various-artists compilation “Sounds From The Matrix 26” and will not be issued elsewhere. “Brutalism (Habitat 67)” followed on 6 September 2026, built around Moshe Safdie’s Habitat 67 in Montreal. The visual is as a digital reinterpretation of the building via “The Hillside Project” by NeoScape, rather than footage of the original structure. “Contextualism (Fallingwater)” was posted on 11 September 2026, pairing the track with Frank Lloyd Wright’s Fallingwater house. The version of “Contextualism” heard in this video appears on the “Minimalism” album, while a separate version of the same track, tied to the AT&T Long Lines Building, features on the lead single “Minimalism,” due 26 September 2026. “Collectionism” was posted on 17 September 2026. Unlike the previous three entries in this video 808 Dot Pop gives more info on a few upcoming fan packages. The ‘Minimalism’ and ‘Maximalism’ project 808 Dot Pop announced “Minimalism” (a white-sleeve album) and “Maximalism” (a black-sleeve album) on its website on 14 August 2026, describing them as “two completely different albums in content.” The lead single, “Minimalism,” is scheduled for 26 September 2026. Two further items are tied to the same releases. “Foundationalism,” a six-track EP featuring exclusive versions, is planned as a fan-shop exclusive on an NFC-equipped “phygital” card format. A 72-page fan book titled “Essentialism,” covering the architectural sites referenced across the campaign, was announced on 11 September 2026, with further details promised but not yet published as of this writing. A full tracklist and confirmed formats for “Minimalism” and “Maximalism” have not been published. About 808 Dot Pop 808 Dot Pop is the solo electronica pop project of Belgian musician Passenger S, also known for his work in Metroland. Side-Line reported his debut under the 808 Dot Pop name on 27 March 2020, in “Metroland’s Passenger S launches debut album under 808 DOT POP moniker”, ahead of the album “The Colour Temperature,” released on download and CD on 5 June 2020 on Alfa Matrix. Further singles followed the same year: “Incandescent,” the second single from “The Colour Temperature,” on 19 June 2020; a tribute cover of D.A.F.’s “El Que” for Alfa Matrix’s “Wir Sind DAF” compilation, released 2 October 2020; and “Kelvin (4200),” the third and final single from the debut album, on 13 November 2020, alongside a bundled triple 7-inch vinyl set covered by Side-Line in “Electro pop act 808 Dot Pop releases triple 7 inch vinyl singles in one bundle + 2 new download only singles” (6 November 2020). Side-Line also ran a ‘Click Interview’ with 808 Dot Pop in July 2020. The project continued with the “Ultraviolet” single campaign (February 2021) ahead of the album “The Cubic Temperature,” the “SunCatcher” EP (early March 2022) and a single dedicated to Guglielmo Marconi (January 2023), the latter featuring lyrics by Gary Hunter (Kraftman) and vocals by Lis Van Den Akker. Side-Line covered the act’s return with three simultaneous albums plus two EPs in “Belgian electronica act 808 Dot Pop back with 3 albums in one go + 2 singles” (27 March 2023) and a further double-EP release in “Electronica pop act 808 DOT POP returns with double EP” (5 June 2023). Most recently, fellow Alfa Matrix artist Cubic issued a rework album built on 808 Dot Pop material, covered by Side-Line in “Cubic drops 808 Dot Pop rework album ‘Back To 808’ on Alfa Matrix” (12 December 2025). The four-video architecture series and the wider “Minimalism”/”Maximalism” campaign mark the act’s first new album cycle since 2023.

items.body: Argentine post-punk project Zudpöl releases the single Disciple: In Control on 11 September 2026, through the Buenos Aires label Catálogo Negro / No Me Escucho Records (NMER). The two-track release pairs the title song “Disciple” with the B-side “In Control”, sitting between dark post-punk and the club sound of the late 1980s and early 1990s. Both tracks were built on a vintage drum machine, a mini analog synthesizer, a pocket sampler, guitar and bass, with software used only for the final edit. No Me Escucho Records describes the approach as “simple hardware and no virtual instruments”, the same method Zudpöl has used on its earlier releases. The Bandcamp page embeds the single below. Disciple: In Control by Zudpöl Zudpöl on Catálogo Negro since its 2022 debut “Disciple: In Control” is issued under the Catálogo Negro imprint of No Me Escucho Records, the label that has released Zudpöl’s catalog since 2022. NMER previously put out the free covers compilation “NMER C-01 2024”, on which Zudpöl contributed a version of Death In June’s “Fall Apart”. About Zudpöl Zudpöl is a post-punk, darkwave and coldwave project released through No Me Escucho Records, the independent label founded in Buenos Aires, Argentina by Darío Martinez and Diego Centurión, joined in 2021 by Ferran Pont Vergés. Zudpöl debuted on NMER in 2022 with the album “A Weaker Sun”, followed in June 2023 by the single “In Fear” and, on 24 November 2023, by the six-track album “Last Lights”, which extended the project’s coldwave core with ethereal and dream-pop textures. In January 2025, Zudpöl contributed a cover of Death In June’s “Fall Apart” to NMER’s free “NMER C-01 2024” covers compilation. All of these releases share the same production method: hardware synthesizers, samplers and drum machines, without virtual instruments. “Disciple: In Control” is Zudpöl’s first single since “Last Lights”, continuing that hardware-based approach on Catálogo Negro.

items.body: Midge Ure releases the compilation “Chapters: The Best Of” on 13 November 2026 via Chrysalis Records. The collection gathers his 1980s hits and key album tracks in new 2026 stereo mixes, alongside first-time studio recordings of two songs long associated with his career, and comes in a 2LP vinyl edition, a single CD, a 3CD deluxe edition and a Super Deluxe Edition exclusive Blu-ray audio disc. “Chapters: The Best Of” follows Ure’s recent studio album “A Man Of Two Worlds” and brings together his solo catalogue with material connected to Visage and Thin Lizzy. For the first time, Ure has recorded new studio versions of Visage’s “Fade To Grey” and Phil Lynott’s “Yellow Pearl”, a song he originally co-wrote. Both tracks open the standard 15-track running order on the 2LP black vinyl and single CD, in a six-panel digisleeve. The 3CD deluxe edition expands the set across three discs. CD1 carries 17 tracks in 2026 stereo mixes, including two bonus tracks not on the standard edition, “When The Wind Blows” and “Hell To Heaven”. CD2, subtitled “Connections”, holds 10 newly commissioned remixes from artists and producers who have worked with Ure over his career: Chris Payne remixes “Fade To Grey”, Richard Barbieri reworks “After A Fashion”, Ure himself remixes “The Man Who Sold The World”, Craig Armstrong remodels “That Certain Smile”, Ty Unwin reconstructs “Call Of The Wild”, Blank & Jones rework “If I Was”, Steve Jansen remixes “Sister and Brother”, Danny Mitchell remixes “Wastelands”, “Answers To Nothing” gets a 2026 rework and Wolfgang Flür and Duggal remix “Dear God”. CD3 collects new instrumental versions of all 17 CD1 tracks. The tracklist includes the UK number one single “If I Was” from the album “The Gift”, along with “Dear God”, “No Regrets”, “The Man Who Sold The World”, “Answers To Nothing”, “Living In The Past”, “That Certain Smile”, “Wasteland”, “Call Of The Wild” and “Remembrance Day”. “After A Fashion” is Ure’s 1984 collaboration with Japan bassist Mick Karn, and “Sister & Brother” is his duet with Kate Bush. Super Deluxe Edition, the SDE shop, offers two exclusives alongside the standard formats: a Blu-ray audio disc and a hand-pressed 2LP on splatter vinyl limited to 250 copies, packaged with an OBI strip and certificate. The Blu-ray carries new mixes of 17 tracks in Dolby Atmos, 5.1 and new stereo, plus matching instrumental mixes, along with seven promo videos with an optional Ure commentary track and seven BBC television appearances, including performances on “Top of the Pops” and “Wogan”. The SDE Blu-ray is available to pre-order for two weeks only, with the window closing on 1 October 2026. “Chapters: The Best Of” is catalogued as entry 79 in SDE’s ongoing Surround Series. Ure recorded a new version of “Fade To Grey” for the collection, embedded below. About Midge Ure Midge Ure moved to London from his native Glasgow in 1977 and joined Glenn Matlock’s Rich Kids. The following year, he and Rich Kids drummer Rusty Egan formed Visage with Steve Strange, completed by John McGeoch, Barry Adamson and Dave Formula from Magazine and Ultravox keyboardist Billy Currie. Visage’s second single, “Fade To Grey”, became a UK Top 10 hit. In 1979, Ure joined Thin Lizzy for a US tour following Gary Moore’s departure, and later co-wrote “Yellow Pearl” with Phil Lynott, which became the theme tune to “Top of the Pops”. That same year, Billy Currie invited Ure to join Ultravox, beginning a six-year run that produced the band’s major UK singles and albums. Alongside Ultravox, Ure built a solo career through the 1980s: his album “The Gift” reached number 2 in the UK and included the number 1 single “If I Was”. He recorded “After A Fashion” with Japan bassist Mick Karn and “Sister & Brother” with Kate Bush. Ure is also known as co-writer and co-creator, with Bob Geldof, of Band Aid’s “Do They Know It’s Christmas?” and as a co-founder of Live Aid. “Chapters: The Best Of” follows his studio album “A Man Of Two Worlds” and gathers the hits, key album tracks and career-spanning collaborations from that period into new 2026 mixes, with “Fade To Grey” and “Yellow Pearl” recorded fresh for the release for the first time.

items.body: French industrial project HORSKH has released “Connected“, a collaboration with Carpenter Brut, on September 10, 2026, ahead of HORSKH’s forthcoming album “MTNT”. HORSKH’s official Bandcamp credits the track jointly to HORSKH and Carpenter Brut, with mixing and mastering by Thibault Chaumont at Deviant Lab Studio and artwork by Johanna Jaskowska. Connected by HORSKH “Connected” also appears on HORSKH’s forthcoming album “MTNT”, listed as a ten-track release scheduled for September 25, 2026, issued through Wire Control under exclusive licence to Blood Blast Distribution. “Connected” and the earlier single “Glow” are both tied directly to “MTNT”. The lyrics give the collaboration a considerably less comfortable meaning than its title suggests. Images of wires, intravenous connection, fear, chemical illusion and an attachment that persists despite attempts to escape recur throughout the song, placing bodily, technological and psychological attachment close together rather than treating “connection” as straightforward communication. The pairing brings together two French projects that approach heavy electronic music from different but intersecting angles. HORSKH’s recent catalogue has increasingly combined guitars, electronic programming and industrial pressure: “BODY” arrived in January 2024, following “WIRE” in 2021 and “GATE” in 2017. Carpenter Brut, meanwhile, released his latest studio album “Leather Temple” on February 27, 2026. The two releases share a technical link as well: “Leather Temple” was mixed and mastered by Thibault Chaumont at Deviant Lab, the same studio and engineer credited on “Connected”. “MTNT” arrives on September 25, 2026. “Connected” is available now through HORSKH’s official Bandcamp and streaming platforms. About HORSKH HORSKH are based in Besançon, France. Their recorded catalogue dates back to the “DAWN” EP, released in October 2014 and followed by an expanded edition in 2015. Their first full-length album, “GATE”, arrived on April 10, 2017, followed by “WIRE” on January 22, 2021 and “BODY” on January 19, 2024. The credits for “GATE” and “WIRE” list Bastien on programming, keyboards, vocals and guitar, Briou on live drums, and Jordan on guitar and keyboards. “WIRE” was mixed by Sam Munnier and Bastien Hennaut and mastered at Deviant Lab Studio, while “BODY” was mixed and mastered by Thibault Chaumont at Deviant Lab Studio. Ahead of “MTNT”, HORSKH released three other singles during 2026: “BAD GLITCH” on January 22, “Hyperhuman” in March and “Glow” in June. “Connected”, featuring Carpenter Brut, followed on September 10. The band have also been active on the European festival circuit in 2026, with appearances listed at Wave-Gotik-Treffen in Leipzig, Castle Party in Bolków and Nocturnal Culture Night in Deutzen, alongside a series of French dates extending into November. The catalogue combines programmed electronics, guitars and live percussion across industrial, EBM and electro-adjacent territory, reflecting the band’s own album credits. About Carpenter Brut Carpenter Brut is the stage name of Franck Hueso, a French darksynth musician from Poitiers active since 2012. He released three EPs, “EP I” (2012), “EP II” (2013) and “EP III” (2015), later compiled as the album “Trilogy” (2015), followed by “Leather Teeth” (2018), the “Blood Machines” soundtrack (2020), “Leather Terror” (2022) and “Leather Temple” (2026). His releases since 2015 have come out through his own label, No Quarter Prod. In live performances, Carpenter Brut is joined by guitarist Adrien Grousset and drummer Florent Marcadet, both also members of the French metal band Hacride.

items.body: New York darkwave duo Ghostbells released “The Silence” on September 17, 2026 through Out Of Line Music, as a digital single with an accompanying music video. It is the second piece of original material Jessica Perry and Jim Finley have put out since their debut EP “Catacouture” arrived in February, following “Curses” in August. The Silence by ghostbells The track returns to the confessional side of the duo’s sound: 80s and new wave melody laid over a 90s EBM pulse, pushed forward by the kind of driving, dancefloor-ready arrangement that keeps its darker moments moving rather than static. The lyric follows someone consumed by sadness and reaching for a version of life that used to feel joyful, with a plea that goes nowhere: Can someone save me / I hear nothing / it’s the silence that takes me. Ghostbells described the writing behind the song directly. “The Silence is about being consumed by sadness and longing for times before, when there used to be a joy for life. There is a cry for help but it seems useless when it goes unanswered.” Jessica Perry named the source more specifically: “Struggles that I have personally endured and some of the lowest times in life.” Ghostbells follow Dark Summer Open Air with ‘The Silence’ “The Silence” lands right after one of the duo’s largest shows to date. On September 12, Ghostbells played Dark Summer Open Air Vol. 2 at Wasserschloss Klaffenbach in Chemnitz, Germany, alongside Blutengel and Chrom, in front of roughly 3,000 people. In just over a year since signing to Out Of Line, the pair have built a run of remix work alongside their own releases, reworking Blutengel’s “Schwarzer Engel”, Cemetery Skyline’s “Torn Away” and Blitz Union’s “Evolution”. The single carries that momentum into a run of US club dates and a full Latin American tour supporting label-mates Hocico, followed by European festival dates into next year. Tour dates for Ghostbells in 2026 and 2027 September 19, 2026 – Los Angeles, CA, USA – Bar Sinister September 23 – October 4, 2026 – Hocico “Unseen Horror Scenes” tour support October 29, 2026 – Fort Worth, TX, USA – Haltom Theatre October 30, 2026 – Houston, TX, USA – Scout Bar November 13, 2026 – Tampa, FL, USA – New World Tampa November 14, 2026 – Miami, FL, USA – Las Rosas November 20-21, 2026 – Wangels, Germany – Plage Noire Festival November 28, 2026 – Essen, Germany – Obsidian Echoes Festival July 24-25, 2027 – Cologne, Germany – Amphi Festival About Ghostbells Ghostbells are a duo from New York City: Jessica Perry on vocals, guitar, bass and synth, and Jim Finley on production, vocals, bass, guitar and synth. The project signed to Berlin label Out Of Line Music in 2025 and released its first single, “Darkness Saves“, that August. Three digital EPs followed before year’s end, and the duo’s debut EP proper, “Catacouture”, arrived on Out Of Line on February 5, 2026, collecting six tracks including “Darkness Saves”, “Ghosts”, “Wrath” and “Cry4Her” and giving the band its first CD pressing. Since then, Ghostbells have kept up a steady release and touring pace: a run of remixes for Blutengel, Cemetery Skyline and Blitz Union, the “Curses” single and video in August, and festival and club dates across the UK, Europe and the US. “The Silence” is their second original track since “Catacouture”, released as the band works toward its debut full-length album, and it opens a touring stretch that runs from Los Angeles through Latin America to the Amphi Festival in Germany next summer.

Ray Noir’s “Gothstar” EP is out digitally and on vinyl and CD. The EP collects the four singles issued since April 2026 and adds two new recordings. items.body: London-based queer alt-metal artist Ray Noir released “Gothstar” on September 17th 2026, a six-track EP that mixes metalcore guitars with rave and electronic club production. Ray Noir’s “Gothstar” EP is out digitally and on vinyl and CD. The EP collects the four singles issued since April 2026 and adds two new recordings. It opens with “Label Whxre” and continues with “Black”, “Boys”, and “Gothstar” featuring Danny Blu, the New York artist and former Echo Black frontman. The new track “Crush” follows, and “Gothstar (Alternative Version)”, a solo version of the title track, closes the record. Ray Noir wrote the material with Jon Cass and Tom Saint, who are also the EP’s producers. The track credits for “Black” and “Crush” list Cass as producer and Saint for additional production, mixing and mastering, with Saint also singing backing vocals on “Crush”. Cass, a member of UK post-hardcore band As Everything Unfolds, previously produced Ray Noir’s 2025 EP “Against The Machine”. The release material describes the EP as dealing with identity, confidence and sexuality, with “Gothstar” as both a character and an attitude at its centre. Ray Noir commented: “Growing up in the Norwegian metal scene, I didn’t really see anyone like me. With Gothstar, I wanted to create the world I wish I’d had back then. It’s gay, it’s heavy, it’s sweaty, it’s camp and it doesn’t take itself too seriously. Basically, if Berghain had a mosh pit, I’d like to think this would be playing.” “Crush” is the focus track of the EP. Ray Noir based it on his own experience of growing up in Norway’s metal scene and on “Heated Rivalry”, Rachel Reid’s gay ice hockey romance novel, which was adapted for television in 2025. The lyrics name the story’s lead couple, Ilya and Shane, and include lines in Norwegian. Four singles ahead of the EP “Label Whxre” opened the “Gothstar” campaign on 2 April 2026. “Black” followed on 14 May 2026 with a video directed by Ray Noir, and “Boys” arrived in June 2026 with a video filmed at Slim Jim’s Liquor Store in Islington, north London. The title track “Gothstar” featuring Danny Blu came out on 13 August 2026 together with an official music video. ‘Gothstar'”‘ release party in London Ray Noir marks the release with a party at Slim Jim’s Liquor Store on Saturday 19 September 2026, the venue where the “Boys” video was filmed. Tom Saint is listed as special guest. Entry is free, with tickets via Ray Noir – Gothstar EP Release Party on DICE. Get the EP as vinyl or CD here! About Ray Noir Ray Noir is a queer alternative artist based in London. His official biography places his background in Oslo’s black-metal underground, and his sound combines metal guitars with electronic club production. He released his first single, “Double Trouble”, in 2014. In October 2023 he issued “Pity Party“, the lead single from the mixtape “Scorpio”, followed on 1 November 2023 by “Latency“. The seven-track “Scorpio” arrived in 2024, and his official biography lists a top-five placement in the German Alternative Charts. A deluxe edition of “Scorpio” followed in July 2024, adding “All Alone” featuring Mariann Rosa of Surferosa, a “Double Trouble” remix by TOVA, remixes by Gothminister, Corlyx and Tension Control, and “You, Me & The Devil” featuring Tom Saint. That August he supported Combichrist at the Underworld in London and played the Electro Night in Oslo at Revolver with Piston Damp on 31 August 2024. On 14 February 2025 he released “Razorblade Romance“, written with Steve Stevens and Madeleine Wood, featuring Stevens on guitar and produced and mixed by Jon Cass. A cover of Tears for Fears’ “Shout” followed in May 2025, with guitar by Arno Von Detritus and backing vocals by Ben Christo of The Sisters of Mercy. “Dead Valentine” came out on 3 July 2025 and announced the EP “Against The Machine”, released on 18 September 2025 with “Razorblade Romance”, “Dead Valentine”, “Mad World” and an alternative version of “YMATD”. A deluxe edition followed in December 2025 with remixes by Tension Control, Verona On Venus, Junkie Kut and Ays Kura, alongside vinyl and CD editions. Ray Noir opened 2026 with the singles “Temptation” in January and “Breathe” in February. “Gothstar” is his second EP after “Against The Machine” and continues his work with Jon Cass, who produced both EPs, and Tom Saint, who also featured on the 2024 “Scorpio” deluxe edition.

items.body: Boston publisher SIGNALS Press launched a Kickstarter campaign on 10 September 2026 for “Industrial Music/Graphics: A Visual History of a Movement“, a 320-page survey of the graphic design that grew up alongside industrial music. The campaign runs through 2 October 2026, with books shipping spring 2027. The book traces the movement’s visual language from post-punk Britain and Cold War Europe through Reagan-era America, across album covers, logos, posters, type studies and ephemera. It documents the graphic identities of bands and labels including Throbbing Gristle and Industrial Records, Cabaret Voltaire, Mute Records, Nettwerk, wax trax!, Einstürzende Neubauten, Skinny Puppy, Front 242, Ministry, KMFDM and Nine Inch Nails. Designers contributing directly to the book include Neville Brody, Rob Sheridan, Richard Borge, Rick Valicenti, Patrick Codenys, Steven R. Gilmore, Simon Granger, Simone Grant, Brian Shanley and Martin Atkins. The Kickstarter’s reward tiers include a pin designed by Simon Granger of Nitzer Ebb Produkt and two shirts by Steven R. Gilmore. “Industrial music didn’t just change how music sounded, it changed how music looked,” said coauthor Chris Grimley. “Designers were sampling medical imagery, military documents, brutalist architecture, and early computer graphics into something coherent and international, and that history has never been collected. It sits in aftermarket bins and collectors’ stacks. This book brings it together.” The book is authored by GR—APP, the shared pseudonym of Chris Grimley and Alan Rapp. Grimley is founder and creative director of SIGNALS Press and has authored, coauthored and designed numerous books; Rapp is editorial director of SIGNALS Press and a former college DJ and music critic. “Industrial Music/Graphics” is produced as a physical object in its own right: 8 x 10.25 inches, 320 pages, Otabind layflat binding, four-color interior and a six-color foil-stamped, offset-printed cover. The Kickstarter campaign carries a Kickstarter “Project We Love” designation. About SIGNALS Press SIGNALS Press is a Boston-based publisher founded and led by Chris Grimley, who has authored, coauthored and designed multiple books and began making music after covering Skinny Puppy in high school. Alan Rapp, the press’s editorial director, is a former college DJ and music critic. Together the pair write as GR—APP, a pseudonym paying homage to the artistic aliases adopted by figures within the industrial scene the book documents. “Industrial Music/Graphics: A Visual History of a Movement” is SIGNALS Press’s Kickstarter campaign running through 2 October 2026, with fulfillment planned for spring 2027.

items.body: Infacted Recordings launches the Zoth Ommog Classix series, a vinyl-only reissue line reviving catalog from the German EBM and electro-industrial label Zoth Ommog. The first release is a limited grey-vinyl pressing of Lights Of Euphoria’s 1995 debut album “Brainstorm“, out 16 October 2026, followed on 23 October by Menschdefekt’s fifth studio album “Into the Void” on CD. Zoth Ommog was founded by Talla 2XLC after he left Techno Drome International. Its first release was Italian electro act Pankow’s “Kunst & Wahnsinn” EP. Talla continued T.D.I.’s early program with artists including Bigod 20, Aircrash Bureau, Leæther Strip, X Marks the Pedwalk and Armageddon Dildos. Torben Schmidt, founder of Infacted Recordings, worked as Zoth Ommog’s label manager from 1995 to 1998. He and Talla launched the Zoth Ommog Classix series together. “Brainstorm” track listing: This Is the Point, Brainstorm, Give Me You, Reaching Out, Energy & Consciousness, Misery, Sacred, Ice Machine (vox version), Serenade (splitter), Subjection (violated), No Tears, Face of a God, Dead Bodies. Menschdefekt’s “Into the Void” arrives 23 October on CD (catalog FACT3483, EAN 4018939613945) in a clear tray jewel box, its first full-length album with vocalist Alex Erbacher. The 14-track, roughly 70-minute record moves between synth pop, dark electro and future pop, and includes two tracks reaching CD for the first time: a cover of Bronski Beat’s “Smalltown Boy” and “Day by Day”, a collaboration with Mark Sousa of Voicecoil, who died earlier in 2026. “Into the Void” will also be released digitally via Bandcamp and on streaming platforms. “Into the Void” track listing: Into the Void, Inside the Machine, Black as Black Can Be, Fragile Existence Part I, Losing Fire, The Book of Life, Reality, This World, Scream in Silence, Smalltown Boy, Oblivion, God, Embrace Your Fate, plus bonus track Day by Day (Album Version feat. Mark Sousa). The Zoth Ommog Classix series also keeps in print earlier Lights Of Euphoria releases “Future Unknown” and “True Life” on vinyl, the “Suicidal” MCD and “Traumatized” CD, plus Menschdefekt‘s “Recombination” CD. About Lights Of Euphoria and Menschdefekt Lights Of Euphoria is a German EBM act that released “Brainstorm” on Zoth Ommog in 1995, one of the label’s catalog titles from its run as a driving force in European electronic music through the 1990s. The album’s Zoth Ommog Classix reissue marks its first-ever appearance on vinyl, 31 years after its original CD release. Menschdefekt build a sound bridging synth pop, dark electro and future pop, marked by clean vocals, trance-inspired synthesizer structures and the band’s spoken-word samples. “Into the Void” is the group’s fifth studio album and its first to feature vocalist Alex Erbacher, presenting a more melodic and accessible side of the band while staying rooted in its electronic origins.

items.body: UK synthpop and dark disco project KN/GHTS released the single “Light The Fuse” on 17 September 2026 via Specchio Uomo. The B-side carries a remix of “Supernatural Lover”, from KN/GHTS’s second studio album of the same name, by Berlin-based artist Daniel Knutz. Light The Fuse by KN/GHTS Specchio Uomo describes “Light The Fuse” as a pulsating and emotionally charged song about loss, recovery and finding yourself again. The track mixes synth pop, dark disco and italo disco elements with classic synth sounds. Daniel Knutz, whose own work draws on darkwave, coldwave, post-punk and minimal electronic, reworks “Supernatural Lover” as the release’s second track. An official video for “Light The Fuse” is out now, directed and edited by independent filmmaker Dirk Roche. It was filmed during the “Supernatural Lover Tour”, with additional footage from KN/GHTS’s live performances in Germany. About KN/GHTS KN/GHTS is the solo project of UK vocalist and songwriter James Knights, previously a singer of electronic pioneers Boytronic and known from his time in Scarlet Soho. Knights launched the project under the name Knight$, releasing the EPs “What’s Your Poison?” (2016) and “Alligator” (2017) before his debut album “Dollar$ & Cent$” came out on Cargo Records in 2019. Side-Line spoke to him about that album in a 2019 interview, in which he described the project as a faster-moving continuation of the sound he built with Scarlet Soho and Boytronic. The project later restyled its name as KN/GHTS and released its second studio album, “Supernatural Lover”, building an audience particularly in Germany, Sweden and Mexico. KN/GHTS combines synth pop, dark disco, electronic music and theatrical performance, and has performed live alongside Drab Majesty and Andy Bell of Erasure. “Light The Fuse”, released via Specchio Uomo, continues the project’s work following the “Supernatural Lover” album and tour.

items.body: Charlotte, North Carolina synthpop project Midniter, the solo vehicle of Nic Pugh, released the single and video “I Could Love You” on September 15, 2026, via Bandcamp and YouTube. It is the fourth and final promotional single ahead of Midniter’s debut album, “Xeno”, due October 27 on SugarTank! Records, the Charlotte label Pugh co-founded. The release coincides with the opening of vinyl LP pre-orders for “Xeno” through the label’s own store. Midniter describes “I Could Love You” as a ballad about unrequited love Pugh traced the song back to an unfinished piano piece: “‘I Could Love You’ came from an old piano tune that I never finished. The bookends of the song are directly from that idea, with the middle evolving into a more synthpop direction for Midniter. To me, it’s a pretty standard ballad about unrequited love – a tale as old as time that everyone can understand.” I Could Love You by Midniter The video for “I Could Love You” favors mood over narrative Pugh said the video leaves its meaning open: “The video is more ambiguous, playing with the question, ‘Is this about desire, obsession, or both?’ It’s ultimately your call to make. Our goal with this video was to focus more on mood than narrative. It was more important to live in these feelings of distance and longing than explain why they linger. The dancers, our friends from Baran Dance, were instrumental in carrying those moods throughout the video with their choreography. Our main actress Dustie Bayer was also incredible in her debut.” Paul Jahn of Yawn Productions filmed and edited the video, co-directing it with Pugh. Choreography comes from Baran Dance members Audrey Baran, Faith Centa and Donovan Granville, with Dustie Bayer in the lead acting role. For the silhouette performance scenes, Midniter expands to a trio with Joe Boyland and Dan Hitzelberger joining Pugh. Filming took place at Petra’s, the Charlotte venue where Pugh works and where Midniter’s 2025 debut single video, “Shoot the Moon”, was also shot, alongside a University of North Carolina dance studio and locations around Charlotte. About Midniter Midniter is the solo indie-electronic project of Charlotte, North Carolina musician Nic Pugh, launched in 2024 after roughly two decades in punk and rock’n’roll bands, including Paint Fumes and Jaggermouth. As Midniter, Pugh mixes synthpop songwriting with indie-electronic production, citing Radiohead, Justice, The Knife, LCD Soundsystem, Aphex Twin, Squarepusher and M83 as reference points alongside an “Indie Sleaze” visual style. Pugh co-founded Charlotte label SugarTank! Records with fellow musician Nic Holman; the label supports LGBTQ+ artists and allies. Midniter’s debut single, “Shoot the Moon”, arrived with a video shot at Petra’s in 2025, and Side-Line covered the project’s “Alarmist” video single that October. “I Could Love You” is the fourth and last of the promotional singles released ahead of Midniter’s debut album, “Xeno”, due October 27 on SugarTank! Records, with vinyl LP pre-orders now open through the label.

items.body: XTC co-founder Colin Moulding releases his new three-track EP, “Want It Bad (The Pep Talks and Playing Fields of Old England)”, on CD via Burning Shed on September 18. The release lands 47 years to the week after XTC’s “Making Plans for Nigel,” the Moulding-written single that gave the band its first UK Top 20 hit in 1979. Presented in a four-panel digisleeve and available exclusively through Burning Shed, “Want It Bad” is a physical-only release; digital files are provided to press for review and airplay purposes only. The EP carries catalogue number CMCD002. The title track is joined by “Something About The Boy (James Bond Demo for Female Voice)” and a stripped-down “Want It Bad (Demo).” “Making Plans for Nigel,” written and sung by Moulding, was released in 1979 as the lead single from XTC’s third album, “Drums and Wires.” It became XTC’s first UK Top 20 hit and remains one of the band’s best-known recordings. The title track began, in Moulding’s words, as something closer to a sports talk than a song. “Although this song started life as a sporting pep talk, it was clear that it could easily be thought of as a mantra for one’s own life ambitions, whatever they may be. If you want something in this life you have to really want it. And if you really want it, you’ll get it — that was my mantra,” he says. The cover artwork, by Andrew Swainson, and the accompanying video, directed by Thomas Walsh, both draw on “Les Coureurs” by French painter Robert Delaunay. Moulding explains how the image came about: “I was scouting around for a cover that would signify human endeavour. I had written ‘Want It Bad’, which basically amounted to a pep talk by a sporting coach to his team. Football perhaps… something made me think of the runners on the beach in the film Chariots of Fire. After many permutations, Andrew, my artwork designer, said ‘What about Delaunay and his runners?’ and when he showed me, there was no doubt.” The second track, “Something About The Boy (James Bond Demo for Female Voice),” traces back to a long-held ambition to write a Bond theme. “I was a big James Bond fan. My father had taken me to see the first three – ‘Dr No’, ‘From Russia with Love’, and ‘Goldfinger’… in the 1960s. I had secretly nursed an ambition that one day John Barry and I would work on a theme together,” Moulding says. “So here then was my idea to put to John Barry. Only trouble was I had to sing it myself to demonstrate the female lead.” The closing “Want It Bad (Demo)” documents the song’s earliest stage. “Quite simply, it’s my working demo knocked out in about an hour with a hand-held 57 microphone, different lyrics, and no bass. This is something for the musos, I guess,” he notes. The EP was written and produced by Moulding, mixed by Stuart Rowe, and mastered by Jason Mitchell at Loud Mastering. Cover artwork is by Andrew Swainson, the video by Thomas Walsh, and press photos by Geoff Winn. “Want It Bad” is Moulding’s second solo EP, following 2021’s “The Hardest Battle,” both released via Burning Shed, where his catalogue with XTC and TC&I is also available. About Colin Moulding Colin Ivor Moulding was born on 17 August 1955 in Swindon, England. He took up bass guitar as a teenager after hearing Free’s “All Right Now,” and in 1972 began jamming with local musician Andy Partridge. Their band went through several names, including Star Park and the Helium Kidz, before settling on XTC in 1975, with Terry Chambers on drums. Moulding wrote several of XTC’s earliest hits: “Life Begins at the Hop” (1979) became the band’s first chart entry, “Making Plans for Nigel” (1979), from the album “Drums and Wires,” gave XTC its first UK Top 20 placing, and “Generals and Majors” (1980), from “Black Sea,” became their first US chart single. In 1980 he also released a solo single, “Too Many Cooks in the Kitchen,” under the pseudonym “The Colonel.” In 1984, Moulding co-founded the Dukes of Stratosphear, XTC’s psychedelic alter ego project, whose recordings anticipated the 1980s Paisley Underground revival. XTC released 14 studio albums before disbanding in 2006, with Moulding contributing songs and bass throughout, including “Wonderland” from “Mummer” (1983), “Grass” and “Dying” from “Skylarking” (1986), and “King for a Day” from “Oranges and Lemons” (1989). Outside XTC, he contributed bass and vocals to recordings by artists including Sam Phillips, Anton Barbeau and Days Between Stations, and appeared on Billy Sherwood-produced tribute projects covering Pink Floyd and Supertramp. In 2017, Moulding reunited with original XTC drummer Terry Chambers as TC&I, releasing the “Great Aspirations” EP. The pair, joined by a full band including Moulding’s son Lee, played a series of shows at the Swindon Arts Centre in 2018, drawing on Moulding’s XTC-era songs; highlights were released in 2019 as “Naked Flames: Live at Swindon Arts Centre.” Moulding released his solo debut EP, “The Hardest Battle,” in 2021. “Want It Bad” is his second solo EP, arriving as XTC’s “Making Plans for Nigel” marks its 47th anniversary.
